lessons.text: Databricks runs Apache Spark, which splits work across many machines. You work with DataFrames: tables with named, typed columns, spread over the cluster. Examples use PySpark 4.0, as in Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS. A notebook gives you a ready spark session. from pyspark.sql import functions as F df = spark.table("research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents") spark.createDataFrame(rows, "region STRING, w DOUBLE") builds a small DataFrame from Python tuples, which is handy in tests. Transformations describe a new DataFrame and run nothing yet: select("region", "w") keeps columns. filter(F.col("w") > 0) keeps rows. A boolean column filters directly: filter(F.col("in_scope")). withColumn("w2", F.col("w") * 2) adds or replaces a column. F.lit(1) is a constant, and F.when(cond, a).otherwise(b) picks a value per row. groupBy("region").agg(F.sum("w").alias("total"), F.count("*").alias("n")) summarises per group. join(other, "region_code", "left") and orderBy("region") join and sort. Actions run the plan and return a result: show() prints rows, count() counts them, collect() returns a list of Row objects to Python, and write saves a table. Spark is lazy: nothing happens until an action, so a typo in a column name may only fail at the action. DataFrames are immutable. Every transformation returns a new DataFrame and leaves the old one unchanged, so always use the result: df = df.withColumn(...) or return df.withColumn(...). Import the functions module as F. Importing sum or max from it by name hides Python's own sum and max. Collect only small results: collect() pulls every row onto one machine. A junior engineer wrote df.withColumn("wave", F.lit("W14")) on its own line and saved df. The wave column never existed, because the result was thrown away. Every later job that grouped by wave failed, and a morning was spent looking at the wrong notebook. Assigning the result, df = df.withColumn(...), is the whole fix. Chain transformations and use their results, let Spark aggregate, and run an action only when you need the answer.

lessons.text: Databricks pipelines mix PySpark with Spark SQL. The examples use Spark 4.0 SQL. Run SQL from Python with spark.sql("SELECT ..."), which returns a DataFrame. Read and filter. SELECT region, final_weight FROM respondents WHERE final_weight > 0 picks columns and keeps rows. Summarise. GROUP BY region makes one row per region. Aggregates work per group: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(final_weight) counts non-NULL values, and SUM and AVG skip NULLs. HAVING SUM(final_weight) > 100 filters groups after they are summarised, where WHERE filters rows before. Join. JOIN regions g ON r.region_code = g.region_code keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL when there is no match. LEFT ANTI JOIN keeps the left rows that have no match, which finds orphan keys in one line. NULL means unknown. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, never true, so WHERE final_weight = NULL matches nothing. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. Pick one row per key. A delivery can repeat a respondent. A window function numbers the rows within each key, newest first, and you keep number 1: SELECT respondent_id, wave_id, final_weight FROM ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY respondent_id, wave_id ORDER BY delivery_version DESC) AS rn FROM bronze_deliveries ) WHERE rn = 1 PARTITION BY sets the groups, ORDER BY ... DESC puts the newest first, and ROW_NUMBER() gives exactly one row the number 1 in each group. DISTINCT would keep both versions, because their values differ. Lessons A3 and A4 add MERGE, GRANT and row filters on top of these. A data-quality check counted missing weights with WHERE final_weight = NULL. It reported zero every night for two months while 1,800 weights were missing, because a comparison with NULL is never true. IS NULL found them on the first run, and the check now catches the problem it was written for. Filter rows with WHERE and groups with HAVING, test NULL with IS NULL, and keep one row per key with ROW_NUMBER, not DISTINCT.

lessons.text: Track A uses a handful of Databricks words on every page. This lesson places each one. Workspace, notebooks, compute, jobs. You work in a workspace, writing code in notebooks. Code runs on compute: serverless compute that Databricks manages for you, or a cluster you configure. Databricks Free Edition offers serverless compute only. A job runs notebooks on a schedule, with parameters (lesson A10-L2). Unity Catalog organises data and permissions with three-level names, catalog.schema.table: a catalog per environment, such as research_dev and research_prod, a schema per layer, such as research_silver, a table, such as nat_respondents. Volumes hold files, such as raw delivery CSVs, under the same names and permissions. Grants go to groups, never to individual users (lesson A4-L2). Delta tables. A table created USING DELTA, the Databricks default, is a folder of Parquet data files plus a transaction log, _delta_log. Each write adds one numbered JSON commit to the log, so the table has versions 0, 1, 2 and so on. DESCRIBE HISTORY t lists them, and SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 1 reads an older one (lesson A3-L3). Readers never see a half-finished write. Medallion layers give each table one job: Bronze keeps every delivery as received, plus audit columns: nat_raw. Silver has clean names and types and one row per respondent per wave: nat_respondents. Gold holds business-ready aggregates with a stated grain: nat_metrics. Data moves forward only. A fix in silver logic means rebuilding silver from bronze, never editing bronze. Module A2 sets the contract for each layer. Two analysts both wrote to a table called respondents, one in the development catalog and one in production, because their notebooks used two-part names and different default catalogs. Production silver received a week of test rows before anyone noticed. Three-level names, with the catalog stated explicitly or set from a job parameter, make the target impossible to mistake. Name every table in full, keep files in volumes, let Delta keep versions, and move data forward from bronze to silver to gold.

lessons.text: A function should do one of five jobs: read, transform, validate, write or log. A sixth kind, the orchestrator, calls the others in order and does nothing else. Single-purpose functions pay off in three ways: Tests. A transform that takes a DataFrame and returns a DataFrame runs on a local SparkSession with three rows. A function that reads a table, transforms it and writes it needs a live catalog. Reuse. filter_in_scope() serves gold, QA and ad hoc analysis. A 200-line process() serves one notebook. Change. When the supplier renames a column, you edit one transform. Nothing else moves. A useful test: describe the function in one sentence without "and". "Aggregate reach by wave and subgroup" passes. "Read silver and compute reach and write gold" fails three times. Names carry the contract. Follow the standard from your reference project: Object Convention Example Function verb_noun, snake_case check_table_health Class PascalCase noun CheckResult Constant UPPER_SNAKE_CASE MAX_WEIGHT_CV Bronze table [tracker]_raw nat_raw Silver table [tracker]_respondents nat_respondents Gold table [tracker]_metrics nat_metrics Job [tracker]_[layer]_pipeline nat_silver_pipeline A name must match what the function does. get_ and check_ promise no side effects. A get_unprocessed_waves() that also deletes rows breaks that promise, and the next reader calls it without knowing. A gold notebook holds one 350-line cell: read silver, filter, weight, aggregate, write, log. A change request asks for a new subgroup. The developer edits the aggregation, and a variable named df later in the cell now points at the new frame. The write step saves the unfiltered data. Gold publishes reach figures that include out-of-scope respondents for two waves. Nobody could test the cell without writing to production tables, so nobody tested it. With filter_in_scope() and aggregate_reach() as separate functions, a three-row unit test catches the mistake before the merge. Each strong function passes the one-sentence test. The weak one needs "and" four times.
lessons.title: Single-purpose functions and clear names

lessons.text: A type hint states a contract. keys: list[str] tells the caller, the reviewer and mypy that keys is a list of column names. A bare list says "some list". No hint says nothing. Use the modern forms, valid from Python 3.10: Built-in generics: list[str], dict[str, int], tuple[str, ...]. Optional values: str None = None. Never str = None, which claims the value is always a string. Fixed sets of strings: Literal["PASS", "WARN", "FAIL"] from typing. mypy then rejects "pass" or "FAILED". A return type on every function, including -> None. Run mypy --strict in CI. Strict mode refuses functions without hints, so gaps cannot creep back. A docstring explains what hints cannot: meaning, units, grain and failure modes. Use the Google style: def weighted_share(df: DataFrame, flag_col: str) -> float None: """Weighted share of rows where flag_col is 1. Args: df: Respondents with final_weight. flag_col: 0/1 column to share. Returns: Share between 0 and 1, or None when the total weight is 0. Raises: ValueError: If flag_col is missing from df. """ The first line fits on one line and says what the function returns or does. Args, Returns and Raises follow. A reviewer reads the docstring, then checks the body against it. A mismatch between the two is a bug in one of them. PySpark is not fully typed, and mypy cannot see column names. Hints still catch the most common mistake: passing the wrong kind of object. The reference upsert_silver takes merge_keys: list. A caller passes the string "respondent_id" instead of ["respondent_id"]. Python iterates a string character by character, so the join builds t.r = s.r AND t.e = s.e AND .... The MERGE fails with a column-not-found error at 02:00, and the on-call engineer spends an hour reading the wrong part of the stack trace. With merge_keys: list[str], mypy flags the call in CI: a str is not a list[str]. The bug never reaches the scheduler. The strong version tells mypy, the reviewer and the caller the same story. The weak version tells three different ones.
lessons.title: Type hints and docstrings a reviewer can trust

lessons.text: Pipeline code should contain logic. Everything that changes between environments, trackers or contract versions belongs in configuration: catalog, schema and table names column maps and type maps thresholds, such as weight_sum_min or a stability tolerance contract rules and their severity Keep configuration in one of two places. Versioned JSON or YAML files in the repository suit values that change with a code release. Registry tables in Unity Catalog suit values that analysts maintain, such as the Variable Registry column map. Load configuration once, at the start of the run, into a typed object. A frozen dataclass or a pydantic model works. Validate on load: every required key present, weight_sum_min below weight_sum_max, names non-empty. Fail at 00:01 with "missing key: silver_table", not at 02:47 with a KeyError deep in a transform. Then pass the object, or the values from it, into your functions. A function that reads a global config dictionary is as hard to test as one with hardcoded strings. Style is part of the same discipline. PEP 8 is the Python style guide. ruff checks it and formats code in one fast tool: ruff check . finds errors and style problems, such as undefined names (F821) or == True (E712). ruff format . rewrites layout consistently. ruff format --check . fails CI when a file needs formatting. Settle the rules once in pyproject.toml under [tool.ruff], run both commands in CI, and stop debating layout in reviews. A developer copies the production silver notebook to test a change in the dev workspace. The notebook hardcodes research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents. The dev run MERGEs half-finished test data into the production table. The morning report shows impossible reach figures, and the team restores the table from Delta history. With the catalog in a config file per environment, the dev run writes to research_dev. The same code runs in both places, and only the config changes. The strong version runs unchanged in dev and prod. The contract file decides the table and the limits.
lessons.title: Config over hardcoded values, and PEP 8 with ruff

lessons.text: Bronze is your evidence. Its contract has four rules. Append only. Every delivery adds rows. Nothing in bronze is updated, deleted or overwritten. A redelivery of wave W14 appends again, with a new ingestion_id. As received. No cleaning, filtering, renaming or type casting. Read CSV columns as strings. inferSchema guesses types, and a guess can destroy data: the ID 00123 becomes the integer 123, and the leading zeros are gone for good. Audit columns. Add four columns to every row: ingestion_id (one UUID per load), source_file, ingestion_timestamp and delivery_version. Later layers use them to pick the newest version and to trace any number back to a file. Grain. One row per respondent per wave per delivery file. Duplicates across deliveries are expected here. Silver resolves them. Why keep the mess? Because silver logic changes. When you fix a mapping bug in March, you rebuild silver from bronze for every wave since January. You can only do that if bronze still holds the original deliveries. Two practical points for Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS: Count what you wrote from the Delta history instead of calling count() before the write. DeltaTable.forName(spark, table).history(1) returns operationMetrics["numOutputRows"]. A separate count() reads the source file a second time. Open-source Spark defaults saveAsTable to Parquet. Databricks defaults to Delta. Write .format("delta") explicitly, so the code behaves the same in local tests. A bronze job reads supplier CSVs with inferSchema=true. Respondent IDs such as 00123 land as the integer 123. Months later, the supplier sends a correction file keyed on the original IDs, and 18% of rows fail to match silver. The original IDs are not recoverable from bronze, because bronze never held them. The team asks the supplier to resend six months of deliveries. Reading every column as a string keeps 00123 intact. Silver can then cast deliberately, with checks. The strong version keeps every byte the supplier sent, labels every row with its origin, and reads the file once.
lessons.title: Bronze: keep every delivery exactly as received

lessons.text: Silver turns deliveries into a dependable table. Its contract: Canonical names. Rename supplier columns to the names in the Variable Registry, loaded at run time. Declared types. Cast each column to the type in the registry. Grain. One row per respondent per wave. Keep the newest delivery version per key, then MERGE (lesson A3-L1). Two Spark behaviours make the first two steps fail silently or loudly, in the wrong place. Renames skip missing columns. withColumnRenamed("wgt", "final_weight") does nothing when wgt is absent, and so does withColumnsRenamed. No error, no warning. If the supplier renames wgt to weight, silver loses its weight column, and the failure surfaces hours later in gold. Check the source columns yourself before you rename, and raise one error that lists every missing column. Casts under ANSI mode. Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS runs Spark 4.0, which turns ANSI mode on by default. cast("abc" as int) now raises CAST_INVALID_INPUT and stops the job at the first bad value. Older runtimes returned NULL without a word. Neither is what you want in silver. Use try_cast, which returns NULL for a bad value, then count the new NULLs and let a data-quality check decide: under 0.1% is a WARN, above it is CRITICAL. F.col("final_weight").try_cast("double") The pattern is: check columns, rename, try_cast, count cast failures, deduplicate, MERGE. Each step is a small function you can test. A supplier renames wgt to weight without notice. The silver job calls withColumnRenamed("wgt", "final_weight"), which silently does nothing. The type-casting loop skips final_weight because the column is missing. Silver writes the wave with no weight column, since schema evolution is on. At 03:00 the gold job fails with final_weight not found. The morning report shows nothing for the new wave. A column check before the rename fails the silver job at 01:00 with one clear message: "missing source columns: wgt". The on-call engineer knows exactly what to ask the supplier. The strong version fails early and clearly on a changed delivery, and turns bad values into a number you can check instead of a crash or a silent NULL.
lessons.title: Silver: canonical names, checked types, one row per respondent per wave

lessons.text: Gold tables feed Power BI and clients. The contract has three parts. State the grain. Write it in the function docstring and on the table. "One row per tracker x wave x age group x gender x region." Store it as a table comment or a custom table property: COMMENT ON TABLE research_gold.nat_metrics IS 'Grain: tracker x wave x age_group x gender x region'; ALTER TABLE research_gold.nat_metrics SET TBLPROPERTIES ('grain' = 'tracker x wave x age_group x gender x region'); Avoid the property name owner. It is reserved, and Spark 4.0 rejects it with UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.SET_TABLE_PROPERTY. Ownership is set with ALTER TABLE ... OWNER TO. Group by every grain column. If the grain names tracker_id, the groupBy must include tracker_id. Miss one and two trackers' respondents fall into the same row. The numbers look plausible and are wrong. Make aggregates safe. A sum over no matching rows returns NULL, not 0. F.sum(F.when(F.col("reach_flag") == 1, 1)) gives NULL for a subgroup with no reach. Wrap it: F.coalesce(F.sum(...), F.lit(0)). Guard every ratio. F.when(F.col("weighted_base") > 0, reach / base) returns NULL for an empty base instead of an error or an infinite value. Keep the unweighted count next to every weighted figure. Analysts need it to judge whether a subgroup is too small to report. Gold is also where you check totals against silver. The sum of weighted_base across all subgroups for a wave must equal the silver weight total for in-scope respondents. Lesson A6-L3 builds that check. The reference compute_gold_reach_metrics promises "tracker x wave x subgroup grain" but groups by wave and subgroup only. When a second tracker starts writing to the same silver table, its respondents fold into the first tracker's rows. Weighted bases roughly double, and reach percentages blend two audiences. The dashboard shows smooth, believable figures for three weeks, until a client compares a subgroup against its published sample size. Adding tracker_id to groupBy, and a test that checks the output has one row per grain key, prevents it. The strong version cannot merge two trackers, reports a true zero for zero reach, and never divides by nothing.
lessons.title: Gold: state the grain, group by all of it, guard every ratio

lessons.text: A pipeline is idempotent when running it twice with the same input leaves the table in the same state as running it once. Retries, reruns and redeliveries happen every week in production, so idempotence is not optional. An append is not idempotent. Run write.mode("append") twice and every row lands twice. A Delta MERGE is idempotent when two conditions hold: The ON condition covers every column of the table's grain. For a silver table with one row per respondent per wave, that means respondent_id and wave_id. The source holds at most one row per key. The second condition catches people out. When two source rows match the same target row, Delta cannot tell which one should win. It stops the MERGE with the error DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE. When neither row matches a target row, both rows are inserted, and your grain is broken without any error. So deduplicate the source before you merge. Rank the rows for each key by a version column, such as delivery_version or ingestion_timestamp, and keep the newest. Use a window with row_number(). Do not use dropDuplicates(): it keeps an arbitrary row per key, so a rerun keeps a different version with no warning. The pattern for every silver load: Keep the newest source row per key. MERGE on the full grain. whenMatchedUpdateAll() for redelivered rows, whenNotMatchedInsertAll() for new ones. Bronze stays append-only, because bronze records every delivery as received. Silver is where you resolve versions. A supplier redelivers a wave with corrected weights. The file repeats 37 respondents, because the supplier's export joined two tables. The silver job uses the reference upsert_silver, which merges without deduplicating. The MERGE fails at 02:00 with DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE. Gold does not refresh, and the morning Power BI report shows last week's numbers. The on-call engineer "fixes" it by switching the job to append. The next run succeeds. Silver now holds the wave twice. Reach percentages look normal, because both the numerator and the denominator doubled. Weighted population estimates are twice their true size for a month, until a reconciliation check against the weight total catches it. Deduplicating on the full grain before the MERGE prevents both failures. The strong version is idempotent for any source: repeated keys, a retry or a full redelivery. The weak version works only while the supplier never repeats a row.
lessons.title: Idempotent MERGE, and why you deduplicate the source first

lessons.text: A Delta table has a schema, and writes must match it. This is schema enforcement, and it is on by default. Tested on delta-spark 4.0.1: Write Result Append with an extra column Fails: schema mismatch Append with a column missing Succeeds: the missing column is NULL Append with a clashing type (INT into DOUBLE) Fails: DELTA_FAILED_TO_MERGE_FIELDS Overwrite with a different schema Fails unless overwriteSchema is true MERGE with updateAll/insertAll and an extra source column Succeeds, and silently drops the extra column Enforcement is your friend. A failing write is a cheap, early signal that a delivery changed. Schema evolution changes the table's schema to accept the new shape. Delta offers it per write: Append: .option("mergeSchema", "true") adds new columns. MERGE: .withSchemaEvolution() on the merge builder adds new source columns. Planned change: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN (region STRING) in a reviewed migration. Evolve on purpose, never by default. Two habits cause trouble: Leaving mergeSchema on every silver write. A supplier typo such as final_wieght becomes a new, permanent column, and the real weight is NULL for that wave. Setting spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled for the session, which Databricks now labels legacy. It turns evolution on for every MERGE in the job, including ones you did not think about. The safe pattern: validate the incoming columns against the registry first (lesson A2-L2). If a column is new and expected, add it with ALTER TABLE or evolve that one write. If it is unexpected, fail the run and ask the supplier. Note the silent MERGE case in the table. Enforcement does not protect you there. Your column check does. A silver job appends with mergeSchema always on, "to avoid schema errors". A supplier's export misspells final_weight as final_wieght for one wave. The append succeeds. Silver gains a permanent final_wieght column, and final_weight is NULL for 2,000 respondents. Gold sums NULL weights to a smaller base, and weighted reach for that wave is computed on the wrong population. Without mergeSchema, the append fails with a schema mismatch naming the unexpected column. The fix takes minutes, and silver never holds the bad wave. Schema changes become decisions a person reviews, not accidents a delivery causes.
lessons.title: Schema enforcement is on by default. Evolve on purpose.

lessons.text: Every Delta write creates a new table version. The transaction log keeps the list, and you can read any version still on storage. DESCRIBE HISTORY t lists versions with the operation, user and metrics. spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 12).table("t") or SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 12 reads an old version. timestampAsOf and TIMESTAMP AS OF work by time. RESTORE TABLE t TO VERSION AS OF 12 makes version 12 current again, as a new version. History is kept, so you can undo the restore. Time travel is your first response to a bad write: compare the versions, restore, then fix the job. Two maintenance commands keep tables fast and storage bounded. OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer large ones. Frequent small appends leave thousands of tiny files, and every query pays to open them. OPTIMIZE t ZORDER BY (wave_id) also co-locates rows by a column. On Unity Catalog managed tables, Databricks recommends liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY, or CLUSTER BY AUTO) with predictive optimization, which runs OPTIMIZE and VACUUM for you. VACUUM deletes data files that no current version needs and that are older than the retention window. The window comes from delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration, which defaults to 7 days. Delta blocks VACUUM t RETAIN 0 HOURS with a safety check, because a running reader or writer might still need those files. VACUUM limits time travel. After it runs, versions whose files it removed can no longer be read. The log itself keeps entries for delta.logRetentionDuration, 30 days by default. From Databricks Runtime 18.0, time travel beyond deletedFileRetentionDuration is blocked outright. If you need 30 days of recoverable history, set both properties to at least 30 days. A developer runs a gold rebuild against the wrong wave filter and overwrites three weeks of metrics. The team wants to restore, but a clean-up job ran VACUUM ... RETAIN 0 HOURS nightly, with the retention check switched off "to save storage". The overwritten files are gone. Three weeks of gold are rebuilt from silver overnight, and two client extracts go out late. With the default 7-day retention, RESTORE TABLE research_gold.nat_metrics TO VERSION AS OF the last good version takes seconds. History turns a data incident into a two-minute restore. Keep it long enough to be useful.
lessons.title: Time travel, RESTORE, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM

lessons.text: Unity Catalog names every table with three parts: catalog.schema.table. research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents Use each level for one purpose: Catalog = environment (or a major business domain): research_dev, research_test, research_prod. Permissions and storage attach at this level, so a dev job with no rights on research_prod cannot damage it. Schema = layer or subject: research_bronze, research_silver, research_gold, research_governance. Table = content at a stated grain: nat_raw, nat_respondents, nat_metrics. Always write the full three-part name in pipeline code, built from configuration. A two-part name such as research_silver.nat_respondents resolves against the session's current catalog. That depends on the workspace default, a USE CATALOG somewhere earlier in the notebook, or a job setting. The same code then reads a different table in each place it runs. Build names in one function from config, so no code concatenates strings on its own: def table_name(catalog: str, layer: str, tracker: str) -> str: suffix = {"bronze": "raw", "silver": "respondents", "gold": "metrics"}[layer] return f"{catalog}.research_{layer}.{tracker}_{suffix}" In a notebook, spark.catalog.currentCatalog() tells you which catalog a two-part name would use. It is useful for checks, never as a substitute for naming the catalog. Workspaces created before Unity Catalog also show hive_metastore, the legacy two-level store. Treat it as read-only history while you migrate. A shared all-purpose cluster has research_prod as its default catalog. A developer tests a silver fix from a notebook that writes to research_silver.nat_respondents, a two-part name, believing the notebook "runs in dev". The MERGE lands in production. The fix was only half finished, and 1,400 rows get wrong region codes before anyone notices. With a three-part name built from a dev config file, the same notebook writes to research_dev.research_silver.nat_respondents. The developer's lack of MODIFY on research_prod would also have blocked it. The strong version reads exactly the table its config names, whatever the session's current catalog is.
lessons.title: The three-level namespace, one catalog per environment

lessons.text: Unity Catalog controls access with privileges on securable objects. Four privileges cover most pipeline work: Privilege On Lets the principal USE CATALOG catalog see into the catalog. Grants no data access by itself. USE SCHEMA schema see into the schema. Grants no data access by itself. SELECT table, or schema read data MODIFY table, or schema insert, update and delete data To read a table, a principal needs all three: USE CATALOG on its catalog, USE SCHEMA on its schema and SELECT on the table. MODIFY also needs SELECT and both USE privileges. Grant at the container. A privilege granted on a schema is inherited by every current and future table in it. GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA research_prod.research_gold covers next month's new gold table without another ticket. Grant to groups, never to individual users. People join, move and leave. A group grant is managed once, in one place. A user grant outlives the reason it was made, and nobody finds it until an audit. Run pipelines as a service principal. Jobs that write bronze, silver and gold run as a service principal with MODIFY on those schemas. People get SELECT on the layers they need, and no person needs MODIFY on production. GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG research_prod TO research_analysts; GRANT USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA research_prod.research_gold TO research_analysts; SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA research_prod.research_gold; Avoid ALL PRIVILEGES outside sandboxes. It includes privileges you did not think about, and future privileges too. During a deadline, an analyst gets MODIFY on research_prod.research_silver "for one day" to patch a mapping by hand. The grant is to their user account. Eight months later they run a clean-up notebook against what they believe is a dev copy and delete 12,000 silver rows. Nobody remembered the grant, and silver had to be rebuilt from bronze. With the rule "people get SELECT, pipelines get MODIFY, grants go to groups", the patch would have gone through the pipeline, and the delete would have failed with a permission error. Three rules: groups not users, schemas not tables, SELECT for people and MODIFY for pipelines.
lessons.title: Grant to groups, grant the least, grant at the right level

lessons.text: Grants decide who can read a table. Row filters and column masks decide what each reader sees inside it. Both are SQL user-defined functions that Unity Catalog applies at query time, for every query, from every tool. Row filter. A SQL UDF that returns BOOLEAN. Unity Catalog passes it the columns you name, and drops each row where the function returns FALSE or NULL. CREATE FUNCTION research_prod.research_governance.respondent_filter(tracker_id STRING) RETURN is_account_group_member('research_approved_analysts') OR tracker_id = 'TRK-PUBLIC'; ALTER TABLE research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents SET ROW FILTER research_prod.research_governance.respondent_filter ON (tracker_id); Column mask. A SQL UDF whose first parameter is the column value. It returns the value, or a masked version. CREATE FUNCTION research_prod.research_governance.mask_postcode(postcode STRING) RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('pii_readers') THEN postcode ELSE '*' END; ALTER TABLE research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents ALTER COLUMN postcode SET MASK research_prod.research_governance.mask_postcode; Three rules: Use is_account_group_member(). It checks account-level groups, which Unity Catalog uses. is_member() checks workspace-local groups. Test group membership, never current_user() = 'someone@example.org'. A named user in a function is a hidden grant nobody reviews. Keep filter and mask functions in a governance schema, so their owners and grants are separate from the data. Your reference script uses CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY. That is Snowflake syntax. Databricks rejects it. Where many tables share one rule, Databricks also offers attribute-based policies on governed tags. The reference unity_catalog.sql was written with an AI assistant and never run. Its row-level security uses CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY, which does not exist in Databricks. The deployment script stops at that statement, and the PII table goes live without a filter, because the grants earlier in the script had already succeeded. Every analyst with SELECT on silver can read restricted respondent rows until someone notices the failed step. A SQL UDF with SET ROW FILTER, tested in dev, applies the rule where Databricks enforces it. The strong script runs on Databricks, names groups instead of people, and uses three-part names throughout.
lessons.title: Row filters and column masks in Unity Catalog

lessons.text: Spark splits DataFrame operations into two kinds. Transformations build a plan and return a new DataFrame at once: filter, select, withColumn, join, groupBy().agg(). Nothing is read yet. Actions run the plan and return a result: count(), collect(), show(), first(), toPandas(), and every write. This is lazy evaluation. It lets the optimiser see the whole plan before running it, so it can push filters into the file scan and skip columns you never use. The cost is easy to miss: each action runs the whole plan again, from the source. Nothing is kept between actions unless you ask for it. A local test shows it plainly: a Python function counted its own calls inside a plan over 1,000 rows. After the first count(), it had run 1,000 times. After a second count(), 2,000. Your reference data-contract validator calls count() more than ten times on the same uncached DataFrame: once for the row count, once per mandatory column, once per key and so on. Each call rereads the delivery from storage. Three fixes, in order of preference: Combine the questions into one action. One agg with many expressions answers them all in a single pass: df.agg( F.count("*").alias("rows"), F.count_if(F.col("final_weight").isNull()).alias("null_weights"), F.sum("final_weight").alias("weight_sum"), ).collect()[0] Materialise an expensive intermediate result to a Delta table, then read that table for the follow-up actions. Cache with df.cache() on classic clusters only. Serverless compute, which Free Edition uses, does not support cache APIs. A contract validator checks a 40-million-row delivery with 23 separate count() calls, one per check. Each call rescans the source files in cloud storage. The validation step takes 38 minutes, longer than the transform it protects, and the team starts skipping it "for small redeliveries". A redelivery with duplicated keys then goes straight to silver. Rewritten as one agg with 23 expressions, the same checks run in a single scan of about two minutes, and nobody has a reason to skip them. Four questions, one scan. The strong version reads the delivery once, however many checks you add.
lessons.title: Lazy evaluation, and why every count() re-runs the plan

lessons.text: A Python UDF runs your Python function once per row. Spark must send each value from the JVM to a Python worker process, run the function, and send the result back. The physical plan shows this as a BatchEvalPython step. A built-in function from pyspark.sql.functions runs inside the JVM, in Spark's generated code, with no round trip. Measured on 2 million strings (PySpark 4.0.4, two local cores): Approach Time F.upper(col) 0.30 s pandas UDF (ArrowEvalPython) 1.16 s Python UDF (BatchEvalPython) 1.82 s The Python UDF was six times slower, and the gap grows with cluster size and data volume. Speed is one reason. There are three more: Nulls. Built-ins return NULL for NULL input. A UDF receives None and must handle it. lambda s: s.strip() fails the whole job with a PythonException on the first NULL. Optimisation. The optimiser cannot see inside a UDF, so it cannot push a filter on the UDF's output into the file scan. Readability. F.when(...).when(...) states a rule in one expression a reviewer can check. Most UDFs in pipelines replace functions that already exist: F.upper, F.trim, F.regexp_replace, F.regexp_extract, F.split, F.to_date, F.coalesce, F.when, F.concat_ws, F.lpad. Search the functions reference before you write one. When no built-in fits, prefer a pandas UDF: it moves data in Arrow batches and runs vectorised pandas code. Use a row-by-row Python UDF only as the last resort, and handle None first. A silver job cleans postcodes with a Python UDF: lambda s: s.replace(" ", "").upper(). It runs for months on deliveries where every postcode is present. Then a supplier sends a wave with 40 blank postcodes, which arrive as NULL. The first NULL raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'replace' inside a Python worker, and the whole silver job fails at 02:00. F.upper(F.regexp_replace("postcode", r"\s+", "")) returns NULL for NULL, runs faster, and would never have failed. The strong version runs in the JVM, survives NULLs and reads as a rule. Functions that return Column expressions give you the reuse that UDFs promised.
lessons.title: Built-in functions over Python UDFs

lessons.text: A join between two large tables needs a shuffle: Spark moves rows across the network so equal keys meet on the same executor, then sorts and merges them. The plan shows this as SortMergeJoin with Exchange steps. Shuffles are the most expensive thing Spark does. When one side is small, such as a lookup of 200 region codes, Spark can broadcast it: send a full copy to every executor and join locally, with no shuffle of the large side. The plan shows BroadcastHashJoin. Spark broadcasts automatically when it estimates a side is under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, 10 MB by default in Spark 4.0. Adaptive query execution (AQE), on by default, can switch a join to broadcast at run time once it sees real sizes. You can force it with F.broadcast(small_df) or small_df.hint("broadcast"). Do this for lookups you know are small. Never broadcast something that grows with your data. Read the plan before you tune. df.explain() prints the physical plan. df.explain(mode="formatted") adds details per step, including PushedFilters, which confirm that a filter reached the file scan. Partitions decide parallelism. repartition(n) shuffles to exactly n partitions. coalesce(n) merges partitions without a shuffle, and only reduces the count. repartition(1) or coalesce(1) before a large write puts all the work on one task. Avoid it outside tiny outputs. For table layout on Unity Catalog managed tables, prefer liquid clustering over partitionBy. If you do partition a table, choose a low-cardinality column such as wave_id, never an ID. Caching: df.cache() helps on classic clusters when several actions reuse a result. Serverless compute does not support it. There, write the intermediate result to a Delta table. A gold job joins 40 million respondent rows to a 200-row region lookup. Auto-broadcast does not kick in, because the lookup is read through a view whose size Spark overestimates. Every run shuffles all 40 million rows across the cluster, and the join takes 22 minutes. explain() shows SortMergeJoin with two Exchange steps. Wrapping the lookup in F.broadcast() turns it into BroadcastHashJoin, and the join drops to under two minutes. Five minutes reading the plan saved twenty minutes on every run. One broadcast join replaces a collect, a dict and a UDF, keeps the work distributed, and shows up clearly in the plan.
lessons.title: Joins, broadcast, partitions and reading the plan

lessons.text: A data contract states what a delivery must look like before it may enter silver: row count range, mandatory columns, weight total, unique keys, allowed categories, expected distributions. Your reference project keeps each contract as versioned JSON, such as nat_contract_v2.json. Every check produces a structured result, never a sentence: CheckName = str Status = Literal["PASS", "WARN", "FAIL", "SKIP"] Severity = Literal["CRITICAL", "HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW"] @dataclass(frozen=True) class CheckResult: check_name: CheckName status: Status severity: Severity expected: str actual: str Records can be counted, stored in a Delta table, charted and compared across waves. A narrative such as "weights look a bit high" cannot. Severity decides what happens next. A failed CRITICAL check stops the pipeline: raise an exception, so the job fails and silver stays untouched. Row count out of range, null keys, duplicate keys and a weight total outside limits are CRITICAL. A WARN logs the result and the run continues. Unexpected category values and distribution shifts are warnings: worth a look, not worth a missed report. Evaluate every check first, store all the results, then decide. If you raise on the first failure, you learn about one problem per run. Keep the contract in data and the logic in code. A new contract version changes JSON, not Python. On Databricks, Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines offer the same idea declaratively: @dp.expect records violations, @dp.expect_or_drop removes violating rows, and @dp.expect_or_fail stops the update. Use them when your pipeline runs in that framework. The contract pattern here works in any job. A contract validator raises on the first failed check. A redelivery has a row count 2% below the minimum, so the run stops at check 1. The supplier fixes the count and resends. The next run stops at check 4, duplicate keys. The third run stops at check 6, a weight total outside the range. Three round trips with the supplier cost four days. Evaluating every check, storing all results, and then raising once for all CRITICAL failures gives the supplier one complete list on the first day. Results are data, severity decides the action, and one run reports every problem.
lessons.title: Data contracts with severity levels and structured results

lessons.text: Statistical QA runs on every wave, including the strange ones: an empty delivery, a subgroup with one respondent, a metric that drops to exactly zero. A check that crashes on those cases fails exactly when you need it. Know what Spark 4.0 returns at the edges (all tested on PySpark 4.0.4): Case Result F.mean, F.stddev, percentile_approx on an empty DataFrame NULL F.stddev on one row NULL (it is the sample standard deviation) F.col("a") / F.col("b") where b is 0, ANSI mode on Error: DIVIDE_BY_ZERO, even for DOUBLE F.try_divide(a, b) where b is 0 NULL Python round(None, 4) TypeError So a weight-spread check built as round(stats["stddev"] / stats["mean"], 4) fails three ways: NULL mean on an empty wave, NULL stddev on one row, and round(None) in Python. Four habits make checks robust: Compute the count with the statistics, in the same agg, and decide early. Fewer than two rows: return a SKIP result that says why. Divide with F.try_divide or guard with F.when(denominator > 0, ...). Never a bare / on data you do not control. Test for None with is None in Python. if cv: treats a real CV of 0.0 as missing, and if current_pct and prior_pct: skips a share that fell to 0.0 (reference defect 8). Return a result for every check, including SKIP. A check that silently returns nothing looks exactly like a check that passed. A new tracker's first wave has one respondent in a small region, because of a routing test. The weight-spread check computes the sample standard deviation for that region: NULL. Python then runs round(None, 4) and raises TypeError. The QA job fails, and because QA gates publication, the whole wave's reporting is delayed by a day while someone reads the stack trace. With the count checked first, that region gets a SKIP result, "fewer than 2 respondents", and every other region is checked as normal. The strong version returns a result for every wave and every subgroup, and says why when a statistic is undefined.
lessons.title: Statistical checks that survive empty, single-row and zero data

lessons.text: Each layer transforms data, and each transformation can lose or duplicate rows. Reconciliation checks that what came out of one layer matches what went into the next, for every wave you load. Compare quantities that must agree by design: From To Must match Bronze, wave W Silver, wave W Distinct (respondent_id, wave_id) keys in bronze = silver rows Silver, wave W, in scope Gold, wave W Sum of final_weight = sum of weighted_base over all subgroups Silver, wave W, in scope Gold, wave W Row count = sum of unweighted_n Pick the right bronze figure. Bronze holds every delivery, redeliveries included, so its raw row count is larger than silver's by design. Compare distinct keys. Compare totals with a tolerance. Floating-point sums depend on the order Spark adds values in, which varies with partitioning, so two correct totals can differ in the last digits. In Python, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False. Use math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-6). The abs_tol handles totals near zero, where a relative tolerance means nothing. Compute each side with one aggregation, record the result as a structured check (expected, actual, status), and treat a failed reconciliation as CRITICAL. If gold does not add up to silver, every published figure for that wave is suspect. Run reconciliation after each layer loads and before anything downstream reads it. Store the results with the run log, so you can show that every published wave reconciled. A gold job joins silver to a region lookup with an inner join. A supplier introduces a new region code, NI, that the lookup does not have. 312 respondents drop out of gold without an error. Weighted reach for the wave looks plausible, because the base shrank along with the reach. A reconciliation of silver's in-scope weight total against the sum of gold's weighted_base catches the 1.8% gap on the same run. The alert names the wave and the size of the difference, and the fix is a lookup update, not a client complaint. Silver and gold totals are computed the same way and compared with tolerance. A mismatch becomes a CRITICAL result with numbers, not a print.
lessons.title: Reconcile counts and totals between layers

lessons.text: print writes text to standard output, with no level, no source and no context. In a scheduled job, that text lands in a driver log that nobody searches until something breaks. Python's standard logging module fixes all three problems. One logger per module. log = logging.getLogger(name) names the logger after the module, such as pipelines.silver. Every line then says where it came from. Levels. DEBUG for detail while developing, INFO for normal milestones, WARNING for something odd that did not stop the run, ERROR for a failure, CRITICAL for a failure that stops everything. Loggers pass WARNING and above by default, so log.info(...) prints nothing until you configure a level. Context on every line. Include the identifiers you will search for later: run_id, tracker_id, wave_id, layer. A LoggerAdapter attaches them once, and a format string prints them: base = logging.getLogger(name) log = logging.LoggerAdapter(base, {"run_id": run_id, "wave_id": wave_id}) log.info("merged rows=%d", n) INFO pipelines.silver run_id=7f3c wave_id=W14 merged rows=1832 Three more rules: Pass values as arguments, log.info("rows=%d", n), not pre-built f-strings. The logger formats them only when the line is actually emitted. Inside except, call log.exception("..."). It logs at ERROR and appends the full traceback. Configure handlers and formats once, in the entry point, never inside library functions. Logs are for people reading one run. Metrics you want to compare across runs, such as row counts and statuses, also go to the run log table (lesson A7-L2). A silver job prints "done" at the end of each step. One night it finishes "successfully" with zero rows merged, because an upstream filter used the wrong wave ID. The driver log for that run holds 400 lines of "done" and Spark noise, with no wave ID and no row counts. With log.info("merged rows=%d", n) and the wave ID on every line, the zero is visible in one search, and a WARNING for an empty merge would have flagged it at 02:00. Every line says what, where, which run and which wave. Failures keep their traceback and still fail the job.
lessons.title: Structured logging with the logging module, not print

lessons.text: Logs describe one run. A run log table lets you compare every run: which waves loaded, how many rows, how long, and which failed. It is a Delta table, append-only, with one row per pipeline run per layer. A useful schema: Column Type Notes run_id STRING, not null str(uuid.uuid4()), shared by every log line of the run pipeline_name STRING, not null nat_silver_pipeline tracker_id, wave_id, layer STRING what the run touched rows_processed BIGINT, not null from Delta commit metrics status STRING, not null SUCCESS or FAILED error_message STRING, nullable NULL on success started_at, finished_at TIMESTAMP, not null UTC Build the record against an explicit StructType. Your reference log_pipeline_run builds a DataFrame from a dict and lets Spark infer types. That fails on every successful run: error_message is None, and Spark raises CANNOT_DETERMINE_TYPE because it cannot infer a type from a column of only nulls. The explicit schema also rejects a wrong type, such as "12" for rows_processed, before anything is written. Take timestamps with datetime.now(timezone.utc). datetime.utcnow() is deprecated from Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime that carries no timezone. Import everything you use. The reference function calls uuid and datetime without importing them, a NameError on its first run. ruff check (rule F821) catches it in CI. Write the log record in a finally block, or in both the success and failure paths, so failed runs are logged too. A run log that only records successes cannot tell you how often the pipeline fails. The reference log_pipeline_run has never succeeded. It fails first with NameError: name 'uuid' is not defined. Once someone adds the imports, it fails on every successful run with CANNOT_DETERMINE_TYPE, because error_message=None is the only value in its column. The orchestrator catches that error "so logging never breaks the pipeline". Months later the team wants to show a client every load of 2025. The run log table is empty. An explicit schema, imported names and a test that writes one record on a local SparkSession prevent all three problems. The strong record builds on every run, success or failure, and its types never depend on the values in one row.
lessons.title: A pipeline run log table with an explicit schema

lessons.text: An alert is useful when it fires for real problems, reaches the person who can act, and says enough to start. Pipelines need two kinds. Loud failures: the job fails. Databricks job notifications send an email or a webhook message when a run fails. In a job definition or bundle: email_notifications: on_failure: data-oncall@example.org These fire only if the job actually fails. Every except block that logs and carries on silences them. Log, record the run as FAILED, then re-raise (lesson A7-L2). Job-level notifications are not sent when a failed task is retried. If you want a message for every failed attempt, add task-level notifications. Silent failures: the job succeeds, but the data is wrong or missing. A job that never starts, a MERGE that writes 0 rows, a wave with a WARN on every contract check. No job fails, so no notification fires. Detect these with queries on your run log and QA results tables, run on a schedule, for example as Databricks SQL alerts: No SUCCESS run for a pipeline in the last 26 hours (a daily job plus slack). A run with rows_processed = 0. More WARN results for a wave than the last five waves' average. Write each alert query against the exact values your tables hold. A query for status = 'FAIL' never fires on a table that stores FAILED. Send alerts to a group address or channel, never to one person's inbox. Include the pipeline, the wave, the run ID and a link, so the reader can start without searching. A nightly bronze job's schedule is paused during a workspace migration and never resumed. The job does not fail, because it never runs, so no failure email arrives. Silver and gold keep succeeding on the old data. Eleven days later a client asks why the dashboard has not moved. A scheduled query, "no SUCCESS for nat_bronze_pipeline in 26 hours", would have alerted the on-call group on the second morning. Job notifications catch runs that fail. Scheduled queries catch runs that do not happen, or that succeed at doing nothing.
lessons.title: Alert on failures, and on the silence that hides them

lessons.text: Incremental loading means each run handles only new work: waves in bronze that silver does not have yet. It saves compute, and it keeps reruns cheap. It is also easy to get subtly wrong. The pattern: def unprocessed_waves(spark, bronze, silver, tracker_id) -> list[str]: source = spark.table(bronze).filter(F.col("tracker_id") == tracker_id).select("wave_id").distinct() done = spark.table(silver).filter(F.col("tracker_id") == tracker_id).select("wave_id").distinct() return sorted(r.wave_id for r in source.join(done, "wave_id", "left_anti").collect()) Four rules: Filter both sides the same way. Your reference get_unprocessed_waves filters bronze by tracker but reads silver for every tracker. If tracker B already has wave W14 in silver, tracker A's W14 is treated as done and never loads. Scope both sides with the same keys. Use a left anti join ("left_anti"): rows on the left with no match on the right. It says exactly what you mean, and it works for multi-column keys. Handle the first run. When silver does not exist yet, every bronze wave is new. Check with spark.catalog.tableExists(silver). Keep each wave's load idempotent. Detection can be wrong after a partial failure, for example if silver has half a wave. Because the silver MERGE is idempotent (A3-L1), reprocessing a wave is always safe. Design for "process again", not "process exactly once". Deciding by "waves not in silver" misses redeliveries of a wave silver already has. Either compare the latest ingestion_timestamp per wave in bronze with the one recorded when silver loaded it, or read bronze incrementally with change data feed (A8-L3) or Auto Loader (A8-L2). Two trackers share one silver table. Tracker B loads wave W14 on Monday. Tracker A's W14 arrives on Tuesday. The reference get_unprocessed_waves compares tracker A's bronze waves against silver waves for all trackers, finds W14 already present, and skips it. Tracker A's dashboard shows no W14, and no job fails. The gap is found nine days later, by a client. Filtering silver by tracker_id too makes the comparison correct, and a reconciliation of bronze keys against silver rows (A6-L3) would have flagged it on Tuesday. Same filters on both sides, an explicit anti join, a first-run branch, and an idempotent load behind it.
lessons.title: Process only the waves you have not processed, correctly

lessons.text: Suppliers drop files into a landing folder. You want each file loaded into bronze exactly once, whenever it arrives, without keeping your own list of processed files. Auto Loader does this on Databricks. It is a Structured Streaming source called cloudFiles. ( spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv") .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", schema_path) .option("header", "true") .load(landing_path) .select("*", F.col("_metadata.file_path").alias("source_file")) .writeStream .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path) .trigger(availableNow=True) .toTable("research_prod.research_bronze.nat_raw") ) What each piece does: Checkpoint location. Auto Loader records every discovered file in a key-value store (RocksDB) under the checkpoint. After a failure it resumes where it stopped, and each file path is processed once. One checkpoint per stream, never shared, never deleted casually: deleting it reloads every file. Schema location. Auto Loader infers the schema once, stores it there, and tracks changes. Without a schema you provide, the default mode is addNewColumns: when a new column appears, the stream stops with UnknownFieldException after recording the new schema, and the next start includes the column. Run it from a job that retries, so the restart is automatic. Rescued data. When Auto Loader infers the schema, it adds a _rescued_data column that captures values that do not fit, such as a type mismatch. Count non-null _rescued_data in your contract checks. trigger(availableNow=True) processes every file that has arrived, then stops. Schedule it as a batch job: incremental logic, batch cost. _metadata.file_path gives each row its source file, for the bronze audit columns. Keep checkpoints and schemas in a Unity Catalog volume, such as /Volumes/research_prod/research_bronze/checkpoints/nat_raw. A bronze notebook lists the landing folder, compares file names with a hand-maintained "processed.txt", and loads the rest. A timeout kills the notebook after it has loaded a file but before it has updated the list. The next run loads the same file again. Bronze now holds the delivery twice with two ingestion IDs, and silver's newest-version logic cannot tell them apart, because both carry the same delivery_version. Auto Loader's checkpoint records files and commits the Delta write together, so a restart after a failure neither skips nor repeats a file. Auto Loader replaces a fragile processed-files list with a checkpoint that commits together with the Delta write.
lessons.title: Auto Loader for file ingestion into bronze

lessons.text: When silver changes, gold should reprocess only the rows that changed, not the whole table. Change data feed (CDF) makes a Delta table record row-level changes for every write. Turn it on per table: ALTER TABLE research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true); Read the changes since a version: changes = ( spark.read.option("readChangeFeed", "true") .option("startingVersion", last_version + 1) .table("research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents") ) Each row carries three extra columns: _change_type: insert, update_preimage (the row before an update), update_postimage (the row after), or delete. _commit_version and _commit_timestamp: which commit made the change. Two rules make CDF consumers correct: Drop update_preimage rows before you use the changes. An update produces two rows, old and new. Keep the old one and every updated respondent is counted twice. Keep one row per key: the latest by _commit_version. A respondent updated in three commits since your last run appears three times. Track progress. Either store the last processed version in a state table, or read the feed as a stream (readStream with readChangeFeed) and let the checkpoint remember it. Change data only exists from the version where you enabled it. Asking for an earlier version fails with DELTA_MISSING_CHANGE_DATA. VACUUM also removes old change files after the retention window. For gold, collect the waves and subgroups the changes touch, then recompute just those aggregates. Aggregates cannot be patched row by row. A gold job rebuilds weighted metrics for every wave every night: 180 waves, 40 minutes. Most nights, only one wave changed. When a late correction arrives mid-afternoon, the team cannot refresh gold before the client call, because a full rebuild takes too long. With CDF on silver, the job reads the day's changes, finds the one wave they touch, and recomputes it in under two minutes. The same job also stops double counting, because it drops update_preimage rows before aggregating. Read after the last version, drop pre-images, keep the newest change per key, and recompute only what the changes touch.
lessons.title: Change data feed, so downstream layers read only what changed

lessons.text: pytest finds files named test_*.py, runs every function named test_*, and reports each failing assert with the values on both sides. No classes or special assert methods are needed. def test_weighted_share_uses_weights() -> None: assert weighted_share([1, 0], [3.0, 1.0]) == 0.75 Fixtures provide what tests need. A test names a fixture as a parameter, and pytest builds it and passes it in. For Spark, one fixture creates the session: @pytest.fixture(scope="session") def spark() -> Iterator[SparkSession]: session = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate() yield session session.stop() scope="session" builds it once for the whole test run. Starting Spark takes several seconds. Once per test, and a 40-test suite spends minutes on start-up alone. yield hands the value to the tests. The code after yield runs once at the end, which is where you stop the session. Put shared fixtures in conftest.py. pytest loads it automatically for every test in that folder and below. @pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test with several inputs, and each input is reported as its own test: @pytest.mark.parametrize(("flags", "weights", "expected"), [([1], [2.0], 1.0), ([0, 0], [1.0, 1.0], 0.0)]) def test_share(flags, weights, expected): ... A good test fails for the bug you fear. Write it against the known answer on small data, including the edge cases: empty input, zero totals, missing values. Check it by breaking the code on purpose and watching the test fail. A team's test for weighted_share checks that the result is between 0 and 1. The function is later rewritten and accidentally returns the unweighted share. The result is still between 0 and 1, so the test passes, and weighted reach in the dashboard is wrong for a month. A test with a known answer, weighted_share([1, 0], [3.0, 1.0]) == 0.75, fails the moment the weights are ignored, because the unweighted answer is 0.5. One session-scoped fixture, and tests with known answers that fail for the bugs you care about.
lessons.title: pytest basics, and a SparkSession fixture shared by every test

lessons.text: Unit tests for PySpark run on your laptop and in CI, not on a cluster. A local session that starts in seconds and runs small jobs fast needs a few settings: builder = ( SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]") .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "2") .config("spark.ui.enabled", "false") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension") .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog") .config("spark.sql.sources.default", "delta") ) spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder).getOrCreate() local[2] runs Spark in one process with two worker threads. Two threads, not one, so bugs that depend on partitioning still show up. spark.sql.shuffle.partitions defaults to 200. On ten test rows, every shuffle creates 200 tiny tasks. Two is plenty. configure_spark_with_delta_pip from delta-spark adds the matching Delta JAR. The two config lines enable Delta SQL and the Delta catalog. Open-source Spark writes saveAsTable as Parquet by default. Databricks uses Delta. Set the default so tests behave like production. Test data. Build it with an explicit schema, as a DDL string such as "respondent_id STRING, final_weight DOUBLE". Inference guesses types from values, fails on a column of only None (CANNOT_DETERMINE_TYPE), and turns 2 into a LONG where production has DOUBLE. A test data builder keeps tests short: one function returns a valid row with sensible defaults, and each test overrides only the field it is about. def respondent(**overrides: object) -> dict[str, object]: row = {"respondent_id": "R1", "wave_id": "W1", "final_weight": 1.0, "in_scope": True} row.update(overrides) return row A test that says respondent(final_weight=None) tells the reader exactly what it is testing. A project's Spark tests take 14 minutes in CI, so developers stop running them locally. The session uses the default 200 shuffle partitions, and each of the 60 tests runs two or three shuffles on a handful of rows. Most of the time goes into scheduling empty tasks. A MERGE bug that a test would have caught ships to production, because nobody waited for the suite. With local[2] and two shuffle partitions, the same suite runs in under two minutes, and people run it before every push. A tuned local session makes tests fast enough to run on every change. Builders with explicit schemas make them short and exact.
lessons.title: A fast local SparkSession and readable test data

lessons.text: Comparing DataFrames by hand is harder than it looks. actual.collect() == expected.collect() fails when the rows come back in a different order, which Spark never guarantees. It also fails when a float is 0.30000000000000004 instead of 0.3. Sorting both sides fixes the order but not the floats, and neither checks the schema. pyspark.testing (PySpark 3.5 and later) handles all of this: from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual, assertSchemaEqual assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected) Tested on PySpark 4.0.4: Row order is ignored by default. Pass checkRowOrder=True when order is the point, as in a top-10 list. Floats compare with a tolerance (rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8 by default). Schemas must match: INT against BIGINT fails with DIFFERENT_SCHEMA. Duplicates count: two identical rows do not equal one. expected can be a list of Row objects, which is handy for snapshots. Failures raise PySparkAssertionError, a subclass of AssertionError, so pytest reports them as ordinary test failures, with a diff. assertSchemaEqual(actual.schema, expected.schema) checks only the structure. Testing MERGE. The property that matters is idempotence. The test: Create an empty Delta table with the target schema. Run the load once, and take a snapshot: first = spark.table(t).collect(). Run the same load again. assertDataFrameEqual(spark.table(t), first). Add cases for the failures you fear: a repeated key in the source, a redelivery with a newer version, and the same respondent in two waves. Each one takes a few rows and a second or two. In the practice harness, PySpark 4.0.4 needs pandas 2.x. With pandas 3.x, assertDataFrameEqual fails to import. A silver test compares actual.collect() == expected.collect(). It passes on a developer's laptop and fails one CI run in five, because the order of rows varies with partitioning. The team marks it flaky and skips it. A month later a real regression in the MERGE, duplicate rows after a retry, ships untested. assertDataFrameEqual ignores order, so the test is stable, and an idempotence test that runs the load twice catches the regression. One helper compares DataFrames the right way, and one small test proves a MERGE survives a retry and a repeated key.
lessons.title: Compare DataFrames properly, and test that MERGE is idempotent

lessons.text: Production pipeline code lives in Git, not in someone's workspace folder. Databricks Git folders connect a workspace folder to a remote repository, so you can edit, commit, pull and switch branches from the workspace. The workflow Databricks documents: Each developer clones the repository into their own Git folder under /Workspace/Users/<email>/ and works on their own branch. Use a trunk-based strategy: short-lived feature branches off main, merged through a pull request with review and CI checks. Production Git folders are different. An admin creates them outside user folders. They hold a deployment branch, and only automation updates them, after a pull request merges. Nobody edits code there by hand. For deploying jobs and their configuration together, Databricks recommends Declarative Automation Bundles (lesson A10-L2). Store notebooks as source files (.py with # Databricks notebook source headers, or .ipynb). Put reusable functions in plain Python modules that notebooks import, so tests can import them too. Secrets never go into the repository. Not in code, not in config files, not in notebook outputs. Git keeps every version forever, and removing a token in a later commit does not remove it from history. Rotate any secret that was ever committed. In Databricks, read secrets at run time: api_key = dbutils.secrets.get(scope="research", key="supplier_api_key") Databricks redacts secret values read this way, showing [REDACTED] if you print them. Redaction does not stop deliberate transformations, so never try to display a secret. In CI, secrets come from the CI system's secret store as environment variables. Add a .gitignore for local files (.venv/, pycache/, .env), so credentials and environments never get staged by accident. A developer tests a supplier API from a notebook with a hardcoded token, then commits the notebook to share the code. A week later they replace the token with a secret lookup in a new commit, believing the problem is fixed. The repository is later mirrored to a partner, and the token is still in the history. The supplier revokes the key after detecting unusual use, and every ingestion job that depends on it fails for two days. With dbutils.secrets.get from the first line, there is nothing to leak. Code flows from a branch, through review and CI, to production. Secrets flow from a secret store at run time, never through Git.
lessons.title: Git folders, one branch per change, and no secrets in the repository

lessons.text: A job built by clicking in the UI exists only in one workspace, with no history and no review. Declarative Automation Bundles describe jobs, their tasks, parameters and notifications as YAML files in your repository. Databricks renamed them from Databricks Asset Bundles on 16 March 2026. The databricks bundle commands and databricks.yml did not change. A bundle has one databricks.yml at its root: bundle: name: research_pipelines variables: catalog: description: Catalog the pipelines write to. resources: jobs: nat_silver_pipeline: name: nat_silver_pipeline parameters: name: catalog default: ${var.catalog} tasks: task_key: silver notebook_task: notebook_path: ./notebooks/silver_nat_transform.py targets: dev: mode: development default: true variables: catalog: research_dev prod: mode: production variables: catalog: research_prod Targets are environments. One code base deploys to each with different values. Variables hold what differs per target. They resolve from --var, then BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables, then target mappings, then defaults. Job parameters reach notebook tasks, which read them with dbutils.widgets.get("catalog"). Dynamic references such as {{job.run_id}} fill in values at run time. mode: development prefixes job names with [dev <your name>] and pauses schedules, so your test deployment never runs on the production timetable. The commands: databricks bundle validate -t dev databricks bundle deploy -t dev databricks bundle run -t dev nat_silver_pipeline Deploy to prod only from CI, as a service principal (lesson A10-L3). A team manages its jobs in the UI. Someone changes the production silver job's notebook path to test a branch, meaning to change it back. They forget. For a week, production runs a half-finished branch. Nobody can say what changed or when, because the UI keeps no diff and nothing was reviewed. With the job in a bundle, the path is a line in databricks.yml. Changing it needs a pull request, CI validates it, and Git shows exactly what changed. One reviewed file describes the job for every environment. The target decides where it writes.
lessons.title: Declarative Automation Bundles and parameterised jobs

lessons.text: Continuous integration (CI) runs the same checks on every change, before a human reviews it. For a Databricks pipeline repository, run four checks on each pull request: Lint and format: ruff check . and ruff format --check . Type-check: mypy Unit tests: pytest, with a local SparkSession (lesson A9-L2). Install Java in the CI runner first. Bundle validation: databricks bundle validate -t dev. It catches YAML errors and broken references before anything is deployed. On merge to main, a separate job deploys: databricks bundle deploy -t prod. Only CI deploys to production, and it does so as a service principal, never as a person. Authenticating CI. Databricks recommends OAuth machine-to-machine authentication for a service principal. The CLI reads the workspace and credentials from environment variables, filled from the CI system's secret store: env: DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ vars.DATABRICKS_HOST }} DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID }} DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET }} Workload identity federation goes a step further: with DATABRICKS_AUTH_TYPE: github-oidc, GitHub proves the workflow's identity, and no client secret is stored at all. Prefer it where your workspace supports it. Two rules keep CI trustworthy: CI must be able to fail. A test step with continue-on-error: true, or a true after a command, reports success whatever happens. Protect main. Require the CI checks to pass before a pull request can merge. Otherwise CI only reports problems, and nothing stops them. Install the CLI with the databricks/setup-cli action, and pin its version so a CLI release cannot change your pipeline's behaviour overnight. A team adds CI but marks the test step continue-on-error: true "until the flaky tests are fixed". Six weeks later, every pull request shows a green tick. A change that breaks the silver MERGE key merges on a Friday. The failing test had run and failed, but the step's failure no longer failed the job. Production double-counts a wave over the weekend. With the test step allowed to fail and main protected by required checks, the pull request could not have merged. Every pull request is linted, typed, tested and validated. Only a merge to main deploys, as a service principal, with nothing secret in the file. The CLI version shown is an example: pin the version you tested.
lessons.title: CI: lint, type-check, test and validate on every pull request

lessons.text: This track assumes you can read and write everyday Python 3.11 or later. Here is the core it relies on. Values and collections. Numbers are int or float, text is str, and True and False are bool. None means "no value". A list holds items in order, [1.5, 2.0]. A dict maps keys to values, {"R1": 1.5, "R2": 2.0}. A tuple is a fixed group, such as (lower, upper). Functions take inputs and return a result. Type hints say what goes in and out, and a docstring says what the function does: def mean_weight(weights: list[float]) -> float None: """Average weight, or None for an empty list.""" if not weights: return None return sum(weights) / len(weights) Loops and comprehensions. for rid, w in weights.items(): walks through a dict's keys and values together. A comprehension builds a new list in one line: [w for w in weights if w > 0]. f-strings put values into text: f"{name}: {share:.1%}" prints North: 12.5%. The part after the colon sets the format. Truthiness. In an if, Python treats 0, 0.0, "", empty collections and None as false. That is handy for "is this list empty?", and dangerous for numbers. A share of 0.0 is real data, so test for a missing value with is None, never with if not share. Errors. raise ValueError("negative weight for R2") stops the function with a message. try: ... except ValueError: catches it where you can handle it. Raise early, with a message that names the bad input. Imports. import math or from pathlib import Path bring in standard library modules. Install other packages, such as pandas, with pip (lesson B1-L2). A brand tracker counted brands "with no data" using if not share:. Brands with a real 0% share counted as missing, so the report said 14 brands lacked data when only 9 did. The client asked why five brands had vanished from the chart. One is None fixed both the count and the chart. Put logic in typed functions that return results, use comprehensions to filter, and test for missing values with is None.
lessons.title: Python essentials for data work
lessons.where: B0 Start here: foundations for data science

lessons.text: pandas holds tables as DataFrames: named columns over a row index. One column is a Series. The examples use pandas 3.0, where text columns get the str dtype. import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv("respondents.csv") Select columns. df["w"] returns one column as a Series. df[["id", "w"]] returns a smaller DataFrame. Filter rows. A comparison on a column gives a Series of True and False, a mask. Indexing with it keeps the True rows: df[df["w"] > 0]. Combine masks with & (and), (or) and ~ (not), and put each condition in brackets: df[(df["w"] > 0) & df["in_scope"]]. Python's and raises an error on a Series. Add columns. df.assign(w2=df["w"] * 2) returns a new DataFrame with the extra column and leaves df unchanged. Missing values show as NaN or <NA>. df["w"].isna() marks them. sum() and mean() skip them. Group and summarise. df.groupby("region")["w"].sum() adds up the weights per region. For several results at once, name each one: df.groupby("region", as_index=False).agg( n=("w", "size"), # rows, missing or not recorded=("w", "count"), # non-missing values total=("w", "sum"), ) as_index=False keeps region as a normal column. Join tables. df.merge(regions, on="region_code", how="left") adds the columns of regions to every row of df. how="left" keeps rows with no match, filling the new columns with missing values. The default, how="inner", drops them. Tidy the result. sort_values("region") orders rows, and reset_index(drop=True) renumbers them 0, 1, 2. An analyst joined respondents to a region lookup with the default inner merge. 312 respondents had a region code missing from the lookup, and they disappeared from every regional table without an error. The national total no longer matched the sum of the regions. A left merge, followed by a count of rows with a missing region, shows the problem in one line. Filter with bracketed masks, summarise with groupby and named aggregations, and merge with how="left" when every row must survive.
lessons.title: pandas essentials
lessons.where: B0 Start here: foundations for data science

lessons.text: Survey and model results are estimates from a sample, used to say something about a population. Five ideas carry most of this track. Mean and spread. The mean is the average. The standard deviation (SD) measures how far values sit from it. The sample SD divides by n - 1. Watch the defaults: NumPy 2's np.std(x) divides by n, while pandas 3's Series.std() divides by n - 1. For [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9] they give 2.0 and 2.138. Standard error (SE). Another sample would give a slightly different estimate. The SE says by how much, on average: for a mean: SD / sqrt(n), for a share p: sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n). A share of 50% from 1,000 people has an SE of about 0.0158, 1.6 points. Four times the sample halves the SE. Confidence interval. A 95% interval is roughly the estimate plus or minus 1.96 SEs: 50% plus or minus 3.1 points. Lesson B8-L2 shows better intervals for small samples and shares near 0 or 100%. p-value. It is the probability of a difference at least as large as the one you saw, if there were no true difference. It is not the probability that your hypothesis is true. A p-value of 0.03 means "this would be unusual if nothing were going on", nothing more. Effect size. A tiny difference becomes "significant" in a huge sample. Always report how big the difference is, with its interval, next to any p-value. Survey weights change all of these. Lesson B8-L1 shows how. A monthly report flagged every brand whose awareness changed with p < 0.05.
