With 20,000 respondents a month, a change of 0.6 points was "significant", and the client reacted to noise-sized moves that no campaign could explain. Reporting each change with its interval, and agreeing in advance on the smallest change worth acting on, ended the false alarms. Report an estimate with its standard error or interval, know which SD your library computes, and read a p-value for what it is.
lessons.title: The statistics you need for this track
lessons.where: B0 Start here: foundations for data science

lessons.text: A data science project starts as a notebook and a CSV. By month three it has helper modules, tests, a model, and three people asking how to run it. The fix is structure from day one. pyproject.toml is the one configuration file for a modern Python project. It holds: [project]: name, version, requires-python, and runtime dependencies. [dependency-groups] (PEP 735): named groups for development only, such as test or lint. They never ship with the package. Install one with pip install --group test (pip 25.1 and later). [tool.*] tables for tools: [tool.ruff], [tool.mypy], [tool.pytest.ini_options]. One file replaces setup.py, requirements.txt, setup.cfg, .flake8 and pytest.ini. The src layout puts importable code under src/: reach_model/ ├── pyproject.toml ├── src/reach_model/ # importable package │ ├── init.py │ ├── features.py │ └── train.py ├── tests/ # pytest, imports reach_model ├── notebooks/ # exploration; imports reach_model, holds no logic └── data/ # small samples only; real data stays out of Git With src/, Python can only import your package after you install it (pip install -e .). Tests then run against the installed package, exactly as a user or a job would. Without it, tests silently import whatever sits in the working directory, and "works on my machine" follows. Notebooks explore and present. Functions that matter move into src/, where tests and type checks reach them. A notebook that defines the feature pipeline inline cannot be tested or reused by the training job. Pin requires-python to the versions you test, for example ">=3.11", so pip refuses an interpreter you never tried. A team trains a churn model from train.ipynb, which defines build_features() in a cell. The scoring job copies the function into score.py. A month later someone fixes a leakage bug in the notebook version only. Training and scoring now compute features differently, and live accuracy drops 9 points while offline metrics look fine. With build_features() in src/churn/features.py, imported by both the notebook and the job, one fix reaches both, and one test protects it. Logic lives once, in an installable package. Notebooks, jobs and tests import it.
lessons.title: One pyproject.toml and a src layout

lessons.text: A virtual environment is a folder with its own Python interpreter link and its own site-packages. Packages you install there do not touch the system Python or any other project. python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -e . --group dev Rules that prevent most "it worked yesterday" problems: One environment per project. Two projects that share an environment share their version conflicts. Upgrading pandas for one breaks the other. Never install into the system Python. Operating systems and other tools depend on it. Use python -m pip, not bare pip. Bare pip runs whichever pip comes first on your PATH, which may belong to a different interpreter. python -m pip always installs into the interpreter you are about to run. Keep .venv/ out of Git. It is large, machine-specific and rebuildable. Commit pyproject.toml and a lock file instead (lesson B6-L3). In code, sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is True inside a virtual environment. A script that must not run against the system Python can check it and stop. Sometimes one project needs two environments, because two dependencies cannot live together. A real case from this course's own build: PySpark 4.0.4 fails to import its pandas integration with pandas 3.x, so the Spark test harness runs in its own environment pinned to pandas 2.x, while the rest uses pandas 3. Separate environments, each fully pinned, beat one environment held together by guesswork. Tools such as uv create and sync environments much faster, and conda manages non-Python libraries. The principles are the same. An analyst runs pip install statsmodels in a terminal, then python analysis.py in the same terminal, and gets ModuleNotFoundError. pip belonged to one Python, and python to another. They try sudo pip install, which upgrades NumPy in the system Python and breaks a command-line tool the operating system uses. Two hours are gone. python -m venv .venv, activation, and python -m pip install make the interpreter that installs and the interpreter that runs the same one. One environment per project, created from pyproject.toml, with python -m pip so installing and running use the same interpreter.
lessons.title: One virtual environment per project, and python -m pip

lessons.text: Two tools catch most mistakes before a test runs. ruff lints and formats. On a ten-line sample it reported three real problems: m.py:1:1: I001 [*] Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted m.py:1:8: F401 [*] os imported but unused m.py:9:30: B905 zip() without an explicit strict= parameter B905 matters for data work: zip(flags, weights) silently stops at the shorter list, so a missing weight drops a respondent without an error. zip(..., strict=True) raises instead. mypy checks types. On the same file, strict mode found: m.py:14: error: Unsupported operand types for * ("None" and "int") [operator] m.py:17: error: Function is missing a type annotation [no-untyped-def] Line 14 multiplies a float None by 100. When the total weight is zero, the function returns None and the report crashes. mypy found the zero-weight bug without any test data. Daily habits: Configure both once in pyproject.toml ([tool.ruff] with the rule sets you want, [tool.mypy] with strict = true). Run ruff check --fix . and ruff format . before each commit. --fix applies only safe fixes. Run mypy on src/ and tests/. Fix errors by handling the case, not by adding # type: ignore. Run the same commands in CI (lesson A10-L3), so the rules are not optional. Libraries without type information show import-untyped or missing-stub notes. Install the stub package if one exists, or add a targeted [[tool.mypy.overrides]] with ignore_missing_imports = true for that module only. A reporting script formats a weighted share as f"{share * 100:.1f}%". For eleven months every subgroup has respondents. Then a new region with no fieldwork yet appears in the sample frame, its total weight is zero, weighted_share returns None, and the monthly client pack fails to build on deadline day. mypy flags None * 100 the first time it runs on the file. The fix is two lines, written months before the failure. ruff and mypy found an unused import, a silent truncation and a crash on zero weight, before anyone wrote a test.
lessons.title: ruff and mypy in daily work

lessons.text: A pure function returns a value that depends only on its arguments, and changes nothing outside itself: no file writes, no global variables, no mutation of the inputs, no printing, no clock or random calls it does not receive. def weighted_mean(values: list[float], weights: list[float]) -> float: return sum(v * w for v, w in zip(values, weights, strict=True)) / sum(weights) Pure functions are easy to test (inputs in, answer out), safe to reuse, and safe to run twice. Most analysis logic can be pure: cleaning, feature building, statistics, scoring. Some work is not pure by nature: reading files, calling APIs, writing tables, logging, reading the clock. Push that work to the edges of the program, into a thin layer that gathers inputs, calls the pure core, and writes results. read (impure) -> transform, compute (pure) -> write (impure) Three side effects hide easily in data code: Mutating an argument. df["x"] = ... or rows.append(...) inside a function changes the caller's object. The caller did not ask for that. Return a new object instead: df.assign(x=...), or build a new list. Reading globals. A function that reads a module-level THRESHOLD or TODAY gives different answers after someone changes it. Pass it in. Hidden time and randomness. datetime.now() or np.random.rand() inside a function makes its output untestable. Pass a date, or a numpy.random.Generator. In pandas 3, Copy-on-Write is always on, so many operations already return new objects. Assigning a column with df[col] = ... still changes df itself, which is exactly the mutation to keep out of shared functions. A feature function adds age_group to the DataFrame it receives, in place. The training script calls it, then passes the same DataFrame to a stratified split on age_group. Later, someone reorders the calls so the split runs first. The split fails with a KeyError on one laptop and works on another, depending on which notebook cells ran before. A pure add_age_group(df) -> DataFrame that returns a new frame gives the same result in every order, and its test needs three rows. The pure core is tested with three rows and a fixed year. The edge is a few lines that are easy to read.
lessons.title: Pure functions, side effects at the edges

lessons.text: Analysis code needs settings: a minimum base size, a weight column, a list of waves. Passing them around as a loose dict has three costs. A typo in a key ("min_bse") fails late or not at all. Nothing states which keys exist. Any function can change a value half way through a run. A dataclass (Python 3.7 and later) turns the settings into a named, typed object. from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass(frozen=True) class ReportConfig: weight_col: str min_base: int = 50 waves: tuple[str, ...] = () def post_init(self) -> None: if self.min_base <= 0: raise ValueError(f"min_base must be positive, got {self.min_base}") What you get: Named fields. cfg.min_bse raises AttributeError at once. Your editor and mypy see the fields. frozen=True. Assigning a field raises dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError. Settings stay fixed for the run. Use dataclasses.replace(cfg, min_base=30) to build a changed copy. post_init. Runs after the generated init. Put checks here so a bad config fails at load time, not in hour three. Two traps: Type hints are not checked at runtime. ReportConfig(weight_col="w", min_base="30") builds without error. Convert or check types in post_init, or use pydantic (lesson B5-L2) when input comes from files. Mutable defaults. waves: list[str] = [] raises ValueError when the class is defined. Use field(default_factory=list), or an immutable tuple. Load the config once at the edge, from YAML, JSON or arguments, and pass the object to the pure core. A weighting script reads config["min_base"] from a dict built in a notebook cell. An analyst edits the cell to config["minbase"] = 30 for a test and forgets to revert. The script keeps using the old default of 50, so 14 subgroups the client asked to see are suppressed in the published tables. Nobody notices for two waves. With a frozen dataclass, ReportConfig(minbase=30) raises TypeError: unexpected keyword argument at the first run. A frozen dataclass names every setting, rejects unknown ones, and checks values once, when you build it.
lessons.title: Dataclasses as configuration objects

lessons.text: Python does not require classes. Many data science classes are functions in disguise: an init that stores arguments, and one method that uses them. class Normaliser: def init(self, col): self.col = col def run(self, df): return df.assign(**{self.col: df[self.col] / df[self.col].sum()}) Every caller writes Normaliser("spend").run(df). A function, normalise(df, col), says the same thing in one call, with nothing to construct. A class earns its place when at least one of these holds: State that outlives one call. A weighting model learns targets in fit and applies them in transform. scikit-learn's StandardScaler stores mean_ and scale_ between the two calls. An invariant to protect. A Weights object guarantees values are positive and sum to the sample size. Code that builds one through its constructor cannot break that rule. Several operations on the same data. A SurveyDesign with mean(), ci() and subgroup() that all need weights, strata and clusters. A shared interface. Several classes with the same method, such as load(), so the caller swaps one for another. Settings with no behaviour belong in a dataclass (lesson B2-L2). A single step belongs in a function (lesson B2-L1). Test a design by asking: if you delete the class and keep its methods as functions, what breaks? If nothing, keep the functions. A team wraps each cleaning step in a class: DropDuplicates, FixDates, RenameColumns, each with init and run. A new analyst adds a self.seen_ids set to DropDuplicates to speed up a second call. The pipeline object is reused across two tracker waves, so wave 2 silently drops every respondent who also took part in wave 1: 38% of the sample. Pure functions have no self to keep stale state between calls. Functions by default. A class when state lives across calls, an invariant needs guarding, or several methods share the same data.
lessons.title: When a class earns its place

lessons.text: Every pandas column has a dtype. The wrong dtype gives wrong answers without an error: IDs that lose leading zeros, counts that turn into floats, text that sorts as numbers. Three facts about pandas 3.0: Text columns default to the str dtype. pd.Series(["a", None]).dtype prints str, not object. Missing values in it are NaN. Only strings are allowed, so a stray integer no longer hides in a text column. A missing value turns an integer column into float64, unless you ask for a nullable dtype. pd.Series([1, None]) is float64. pd.Series([1, None], dtype="Int64") keeps integers and shows the gap as <NA>. Setting a value that does not fit raises. Assigning 1.5 into an int64 Series raises TypeError instead of silently upcasting the column. (Assigning NaN still upcasts to float64.) The capital letter matters. int64 is NumPy's integer with no missing values. Int64, Float64 and boolean are pandas nullable dtypes that hold pd.NA. Set dtypes where data enters, not later: df = pd.read_csv( path, dtype={"respondent_id": "str", "postcode": "str", "household_size": "Int64"}, ) Without the dtype map, read_csv reads a postcode such as 01234 as the number 1234.0 once any row is blank. With it, "01234" stays a string. Check the result with df.dtypes right after loading. df.convert_dtypes() switches every column to the nullable equivalents in one call, useful for exploration. An explicit map is better in pipelines, because it fails loudly when the source changes. A panel file stores respondent IDs such as 00731. One wave has a blank ID row, so read_csv infers float64 and the ID becomes 731.0. The join to the previous wave, where IDs were read as text, matches nothing. The longitudinal report shows 0% retention for a panel that kept 82% of its members. dtype={"respondent_id": "str"} at load time keeps 00731 as written in every wave. Decide dtypes at load time. IDs and codes as str, counts with gaps as Int64.
lessons.title: Dtypes in pandas 3, nullable and string

lessons.text: pandas stores each column as an array. A vectorised operation, such as df["a"] * df["b"], np.where() or pd.cut(), runs one compiled loop over the whole array. df.apply(func, axis=1) does the opposite. It builds a Series for each row and calls your Python function once per row. The gap is large. On one million rows, a row-wise apply that picks a weight when a flag is set took 4.0 seconds. np.where did the same job in 7.5 milliseconds, about 500 times faster. (pandas 3.0.6, NumPy 2.4.6, one laptop core.) Speed is not the only gain. Vectorised code states the rule for the whole column in one line, so a reviewer checks one expression instead of a branching function. Reach for these first: Task Vectorised tool Arithmetic between columns +, -, *, / on Series Two-way choice np.where(cond, a, b) Many-way choice np.select(conditions, choices, default) Numeric bands pd.cut(values, bins, labels, right=False) Lookup from a dict Series.map(mapping) Limits Series.clip(lower, upper) Watch missing values. NaN > 60 is False, so np.where(minutes > 60, "heavy", "light") labels a missing value "light". Handle missing values on purpose: pd.cut keeps NaN as missing, and Series.where(values.notna()) puts it back after np.where. Keep apply for work with no vectorised form, such as calling an external parser on each string. Even then, try Series.map or a list comprehension on one column before apply(axis=1). A weighting script derives 25 columns with apply(axis=1). It ran in 8 minutes on 2 million rows, so nobody noticed. The programme then merged three trackers into one file of 40 million rows. At the measured rate of about 4 seconds per million rows per column, the derivations alone need roughly 67 minutes. The job hit its 60-minute timeout every night for a week, and weighted results for all three trackers were late. The same script also labelled respondents with a missing minutes value as "light" viewers, because the row function used if row["minutes"] > 60. The vectorised rewrite fixed the speed, and review of the one-line rule exposed the missing-value bug. The strong version is shorter, about 500 times faster on large frames, and handles missing ages on purpose.
lessons.title: Vectorise instead of apply

lessons.text: Copy-on-Write (CoW) is always on in pandas 3.0. Every indexing result, such as df[cols], df[mask] or df["a"], behaves as a separate object. Changing it never changes df. pandas copies data only when you write to a shared object, so reads stay cheap. One consequence: chained assignment never works. df[df["age"] < 18]["weight"] = 0 # df unchanged, ChainedAssignmentError warning df.loc[df["age"] < 18, "weight"] = 0 # one step: df changed The first line writes to a temporary copy, which Python then discards. pandas 3 emits a ChainedAssignmentError warning, but the code keeps running. SettingWithCopyWarning no longer exists. CoW rewards a second habit: method chaining. Build the result as one expression of steps that each return a new frame. result = ( raw .rename(columns=COLUMN_MAP) .loc[lambda d: d["age"] >= 18] .assign(weight=lambda d: d["weight"].clip(upper=5.0)) .pipe(add_age_band, bins=BINS, labels=LABELS) ) assign(col=lambda d: ...) refers to the frame at that step, not the original raw. .loc[lambda d: ...] filters on the current step. .pipe(func, **kwargs) calls your own pure function (lesson B2-L1) inside the chain. Chains read top to bottom, leave no half-finished variables (df2, df_tmp, df_final) in the namespace, and do not mutate the input. Keep each chain to about ten steps. Split longer ones into named functions and join them with pipe. To debug a chain, comment out steps from the bottom up, or add .pipe(lambda d: print(d.shape) or d) between steps. An analyst caps extreme weights with df[df["weight"] > 5]["weight"] = 5. On pandas 2 it printed a SettingWithCopyWarning that everyone had learned to ignore. The weights were never capped. Three respondents with weights above 12 moved the reported brand share by 4 points. After the upgrade to pandas 3 the assignment still does nothing, with a different warning. df.assign(weight=df["weight"].clip(upper=5.0)) or a single df.loc[mask, "weight"] = 5 does what the analyst meant. Under Copy-on-Write, write with .loc in one step, or better, build a new frame with a chain of assign, loc and pipe.
lessons.title: Method chaining and Copy-on-Write

lessons.text: Polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust. It runs on all your cores and has no row index. You describe work with expressions: pl.col("weight").sum() is a recipe, not a result. Polars runs it inside a context. import polars as pl shares = ( df.group_by("wave", "brand") .agg(pl.col("weight").sum().alias("brand_weight")) .with_columns(total=pl.col("brand_weight").sum().over("wave")) ) select returns only the expressions you list. with_columns adds or replaces columns. filter keeps rows. group_by(...).agg(...) aggregates. .over("wave") computes a group total and broadcasts it back to each row, like a window function in SQL. pl.when(...).then(...).otherwise(...) replaces np.where. Polars has two modes. A DataFrame runs each step at once. A LazyFrame, from df.lazy() or pl.scan_parquet(path), records the steps and runs nothing until .collect(). Before running, the optimiser rewrites the plan. It pushes filters down to the scan, so rows you drop are never read, and reads only the columns you use. lf.explain() prints the plan. Two behaviours to know (Polars 1.33): sum() of a group with only nulls returns 0, not null. Check null_count() before you trust a total. mean() skips nulls. sum() / pl.len() counts null rows in the denominator and gives a different answer. Use lazy mode for files. Scan, filter, select, aggregate, then collect once at the end. A weekly job reads a 9 GB Parquet extract with pl.read_parquet, then filters to the current wave. Memory peaks at 14 GB and the job fails on a 16 GB runner on the week the extract grows. pl.scan_parquet(path).filter(pl.col("wave") == wave).select(cols).collect() lets Polars skip other waves' row groups and unused columns at read time, so memory scales with one wave, not the whole file. Scan lazily, filter and select early, aggregate with expressions, and collect once.
lessons.title: Polars expressions and lazy frames

lessons.text: DuckDB is an analytical SQL database that runs inside your Python process. There is no server to install. It reads Parquet, CSV and JSON files directly, and it queries pandas and Polars DataFrames that are in scope. import duckdb con = duckdb.connect() # in-memory database rel = con.sql(""" SELECT wave, brand, sum(weight) AS total FROM read_parquet('extracts/*.parquet') GROUP BY wave, brand """) df = rel.df() # pandas; .pl() for Polars, .fetchall() for tuples A glob such as 'extracts/*.parquet' reads many files as one table. Filters and column lists are pushed down to the reader, as in Polars lazy mode. FROM responses finds a DataFrame variable named responses in the calling scope. con.register("responses", df) names it explicitly, which is clearer inside functions. Results come back as a relation. Nothing is materialised until you call .df(), .pl(), .fetchall() or .fetchone(). Pass values as parameters, never with f-strings. con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM responses WHERE wave = ?", [wave]) With f"... WHERE wave = '{wave}'", a value that holds a quote changes the query. In this course's own test, the input w1' or '1'='1 turned a filter for one wave into a count of every row. A ? placeholder (or $name with a dict) sends the value as data, so quotes cannot change the SQL. File paths and table names cannot be parameters. Check those against a list of allowed values. Create the connection at the edge of your program and pass con to functions. The module-level duckdb.sql() uses one shared default connection, a global that tests cannot replace. A dashboard helper built its filter with f"WHERE region = '{region}'". The region list came from a client file. One entry was Hawke's Bay. The apostrophe broke the SQL, and the job failed at 06:00 before the client's morning meeting. A second entry with a crafted value could have read other clients' rows. con.execute("... WHERE region = ?", [region]) handles Hawke's Bay as a plain string. One connection passed in, parameters for values, and a None check on aggregates.
lessons.title: DuckDB, SQL over files and DataFrames

lessons.text: All four tools answer the same questions. Pick by where the data lives and how big it is next to your memory, not by fashion. A measurement from this course's build: a group-by with sum and mean over 10 million rows and 1,000 groups, best of three runs on a 4-core machine. pandas 3.0.6 took 0.22 s, Polars 1.44 took 0.11 s, DuckDB 1.5 took 0.06 s. At this size every tool is fast enough. The choice matters when data outgrows memory. Situation Good default Data fits comfortably in memory, you need the scikit-learn, statsmodels or plotting ecosystem pandas Files larger than you want in memory, heavy transforms, one machine Polars lazy (scan_parquet) SQL is the clearest way to express it, or you join many files ad hoc DuckDB Data already in a lakehouse, or larger than one machine, or a scheduled production job Spark (Track A) The tools share the Apache Arrow memory format, so you mix them at the boundaries: lazy_result = pl.scan_parquet("extracts/*.parquet").filter(...).group_by(...).agg(...) summary = lazy_result.collect().to_pandas() # Polars to pandas for statsmodels rel = con.sql("SELECT ... FROM read_parquet('extracts/*.parquet')") top = rel.pl() # DuckDB to Polars Rules for mixing: Reduce first, convert last. Filter and aggregate in the engine that reads the files. Convert the small result. Watch the index. Polars has no index. pl.from_pandas(df) drops a pandas index unless you pass include_index=True, or call reset_index() first. Check dtypes after each hop. Text becomes str in pandas 3 and String in Polars. Nullable integers need care in both directions. One project, one primary engine. A second tool at a clear boundary is fine. Four tools in one function is not. An analyst sets respondent_id as the pandas index to deduplicate, then hands the frame to a Polars function for a fast join. pl.from_pandas drops the index. The join key is gone, so the analyst joins on row position with hstack. Two waves sorted differently, and 11% of respondents got another person's scores. pl.from_pandas(df.reset_index()) keeps the ID as a column, and the join uses it. One primary engine. Reduce where the data is read. Convert small results at a clear boundary.
lessons.title: Choosing pandas, Polars, DuckDB or Spark

lessons.text: A schema states what a DataFrame must look like: which columns exist, their dtypes, and rules on their values. pandera checks a pandas DataFrame against a schema and raises when it does not match. Examples here use pandera 0.33 with pandas 3. import pandera.pandas as pa RESPONSES = pa.DataFrameSchema( { "respondent_id": pa.Column(str, unique=True), "age": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.in_range(16, 99)), "weight": pa.Column(float, pa.Check.gt(0)), }, strict=True, coerce=True, ) clean = RESPONSES.validate(raw, lazy=True) pa.Column(dtype, checks, nullable=False) is the default: nulls fail unless you set nullable=True. unique=True rejects duplicate keys. strict=True rejects columns the schema does not name. coerce=True converts dtypes before checking. lazy=True collects every failure into one SchemaErrors exception. Its failure_cases attribute is a DataFrame with the column, check and failing value. Without lazy, validation stops at the first SchemaError. SchemaErrors is not a subclass of SchemaError. Catch both when you handle failures. A strict=True violation raises SchemaErrors even without lazy=True. The class syntax, pa.DataFrameModel, does the same with type hints. Add @pa.check_types to a function whose parameters are annotated DataFrame[Model], and pandera validates inputs and outputs on every call. Import from pandera.pandas. The plain import pandera still works in 0.33, but the pandas-specific module is the documented path. pandera does not run in this app's browser runtime. The exercises check your code's structure. Run pytest locally with the dev group to execute schemas for real. A supplier changes a weight export so that non-responders get weight 0 instead of being left out. The weighting script divides by the sum of weights per cell. Three cells now contain only zeros. The script writes NaN shares to the client dashboard, and nobody sees an error. pa.Column(float, pa.Check.gt(0)) on the input fails the run on day one, with the failing rows listed in failure_cases. A schema at the point of entry turns a silent bad input into one loud, detailed failure.
lessons.title: DataFrame schemas with pandera

lessons.text: A dataclass (lesson B2-L2) does not check types. pydantic does. A BaseModel validates and converts data when you build it, and raises one ValidationError that lists every problem. Examples use pydantic 2.12. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field class WeightingConfig(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", frozen=True) weight_col: str min_base: int = Field(default=50, gt=0) cap: float = Field(default=5.0, gt=1.0) cfg = WeightingConfig.model_validate(yaml.safe_load(text)) Field(gt=0, le=10) adds bounds. @field_validator("name") adds your own rule. extra="forbid" rejects unknown keys, so minbase: 30 in a YAML file fails instead of being ignored. The default, "ignore", drops them silently. frozen=True rejects assignment after construction. e.errors() returns a list of dicts with loc, type and msg. Log it as structured data. pydantic runs in lax mode by default. It converts "30" to 30 and 30.0 to 30, but rejects "thirty" and 30.5. It also converts True to 1 for an int field. Set ConfigDict(strict=True) when inputs must already have the right type. One gap: model_copy(update={...}) does not validate. cfg.model_copy(update={"min_base": -1}) returns a config with min_base = -1. To change a validated model, build a new one: WeightingConfig.model_validate({**cfg.model_dump(), "min_base": 30}). Use pydantic for records and settings that arrive from outside: YAML, JSON, API payloads. Use pandera (lesson B5-L1) for whole DataFrames. For a list of records, TypeAdapter(list[Model]).validate_python(rows) validates them in one call. A weighting config file had cap: 0.5 typed where 5 was meant, and minbase spelt without the underscore. The loader used a plain dict. The cap shrank every weight above 0.5 down to 0.5, which flattened the weighting, and min_base stayed at its default. The report went out with unweighted-looking results. WeightingConfig.model_validate with gt=1.0 and extra="forbid" rejects both mistakes in one error message, before any data is read. Validate external settings and records once, at the boundary, with every rule in the model.
lessons.title: pydantic models for config and input records

lessons.text: Validation belongs at boundaries, where data crosses from one owner to another: On the way in. After reading a file, API response or config. Check schema, keys and value ranges (lessons B5-L1 and B5-L2). On the way out. Before writing a table or sending a report. Check the promises you make to the next consumer: grain, row counts, totals, shares that sum to 1. Checks in the middle of a pure transformation add noise. A function that receives validated input and is unit tested does not need to re-check it. Not every failed check should stop a run. Give each check a severity: CRITICAL stops the run. Wrong grain, missing required column, empty input, weights that do not sum to the sample size. WARN records the problem and continues. Missing share above its usual level, a subgroup below its reporting base. Record results as structured data, not prose, so a dashboard or alert filters them: Severity = Literal["CRITICAL", "WARN"] @dataclass(frozen=True) class QaResult: check: str severity: Severity passed: bool observed: float None Run all checks, collect the results, log them, then raise if any CRITICAL check failed. The log keeps every result, even on the run that stops. Two coding rules make checks trustworthy: Guard every division. An empty input has no missing share. Return None, not a ZeroDivisionError. Test None with is None. if share: treats a real share of 0.0 like a missing one, and the check silently never runs. A tracker QA step printed "WARNING: low base in 3 cells" to the notebook output and carried on. Nobody reads notebook output for scheduled jobs. The same step never checked for an empty input. The week a supplier delivered an empty file, the job computed shares from zero rows, divided by zero, and wrote NaN to every cell of the client dashboard. Structured results in a table get alerts. A CRITICAL min_rows check stops the run before the empty file reaches the dashboard. Check at boundaries. Collect structured results. Log them all, then stop on CRITICAL.
lessons.title: Validate at the boundaries, with severity

lessons.text: A result you cannot rerun is a result you cannot defend. Randomness enters analysis through sampling, train/test splits, bootstrap intervals, model initialisation and synthetic data. Control each source. Create a generator and pass it in. NumPy 1.17 introduced numpy.random.Generator. Examples use NumPy 2.4. rng = np.random.default_rng(20260925) # at the edge, once sample = draw_sample(ids, k=500, rng=rng) # the function receives rng np.random.default_rng(seed) gives the same stream of numbers for the same seed, on every run and machine with the same NumPy version. Functions take rng: np.random.Generator as a parameter. They never call np.random.seed() or the legacy np.random.rand(), which share one hidden global state across your whole program and every library you import. One generator, used twice, gives two different draws. That is correct: two samples should differ. Rerunning the whole script gives the same pair. Need independent streams for parallel workers? rng.spawn(n) returns n child generators. Libraries take the seed or generator as a parameter too: train_test_split(..., random_state=42) in scikit-learn, df.sample(n, random_state=rng) in pandas. Two hidden sources of non-determinism: hash() on strings changes between Python processes (hash randomisation, PYTHONHASHSEED). hash(respondent_id) % 10 puts the same respondent in a different bucket on each run. Use hashlib.sha256 for stable buckets. Set iteration order for strings also changes between runs. Sort before you rely on order. Record the seed in the run log with the results, so anyone reruns the exact analysis. A holdout set was defined as hash(respondent_id) % 10 == 0. The model scored AUC 0.81 in the notebook. The scheduled retraining job, a new Python process, put a different 10% in the holdout. Some of the old test respondents were now in training, and the reported AUC rose to 0.84 with no change to the model. The team spent a week chasing an improvement that did not exist. A bucket from hashlib.sha256 of the ID is the same in every process. Seed once at the edge, pass the generator in, and never use hash() for anything that must be stable.
lessons.title: Seeds and random generators

lessons.text: To rerun a result you need three things exactly as they were: the data, the config and the code. Record all three with every run, in a small run manifest. manifest = { "run_id": run_id, "started_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), "input_sha256": file_sha256(input_path), "config_sha256": config_sha256(config), "git_commit": git_commit, "seed": seed, "packages": {"pandas": version("pandas"), "numpy": version("numpy")}, } Data. A file name and a date do not identify content. Suppliers resend files under the same name. A content hash does: hashlib.sha256 over the file bytes changes if any byte changes. hashlib.file_digest(f, "sha256") (Python 3.11 and later) reads the file in chunks, so large files do not load into memory. Keep raw inputs immutable: write each delivery to a new path and never overwrite it. For lakehouse tables, record the Delta table version instead (lesson A3-L3). Config. Hash the config you loaded, not the file on disk, so defaults count. Serialise with json.dumps(config, sort_keys=True) first. Without sort_keys, the same settings in a different key order give a different hash. Code. Record the Git commit. Refuse to produce client output from a working tree with uncommitted changes, or record that it was dirty. Environment. importlib.metadata.version("pandas") returns the installed version. The lock file (lesson B6-L3) covers the rest. Store the manifest next to the output, or as a row in a run log table. When someone asks "why did this number change?", compare two manifests. The field that differs is where to look. A client queried a brand share that moved 3 points between two versions of the same wave's report. The analysis folder held wave12.csv, the config and the notebook, all edited since. Nobody knew whether the supplier had resent the file, a setting had changed, or the code had. Reconstructing the answer took four days. With manifests, the two runs differed in one field: input_sha256. The supplier had resent the file with 212 late completes. Hash the input and the loaded config, record the commit and the seed, and store the manifest with the output.
lessons.title: Record the data, config and code behind every result

lessons.text: pyproject.toml states what your project accepts: pandas>=3.0,<4. A lock file records what was installed: pandas 3.0.6, numpy 2.4.6, and every indirect dependency, each with a file hash. You need both. The ranges in pyproject.toml say which versions your code supports. Keep them honest: a lower bound you have tested, an upper bound at the next major version when the library breaks things across majors. The lock file makes every install identical: your laptop, a colleague's, CI and the scheduled job. Commit it. With uv (examples use uv 0.8): uv lock # resolve pyproject.toml ranges, write uv.lock uv sync --locked # install exactly uv.lock; fail if it is out of date uv lock --upgrade-package pandas # move one package on purpose uv sync --locked exits with an error when pyproject.toml has changed since the lock was written: "The lockfile at uv.lock needs to be updated, but --locked was provided." Use it in CI, so a dependency change without a new lock fails the build instead of resolving something new on the runner. Without uv, pip-compile --generate-hashes (pip-tools) writes a fully pinned requirements.txt with hashes, and pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt refuses any file whose hash differs. pip freeze > requirements.txt is a weaker substitute. It lists what happens to be in your environment, including packages you installed by hand for a one-off test, with no hashes and no record of why each is there. Upgrade on purpose: one dependency at a time, on a branch, with tests. Record the reason in the commit message. Never let a fresh install pick up new versions silently. A forecasting job ran on a fresh container every night. requirements.txt said pandas>=2.0. The night pandas 3.0 was released, the container installed it. The job's text columns switched to the new str dtype, a .str.contains call behaved differently on missing values, and the job filtered out 6% of rows. Nobody had changed a line of code. A committed lock file, installed with uv sync --locked, keeps the old pandas until someone upgrades it deliberately, with tests. Ranges in pyproject.toml, exact versions and hashes in a committed lock file, and --locked in CI.
lessons.title: Pinned dependencies and lock files

lessons.text: Before any chart or model, answer five questions about a new dataset. Each takes one line of pandas, and each catches a class of error that no later step will. Shape and grain. How many rows, and what does one row mean? Check the claimed key is unique: df.duplicated(subset=["respondent_id", "wave"]).sum() should be 0. Dtypes. df.dtypes. IDs read as floats, dates as text and numbers as str all show here (lesson B3-L1). Missingness. df.isna().mean() gives the share missing per column. Look for columns that are nearly empty, and for shares that differ by wave or region. Cardinality. df.nunique(). A gender column with 14 distinct values holds typos. An ID column with fewer distinct values than rows holds duplicates. Ranges. df.describe(). Ages of 999, negative weights, and dates in 1900 are codes for "missing" or errors. Put the per-column answers in one table: def profile(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame: return pd.DataFrame({ "dtype": df.dtypes.astype(str), "missing_share": df.isna().mean(), "n_unique": df.nunique(), }) Two pandas defaults to know (pandas 3.0): nunique() excludes missing values. Pass dropna=False to count NaN as a value. duplicated() marks every repeat except the first (keep="first"). To count every row involved in a duplicate, use keep=False. Save the profile with the analysis. When the next delivery arrives, compare the two profiles. A column whose missing share jumps from 2% to 40% tells you something changed at the source before it changes your results. Libraries such as ydata-profiling build long HTML reports. They are useful for a first look. The five checks above, in code, are what you rerun on every delivery. A satisfaction score was coded 1 to 10, with 99 for "don't know". Nobody profiled the file. The mean score for one region came out at 14.2, above the maximum possible value. The analyst assumed a weighting problem and spent a day on the weights. describe() would have shown a maximum of 99 in the first minute. Shape and grain, dtypes, missingness, cardinality and ranges, in code, before any analysis.
lessons.title: Profile a dataset before you analyse it

lessons.text: Summary statistics hide shape. Anscombe's quartet (1973) is four small datasets with the same means, variances and correlation. Computed in this course's build for the first three: Set mean of y variance of y correlation with x I 7.50 4.13 0.816 II 7.50 4.13 0.816 III 7.50 4.12 0.816 Plotted, set I is a noisy line, set II is a curve, and set III is a perfect line with one outlier. The numbers alone cannot tell them apart. Four plots catch most problems: Histogram of each key numeric column. Shows skew, gaps, spikes at codes such as 99 or 0, and more than one peak. Scatter plot of each pair you will model or correlate. Shows curves, clusters and single points that drive a correlation. Line over time of counts and key rates by wave. Shows breaks in the series when a questionnaire or supplier changed. Bar chart of missingness by column and by subgroup. Make each plot honest: Label both axes with units, and give every figure a title that states what it shows. Choose histogram bins on purpose. Too few hide a spike at 99. Try two or three bin counts. Use a log scale for heavily skewed values such as spend, and say so on the axis. Plot the raw data before you plot the smoothed or aggregated version. Write plotting code as functions that return a matplotlib.figure.Figure (matplotlib 3.10). Build with fig, ax = plt.subplots(), not the global plt.plot() state. A function that returns a figure is testable: a test reads ax.get_xlabel() or counts the bars. The caller decides whether to show it or save it. A team reported a correlation of 0.62 between ad recall and purchase intent across 40 markets, and the client planned a budget shift on it. A scatter plot showed 39 markets in a flat cloud and one market far in the top-right corner. Without that market the correlation was close to zero. The decision was about one market, not 40. Plot distributions, pairs and time series before summarising, with functions that return labelled figures.
lessons.title: Plot before you summarise

lessons.text: Every analysis rests on assumptions: what a row means, how "don't know" is coded, which respondents are in scope, that weights sum to the sample size. Unwritten, they live in one analyst's head and break silently when the data changes. Keep an assumptions log next to the analysis. One entry per assumption, with the same fields each time: id: A3 statement: "score uses 1 to 10; 98 = refused, 99 = don't know" evidence: "Questionnaire v4, Q12; profile of waves 1 to 11 shows only 1-10, 98, 99" handling: "98 and 99 become missing before any statistic" check: "score in 1..10 or missing, after recoding" owner: "analysis team" last_verified: 2026-09-01 Then make the assumption executable. The handling becomes code, and the check becomes a QA result (lesson B5-L3) that runs on every delivery. MISSING_CODES: dict[str, list[int]] = {"score": [98, 99]} # from config, per A3 def recode_missing(df: pd.DataFrame, codes: dict[str, list[int]]) -> pd.DataFrame: return df.assign(**{col: df[col].mask(df[col].isin(vals)) for col, vals in codes.items()}) Recode per column. df.replace(99, np.nan) on the whole frame also blanks a real age of 99. Series.mask(cond) sets values to missing where the condition holds and leaves the rest. Three kinds of assumption to write down every time: Structure. Grain, keys, which columns are required. Coding. Missing codes, scales, units, category lists. Scope. Who is included: age limits, completes only, which markets and waves. When a check fails, the log tells you which belief was wrong and who to ask. When a client asks "why is this respondent excluded?", the answer has an ID. An analyst knew that 99 meant "don't know" on the satisfaction scale and removed those rows by hand in a notebook. The analyst left. The next wave went through the scripted pipeline, which did not know. The regional mean rose from 7.1 to 11.4. It was published, because 11.4 looked like a large improvement rather than an impossible value on a 1 to 10 scale. A logged assumption with an executable check would have failed the run on the first 99. Log each assumption with evidence and owner, implement its handling per column, and check it on every run.
lessons.title: Write assumptions down, then turn them into checks

lessons.text: A survey sample rarely matches its population. If young adults are 20% of the population but 10% of your completes, each young respondent gets a larger weight so the weighted sample matches the population. The weighted mean divides by the sum of the weights, not by the row count: weighted_mean = (y * w).sum() / w.sum() # same as np.average(y, weights=w) Weights have a cost. Unequal weights make estimates less precise than the raw sample size suggests. Kish's effective sample size measures that cost: n_eff = w.sum() 2 / (w 2).sum() design_effect = n / n_eff Equal weights give n_eff = n. A sample of 5 with weights 0.5, 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 has n_eff = 2.98: it carries about as much information as three unweighted respondents. The design effect is 1.68. Rules that prevent the common mistakes: Use weights for population estimates: shares, means and totals you report as "UK adults". Use n_eff, not n, for precision: confidence intervals, significance tests and minimum base rules (lesson B8-L2). Report the unweighted base next to every weighted figure, so readers see how many people stand behind it. Drop rows where the value or the weight is missing before you compute. A missing weight is not zero, and a missing answer is not a zero answer. Guard the division. An empty subgroup or a zero weight total has no mean. Return None. Check weights before using them: all positive, none missing, and a sum equal to the sample size or the population total, whichever the weighting scheme promises. Extreme weights (above about 5 times the mean) are a warning sign. Trimming them is a design decision, logged as an assumption (lesson B7-L3). A brand tracker reported that awareness among 18 to 24s rose from 41% to 52%, "significant at 95%". The test used the 180 raw respondents in the group. Their weights were uneven, and the effective sample size was 71. With 71, the change was well inside the margin of error. The client moved budget on a result the data did not support. Weighted estimates divide by the weight total. Precision uses the effective sample size.
lessons.title: Survey weights and the effective sample size

lessons.text: A share without an interval is a guess with no stated size. Report every estimate with a confidence interval, and every difference with an effect size. Intervals for a proportion. The textbook Wald interval, p ± 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p)/n), fails at the edges. For 0 out of 20 it gives [0, 0], as if you were certain. The Wilson interval behaves well for small n and for shares near 0 or 1. For 0 out of 20 it gives [0, 0.161]. In statsmodels 0.14: from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint low, high = proportion_confint(count=40, nobs=100, alpha=0.05, method="wilson") # (0.309, 0.498) For a weighted share, use the weighted estimate and the effective sample size from lesson B8-L1 in the same formula. The 18 to 24 group from that lesson, with a weighted share of 52% and n_eff = 71, has a Wilson interval of 40.6% to 63.2%. With the raw 180 it would be 44.7% to 59.2%, which looks far more precise than the data is. Effect sizes. A p-value answers "is there any difference?", and with a large sample the answer is nearly always yes. Two groups of 100,000 with shares of 50.5% and 50.0% give p = 0.025, and the difference is too small to matter. State the size: The difference in shares, in percentage points, with its interval. This is what a client reads. Cohen's h, 2*asin(sqrt(p1)) - 2*asin(sqrt(p2)), compares differences across different base rates. Rough guides: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. For means, the difference with its interval, or Cohen's d (difference over pooled standard deviation). Decide before the analysis what size of difference matters for the decision. A significant difference below that size is reported as "no meaningful change". A retailer's panel of 90,000 customers showed satisfaction at 7.62 against 7.58 the previous quarter, p = 0.01. The headline read "Satisfaction significantly up". The store managers' bonus scheme was tied to "significant improvement", and bonuses were paid. The change was 0.04 points on a 10-point scale, smaller than the rounding in the published chart. Wilson intervals with n_eff for weighted shares, and an effect size beside every p-value.
lessons.title: Confidence intervals and effect sizes

lessons.text: At a 5% significance level, each test of a true null hypothesis has a 5% chance of a false positive. Run 20 such tests and the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95**20 = 0.64. A simulation in this course's build agreed: 20 t-tests on pure noise, repeated 2,000 times, gave at least one "significant" result 66% of the time. Survey reports run many tests by default: every brand, every region, every age band, every wave. Some cells will light up by chance every time. Adjust the p-values for the number of tests in the family. In statsmodels 0.14: from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests reject, p_adj, _, _ = multipletests(p_values, alpha=0.05, method="holm") Bonferroni multiplies each p-value by the number of tests m. Simple and strict. Holm is a step-down version of Bonferroni. It controls the same error (any false positive in the family) and always rejects at least as many hypotheses. Prefer it to Bonferroni. Benjamini-Hochberg (method="fdr_bh") controls the false discovery rate: the expected share of false positives among the results you flag. It is less strict and suits screening many cells for follow-up. For p-values 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.04 and 0.20, Bonferroni and Holm reject only the first. Benjamini-Hochberg rejects the first four. Define the family before you look: "the 12 regional comparisons in this chart". Adjust within it. Choosing the family after seeing the results defeats the point. Two habits that reduce the problem at the source: Pre-register the few comparisons that answer the business question. Test those. Label the rest as exploratory. Report how many tests you ran. "3 of 40 regions changed significantly" reads very differently from "Region 7 changed significantly". A monthly tracker tested 14 brands in 9 regions, 126 tests, each at 5%. Every month about six cells were flagged in red on the dashboard. Regional managers were asked to explain their red cells. The following month, different cells turned red. Nobody could explain the pattern, because there was none: 126 tests at 5% produce about six false positives by chance. Holm adjustment within each brand's family of 9 regions removed nearly all the monthly red cells. The few that remained repeated in the next month. Define the family first, adjust within it with Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg, and report how many tests ran.
lessons.title: Many tests, and the false positives they bring

lessons.text: A test with too few people cannot see the effect you care about. It returns "no significant difference", and the team concludes the change did nothing. Decide the sample size before fieldwork, from four inputs: Baseline: the current rate, for example 40% consideration. Minimum detectable effect (MDE): the smallest change worth acting on, for example 5 points, to 45%. Significance level (alpha): usually 0.05, two-sided. Power: the chance of detecting the MDE if it is real. Usually 0.8. For two proportions, the sample per group is: z_a = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2) z_b = NormalDist().inv_cdf(power) p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2 n = ((z_a * sqrt(2 * p_bar * (1 - p_bar)) + z_b * sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2))) / (p2 - p1)) ** 2 Round up. For 40% to 45% at alpha 0.05 and power 0.8: 1,534 per group. statsmodels 0.14 agrees: NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=proportion_effectsize(0.45, 0.40), alpha=0.05, power=0.8) returns 1,533.05. The MDE drives everything. Required n grows with the inverse square of the effect: Change n per group 40% to 45% 1,534 40% to 42% 9,493 Halving the effect you want to detect needs roughly four times the sample. Two adjustments for survey work: Design effect. Weighted or clustered samples carry less information (lesson B8-L1). Multiply n by the expected design effect: with a design effect of 1.5, 1,533.05 × 1.5 rounds up to 2,300. Subgroups. If the decision needs the effect within each of four regions, each region needs the full n, not a quarter of it. Write the power calculation into the research plan, with its inputs. If the budget cannot buy the n, say so before fieldwork, and agree a larger MDE or a different design. A packaging test used 300 respondents per cell to compare purchase intent. The new pack scored 43% against 40%. The report said "no significant difference, keep the current pack". With 300 per cell, the test had about a 1 in 4 chance of detecting a real 5-point lift. The result said nothing about the pack. It said the test was too small. Fix baseline, MDE, alpha and power first, compute n, adjust for design effect and subgroups, then field.
lessons.title: Power and sample size, before fieldwork

lessons.text: An A/B test compares groups that differ only by chance and by the change you made. Keep that property in the analysis. Check the split first. If you assigned 50/50 and got 50,600 against 49,400, something went wrong: a redirect lost users, a bot filter hit one arm, a crash hit one version. A chi-square test on the counts detects this sample ratio mismatch (SRM). For those counts, p = 0.00015. A very small p-value here, below 0.001 by common practice, means stop and find the cause. The treatment effect is not trustworthy until you do. from scipy.stats import chisquare chisquare([50_600, 49_400]).pvalue # 0.000148, SciPy 1.17 Analyse as randomised. Everyone assigned to B stays in B, even if they never saw the new page (intention to treat). Dropping "people who did not see it" from B, but not the matching people from A, breaks the randomisation. Analyse at the unit of randomisation. If you randomised users, compute one outcome per user. Counting page views as independent inflates n and shrinks intervals. Report the difference with its interval. For 1,150 of 10,000 in B against 1,000 of 10,000 in A, the lift is 1.5 points, with a 95% interval of 0.6 to 2.4 points. statsmodels 0.14: from statsmodels.stats.proportion import confint_proportions_2indep confint_proportions_2indep(1150, 10_000, 1000, 10_000) # (0.0064, 0.0236) Compare with the minimum effect you planned for (lesson B9-L1). An interval that lies wholly above the MDE is a clear win. One that straddles it needs more data or a judgement call, stated as such. Fix the primary metric, the analysis and the stopping rule in writing before launch. Secondary metrics are exploratory and are reported as such (lesson B8-L3). A checkout test showed a 4% lift in conversion. Nobody checked the split. Arm B had 3% fewer users than arm A, because a slow script in B timed out on older phones, and those users were logged as never arriving. They were also the users least likely to buy. The "lift" came from losing low-converting users from B. When the script was fixed, the lift disappeared. An SRM check on day one would have flagged the missing 3%. Check the split, keep everyone in their assigned arm, analyse per randomised unit, and report the lift with its interval.
lessons.title: Analyse an A/B test the way it was randomised

lessons.text: A test's 5% false positive rate holds only if you analyse once, at the planned sample size. Common habits break it. Peeking. Checking results every day and stopping the first time p < 0.05 gives the noise ten chances to cross the line. A simulation in this course's build: two identical arms with a 10% conversion rate, 1,000 runs, 200 users per arm per look. One look: 5.2% false positives. Five looks: 12.9%. Ten looks: 18.4%. Fixes, in order of simplicity: Fixed horizon. Compute the sample size (lesson B9-L1), run to it, analyse once. Dashboards during the test show health metrics and the split check, not the lift. Planned interim looks with a group-sequential design, where each look uses a stricter threshold so the overall rate stays at 5%. Plan the number of looks and the boundaries before launch. Always-valid methods designed for continuous monitoring,, offered by some experimentation platforms. Use them as the platform documents them. Novelty and learning effects. Users click a new button because it is new. The lift fades after a week. Run for at least one full weekly cycle, and compare the effect in week 1 and week 2. Too many metrics. Twenty secondary metrics produce about one false positive per test (lesson B8-L3). Name one primary metric and a few guardrails before launch. Stopping for a good result only. A team that stops early when B looks good but runs longer when B looks bad biases every conclusion towards B. Interference. If treated users affect control users, through shared inventory, pricing or social features, the arms are not independent. Randomise at a level that contains the interaction, such as city or store. Write the plan down: primary metric, MDE, sample size, duration, looks, and the decision rule. Then follow it. A growth team ran 30 tests a quarter, checked each daily, and shipped any variant that reached p < 0.05. Their dashboard showed 11 winners, with a combined forecast lift of 9% in sign-ups. Sign-ups over the quarter were flat. With daily peeking over three-week tests, the false positive rate per test was far above 5%, and most of the winners were noise. Plan the sample, duration and looks, analyse once at the horizon, and treat anything else as exploration.
lessons.title: Peeking, novelty and other ways tests mislead

lessons.text: Target leakage happens when a feature carries information that would not exist at the moment you make the prediction. The model learns the leak, scores brilliantly in validation, and fails in production, where the leak is absent. Ask one question of every feature: would I know this value at prediction time? Typical leaks in customer and survey data: Consequences of the outcome. cancellation_reason predicts churn perfectly, because only churners have one. refund_amount predicts complaints. Values measured after the prediction date. calls_to_support_last_30d computed on the extraction date, not the prediction date, includes calls made while the customer was leaving. Proxies from the labelling process. A reviewed_by column that is only filled in for fraud cases. IDs and timestamps that encode order. If churners were loaded in a later batch, a row ID predicts churn. A quick screen catches the worst cases. Compute each feature's AUC on its own against the target. A single feature with an AUC near 1.0, or near 0.0 for an inverse relationship, deserves suspicion before celebration. With scikit-learn 1.8: from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score auc = roc_auc_score(y, X[col]) strength = max(auc, 1 - auc) A screen does not prove leakage, and a leak spread across several features will pass it. The real defence is a feature timeline: for every feature, the date it becomes known, compared with the prediction date. Keep that table in the project and review it with someone who knows how the data is produced. When in doubt, leave the feature out and measure how much the model loses. A feature worth 0.15 AUC on its own that nobody can explain is more likely a leak than a discovery. A churn model scored AUC 0.97 in validation. The top feature was days_since_last_login, computed on the day the training data was extracted. For churned customers, that included the weeks after they had already left. In production, scored on active customers, the model ranked customers little better than chance. The retention campaign built on it spent its budget on the wrong people for two months. For every feature, know when it becomes available. Screen single-feature AUCs, and treat a near-perfect one as a suspect.
lessons.title: Target leakage, features that know the answer

lessons.text: Every step that learns from data must learn from the training rows only: imputation means, scaling parameters, category lists, target encodings, feature selection, even the choice of outliers to drop. If a step sees the test rows, information about them flows into the model, and the test score becomes optimistic. This is train/test contamination. A demonstration from this course's build, with scikit-learn 1.8. Take 100 rows of pure noise: 5,000 random features and a random 0/1 target. Nothing can be predicted. Select the 20 features most correlated with the target on all 100 rows, then cross-validate a logistic regression on them: accuracy 0.85. Put the same selection inside each cross-validation fold: accuracy 0.48, the chance level it should be. The first model did not learn anything real. The selection step had already looked at every test fold's labels and picked the features that happened to fit them. The rule for manual preprocessing: params = fit_preprocessing(train) # learn from train only train_ready = apply_preprocessing(train, params) test_ready = apply_preprocessing(test, params) # reuse, never refit Split first, before any step that learns. In cross-validation, that means refitting the preprocessing inside every fold. Doing that by hand is error-prone. scikit-learn's Pipeline does it for you (lesson B11-L2). Steps that do not learn are safe on the full data: fixed recodes from a codebook, unit conversions, parsing dates. Steps that learn include anything with fit, anything that computes a mean, a quantile, a list of categories or a correlation with the target. A propensity model imputed missing income with the median of the full dataset and scaled every feature on the full dataset before the train/test split. It then selected features by their correlation with the target, also on the full data. The validation AUC was 0.79. On the next month's customers it was 0.66. Most of the gap came from the feature selection: it had fitted the noise in the test rows. Split first. Fit every learning step on training rows. Apply the fitted parameters to everything else.
lessons.title: Fit on training data only

lessons.text: When rows have dates, every feature must be computed as of the row's own date, using only earlier data. Three tools in pandas 3.0 cover most cases. Prior-only aggregates. "Total spend before this order" must exclude the current order. Take the running total and subtract the current value, or shift first: orders = orders.sort_values(["customer", "ordered_at"]) prior = orders.groupby("customer")["spend"].cumsum() - orders["spend"] Point-in-time joins. To attach the latest satisfaction score before each prediction date, use pd.merge_asof. It matches each left row with the last right row whose key is at or before it, within the same by group. Both frames must be sorted on the key. pd.merge_asof(preds.sort_values("as_of"), scores.sort_values("scored_at"), left_on="as_of", right_on="scored_at", by="customer", allow_exact_matches=False) The default allow_exact_matches=True also matches a score recorded at the same timestamp as the prediction. If that score could only be known after the prediction was made, set it to False. A plain merge on customer followed by "take the latest" silently uses scores from the future. Time-based splits. Random splits put next month's rows in training and last month's in test. For anything you will use forward in time, split by date: train on data up to a cut-off, test on data after it. scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit gives expanding windows for cross-validation. Build a small as-of test for every time feature: a customer with events before and after the prediction date, and an assertion that only the earlier events count. It catches most mistakes in a few lines. A next-purchase model used "customer's total orders" as a feature, computed once over the full order table. For each training row, the count included orders placed after the row's date, including the very purchase the model was trying to predict. Validation AUC was 0.91. In production, where the future does not exist yet, it was 0.68. Recomputing the count as prior orders only brought validation down to 0.70. That was the model's true performance, and the team finally had an honest number to improve. Compute every feature as of the row's date, join with merge_asof, and split by time.
lessons.title: Time-safe features and point-in-time joins

lessons.text: Three sets, three jobs: Training rows fit the model. Validation rows, or cross-validation folds within training, choose between models and settings. Test rows measure the final choice, once. Every extra look at the test set turns it into a second validation set, and its score stops being an honest estimate. Split so the test set looks like the data the model will meet. Stratify on the target when a class is rare. train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y) keeps a 3% positive rate at 3% in both sets. Without it, a small test set can end up with very few positives. Group when rows are not independent. A panel respondent answering five waves appears in five rows. A random row split puts some of their waves in training and others in test. The model then recognises the person instead of learning the pattern, and the test score measures memory. A demonstration from this course's build (scikit-learn 1.8, random forest): 200 simulated respondents, 5 waves each, a label that depends only on the person and is unrelated to the features. Random 5-fold CV reported accuracy 0.995. GroupKFold by respondent reported 0.468: chance, which is the truth. from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.2, random_state=7) train_idx, test_idx = next(splitter.split(df, groups=df["respondent_id"])) The group is whatever repeats: respondent, household, store, patient, device. If it will be new in production, keep it out of training in validation too. For time-ordered use, split by time as well (lesson B10-L3). Record the split: the seed, the group column, and the resulting row counts, in the run manifest (lesson B6-L2). A model predicting survey drop-out was validated with a random row split over a panel dataset. It scored AUC 0.93. Deployed on a newly recruited panel, where every respondent was new, it scored 0.61. Each respondent's answering style had let the model match test rows to the same person's training rows. A group split would have shown 0.61 before deployment. Tune on validation, measure once on test, and split by the unit that will be new in production.
lessons.title: Train, validation and test, split by the right unit

lessons.text: Lesson B10-L2 fitted preprocessing on training rows by hand. scikit-learn's Pipeline does it for you, every time, including inside each cross-validation fold. Examples use scikit-learn 1.8. A Pipeline chains steps. Calling fit fits each step on the training rows and passes its output to the next. Calling predict runs the fitted steps on new rows without refitting. Cross-validation, grid search and cross_val_score all refit the whole pipeline per fold, so no fold's test rows leak into its preprocessing. A ColumnTransformer applies different preprocessing to different columns: prep = ColumnTransformer([ ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), NUMERIC), ("cat", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"), OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")), CATEGORICAL), ]) model = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]) Three defaults to know: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="error") is the default. A region that did not appear in training raises ValueError at prediction time. Set handle_unknown="ignore" to encode it as all zeros. ColumnTransformer(remainder="drop") is the default. Columns you do not list are silently dropped. List every column you mean to use, or set remainder="passthrough" on purpose. Output feature names come from get_feature_names_out(), prefixed with the step name: num__age, cat__region_n. Keep the column lists in config (lesson A1-L3), and have one function build the pipeline. The same fitted object is what you save, test and deploy, so preprocessing in production is exactly what was validated. A lead-scoring model was trained in a notebook. Preprocessing ran in a separate cell: median imputation and scaling by hand. The deployment team rewrote the preprocessing from the notebook for production and imputed with the mean. Income was skewed, so the mean was 40% above the median. Scores for every lead with missing income shifted, and the sales team's call list changed without anyone noticing. A single fitted Pipeline, saved and deployed as one object, leaves no second copy of the preprocessing to get wrong. Put every learning step in one Pipeline, split columns with a ColumnTransformer, and deploy the fitted object itself.
lessons.title: Pipeline and ColumnTransformer

lessons.text: Cross-validation (CV) splits the training data into k folds, trains on k - 1 and scores on the remaining one, k times. Report the mean and the spread across folds. A mean AUC of 0.81 with fold scores from 0.70 to 0.90 is a less certain result than 0.81 with scores from 0.79 to 0.83. cross_validate (scikit-learn 1.8) returns several metrics in one pass: res = cross_validate(pipe, X, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=7), scoring=["roc_auc", "average_precision"]) res["test_roc_auc"].mean(), res["test_roc_auc"].std() Hyperparameter search. GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV tries settings and keeps the best by CV score. Inside a pipeline, name parameters as step__param: {"clf__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}. The catch: best_score_ is the best of many tries on the same folds. It is optimistic, for the same reason as picking a model on the test set (lesson B11-L1). A simulation in this course's build: 20 datasets of pure noise, a k-nearest-neighbours grid of 60 settings. The mean best_score_ was 0.598 accuracy. The honest estimate was 0.515. Get the honest estimate with nested CV: an outer CV loop scores the whole search as if it were one model. search = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=inner, scoring="roc_auc") honest = cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=outer, scoring="roc_auc") Or keep a held-out test set that the search never sees, and score the refitted best model on it once. Practical rules: Fix random_state in every splitter, so reruns compare like with like. Search on a log scale for regularisation strengths: 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10. Prefer RandomizedSearchCV when the grid has more than about 50 combinations. Report the chosen settings, the honest score and the fold spread in the run log. A team compared 300 configurations of a gradient-boosted model and reported the top best_score_, AUC 0.842, to the client as expected performance. The model went live and scored 0.80 over the first quarter. Nothing had drifted. The 0.842 had been the luckiest of 300 draws on the same five folds. A nested CV estimate of 0.80 would have set the right expectation from the start. Report CV mean and spread, tune with the reported metric, and estimate performance with nested CV or an untouched test set.
lessons.title: Cross-validation and honest hyperparameter search

lessons.text: A metric is a summary of the mistakes you care about. Choose it from the decision the model supports, before you train anything. Accuracy fails on imbalanced data. A test set from this course's build has 2.4% positives. Predicting "negative" for everyone scores accuracy 0.976. A logistic regression at the default 0.5 threshold scored 0.9755, with recall 0.0: it found no positives at all. Better summaries, all in scikit-learn 1.8: ROC AUC (roc_auc_score): the chance a random positive ranks above a random negative. It ignores the threshold and the class balance. Good for comparing rankers. It hides how many false positives come with each true positive when positives are rare. Average precision, the area under the precision-recall curve (average_precision_score): sensitive to rare positives. A random ranking scores the prevalence, 0.025 here. The same logistic regression scored 0.30, twelve times the baseline. Always quote the baseline next to it. Precision and recall at a threshold: precision is the share of flagged cases that are real. Recall is the share of real cases that are flagged. These map straight onto work: "of 100 customers we call, 30 were going to churn" and "we reach 64% of the churners". Cost-weighted metrics: if a missed fraud costs £400 and a false alarm costs £5 of analyst time, compute the total cost at each threshold and pick the cheapest. Pick the threshold from the decision too. 0.5 is a default of the library, not a business rule. If the team can review 200 cases a day, the threshold is whatever flags 200 cases. Report the metric with the prevalence and the number of positives in the test set. A precision of 0.30 from 12 positives is not the same evidence as from 1,200. A claims triage model was reported as "97.6% accurate". It flagged nothing. Fraud prevalence was 2.4%, so a model that approved every claim scored the same. The number went into a board paper before anyone asked how many frauds it caught. The answer was zero. Choose metrics and thresholds from the decision. Report prevalence and counts beside every number.
lessons.title: Choose the metric from the decision

lessons.text: A model is calibrated when its probabilities mean what they say: of all customers scored 0.30, about 30% churn. Ranking metrics such as ROC AUC ignore calibration. A model can rank perfectly and still say 0.9 where the truth is 0.1. Calibration matters whenever someone uses the number itself: expected revenue (probability × value), a forecast count of churners, a risk shown to a person, or thresholds agreed in probability terms. Check it with a calibration table: group predictions into bins, then compare the mean predicted probability with the observed rate in each bin. scikit-learn 1.8 gives the same with calibration_curve(y, p, n_bins=10). Plot observed against predicted. A calibrated model follows the diagonal. Summarise with the Brier score (brier_score_loss), the mean squared error of the probabilities. Compare it with a constant model that always predicts the prevalence. A common cause of bad calibration is reweighting for imbalance. In this course's build, a logistic regression on data with 2.4% positives had a mean predicted probability of 0.024 and a Brier score of 0.021. The same model with class_weight="balanced" had a mean predicted probability of 0.42, and a Brier score of 0.199, worse than predicting 0.024 for everyone (0.024). Its AUC was slightly higher. Its probabilities were useless as probabilities. Fix it with CalibratedClassifierCV(model, method="sigmoid", cv=5), which fits a calibration map on held-out folds. Use method="isotonic" only with plenty of data, roughly a thousand positives or more, because it overfits small samples. Check calibration again on the test set after fitting. If you only need a ranking or a top-k list, calibration does not matter. Say which one you deliver. A retention team estimated campaign value as the sum of churn probabilities times customer margin. The model had been trained with balanced class weights. Its average churn probability was 0.41 on a base that churned at 3% a month. The business case promised ten times the saves the campaign could deliver, and budget was approved on it. When the probability is used as a number, check calibration, compare the Brier score with a constant baseline, and recalibrate on held-out data.
lessons.title: Calibration, when the probability itself matters

lessons.text: Imbalance. When positives are rare, a model trained as usual predicts low probabilities, and the default 0.5 threshold flags almost nothing. That is a threshold problem, not always a model problem. In this course's build (2.4% positives, logistic regression, scikit-learn 1.8), the plain model at 0.5 flagged 3 cases and found none. Lowering the threshold to 0.1 flagged 284 cases with precision 0.36 and recall 0.42. At 0.02 it reached recall 0.63 with precision 0.04. The same model trained with class_weight="balanced" reached recall 0.64 and precision 0.05 at 0.5: a very similar trade-off, with probabilities that were no longer calibrated (lesson B12-L2). Options, in the order to try them: Train normally and choose the threshold from capacity or cost (lesson B12-L1). Probabilities stay calibrated. Class weights when the model struggles to learn the minority class at all. Recalibrate afterwards if you need probabilities. Resampling (over- or under-sampling) inside the training folds only. Never resample the test set: its class balance must match production. Error analysis. One overall metric hides where a model fails. Break the test results down by segment: region, device, customer tenure, survey mode. For each segment report the count, positives, precision and recall. A model with recall 0.60 overall can have recall 0.15 for new customers, the group the campaign most wants to reach. Then read examples. Take the 20 most confident false positives and the 20 most confident false negatives, and look at them with someone who knows the domain. Patterns in those 40 rows often point to a missing feature, a label error or a leak. Report segment results with their counts. A recall of 0.20 from 5 positives is a question, not a finding. A complaint-routing model reported recall 0.71 overall. Complaints arriving by the new web chat were 18% of the volume and had recall 0.22: the model had been trained mostly on email text, and chat messages were shorter and informal. Urgent chat complaints waited in the general queue for three weeks before a supervisor noticed. A per-channel breakdown at validation would have shown it. Treat rare positives with a chosen threshold first, then break results down by segment and read the worst errors.
lessons.title: Imbalanced classes and error analysis by segment

lessons.text: "Which features matter?" has a trustworthy answer and a misleading one. The misleading one is impurity importance, feature_importances_ on scikit-learn tree ensembles. It is computed on training data and favours features with many distinct values. In this course's build (scikit-learn 1.9, random forest, 3,000 rows), a meaningless column of random IDs with 3,000 distinct values got an impurity importance of 0.335, half as much as the real signal (0.661).
