From Microsoft Learn's role table (checked September 2026): Right Admin Member Contributor Viewer Update or delete the workspace, add or remove admins yes Connect the workspace to Git, create a workspace identity yes Add members or lower roles, allow resharing yes yes Create and change items, run notebooks and pipelines yes yes yes Read lakehouse and warehouse data through Spark and OneLake APIs (ReadAll) yes yes yes Read lakehouse and warehouse data with T-SQL (ReadData) yes yes yes yes Two consequences surprise people coming from Databricks: A Viewer can query a lakehouse through its SQL analytics endpoint, but cannot read the same tables from a Spark notebook or through OneLake APIs. A Contributor can change and delete every item in the workspace, including production lakehouse tables. Contributor in production is powerful. Rules that keep access manageable: Assign roles to Microsoft Entra security groups, not to individuals (as in lesson A4-L2). People join and leave groups. Role assignments stay the same. Least privilege per environment. Engineers are Contributors in dev. In production, deployment runs under an automation identity, and people are Viewers unless they are on call. Keep at least two admins, as groups or named people, so a departure does not lock the workspace. Workspace roles are coarse. For finer control inside an item, use item sharing, SQL permissions, or OneLake security (lesson C9-L2). A contractor was added to a production workspace as Contributor "to look at a notebook". Two weeks later they ran a clean-up notebook against the wrong lakehouse and dropped three tables that reports depended on. Viewer would have let them read the notebook and query the data with T-SQL, and would not have let them change anything. Roles go to groups, write access in production goes to automation, and people read.
lessons.title: Workspace roles, granted to groups

lessons.text: A lakehouse has two top-level areas in OneLake: Tables holds managed Delta tables. Fabric registers them, the SQL analytics endpoint exposes them, and Direct Lake semantic models read them. Files holds anything else: CSV, JSON, Parquet, images, raw deliveries. Only Delta tables in Tables reach the SQL engines. A Parquet or CSV file is invisible to the SQL analytics endpoint, wherever it sits. If you put a folder that is not a valid Delta table under Tables, the lakehouse explorer shows it in an Unidentified area. A broken shortcut also lands there. So the flow for a delivery is: land the raw file in Files (your bronze copy, as received), then read it with Spark and write a Delta table to Tables with saveAsTable. Schemas. New lakehouses created in the portal have schemas enabled by default. Every schema-enabled lakehouse has a dbo schema that you cannot rename or remove. A table written without a schema goes to dbo. Create schemas by domain (sales, hr) to keep a growing lakehouse navigable. In Spark SQL you reference tables with a four-part name: workspace.lakehouse.schema.table. Parts you leave out come from defaults: a bare table name means the dbo schema of the notebook's default lakehouse. For code that others run, name at least the lakehouse and schema, so it does not depend on which lakehouse happens to be attached. One change to note if you learned Fabric earlier: since 5 September 2025, Fabric no longer creates a default semantic model automatically with each new lakehouse. Create semantic models on purpose (lesson C6-L1). An engineer wrote cleaned survey data as Parquet into Files/clean/respondents/, the way they had written to cloud storage before. The Power BI team could not find the table in the SQL analytics endpoint, so they imported the Parquet into a separate dataflow, a second copy with its own refresh. Writing a Delta table to Tables with saveAsTable would have exposed it to every engine with no copy. Raw files in Files, Delta tables in Tables, and schema-qualified names in shared code.
lessons.title: Lakehouse Tables and Files, and schemas
lessons.where: C2 Lakehouse, Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint

lessons.text: Fabric Warehouse speaks T-SQL, and most SQL Server habits carry over: CREATE TABLE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, stored procedures, views, TRUNCATE TABLE, identity columns and explicit transactions. MERGE is generally available. Its tables are Delta tables in OneLake, so Spark and Power BI read them too. The differences cause real bugs. Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026: Keys are not enforced. PRIMARY KEY is supported only as NONCLUSTERED NOT ENFORCED. UNIQUE likewise, and FOREIGN KEY only NOT ENFORCED. The engine uses them as hints for query plans. It does not stop duplicates or orphans. Deduplicate and check keys yourself (lesson A3-L1 for MERGE sources, lesson A6-L1 for contracts). Some data types are missing, with documented alternatives: Not supported Use nchar, nvarchar char, varchar (UTF-8 collation) money, smallmoney decimal datetime, smalldatetime datetime2 (up to 6 fractional digits) tinyint smallint text, ntext, json varchar varchar(max) is limited to 16 MB per value. Some features are absent or in preview. Triggers are not supported. ALTER COLUMN and nested CTEs are in preview. Check the T-SQL surface area page before you port a procedure that relies on them. Porting a SQL Server script is usually a type-mapping job plus one design change: replace constraint enforcement with explicit checks. A team ported a customer dimension from SQL Server, where PRIMARY KEY had rejected duplicate loads for years. In Fabric the same key was created NOT ENFORCED, so a pipeline that ran twice on the same file loaded every customer twice. Sales per customer halved in the joined reports for a week before anyone traced it. A duplicate check after each load would have failed the run on the first rerun. Map the types, declare keys as NOT ENFORCED hints, and check uniqueness yourself after every load.
lessons.title: Warehouse T-SQL, and where it differs from SQL Server
lessons.where: C2 Lakehouse, Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint

lessons.text: Fabric gives you three ways to hold and query tables. All three store data as Delta tables in OneLake. They differ in who writes the data and in which language. Lakehouse. You write with Spark: notebooks, Spark job definitions, Dataflows Gen2 or pipelines. It holds files and Delta tables side by side. Choose it for raw files, PySpark transformations and data science. This is the closest match to your Databricks work. SQL analytics endpoint. Every lakehouse gets one automatically. It gives a read-only T-SQL surface over the lakehouse's Delta tables. You can SELECT, and you can create views, functions and stored procedures. You cannot INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE table data through it. It picks up new or changed tables through a metadata sync. Microsoft documents the usual lag as under one minute, but it varies. Warehouse. You write with T-SQL. It supports full DML and DDL, and multi-table transactions. Choose it when a team works in T-SQL, loads data with stored procedures, or needs several tables to change together or not at all. One rule decides most cases: who writes the data, and in which language? Spark writers go to a lakehouse. T-SQL writers go to a warehouse. T-SQL readers of lakehouse data use the SQL analytics endpoint. You do not have to copy data between them. A warehouse query reads lakehouse tables in the same workspace with a three-part name: lakehouse_name.schema.table. Direct Lake semantic models read from either. Check the status of each feature you rely on in VERSIONS.md before you build. Fabric changes monthly. A team moves a finance reconciliation from SQL Server to Fabric. They land every table in a lakehouse, because the Databricks team already uses lakehouses. The month-end stored procedure updates three tables. On the SQL analytics endpoint it fails on its first UPDATE, because the endpoint is read-only. Under deadline, someone rewrites it as three separate Spark notebook writes. On one month-end the second notebook fails. Table one holds the new month and table three holds the old one, and the reconciliation report shows a balance that does not tie. A warehouse transaction would have rolled back all three tables together. The data and the logic are the same. The item type decides whether the procedure runs at all, and whether a failure leaves the tables consistent.
lessons.title: Lakehouse, Warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint
lessons.where: C2 Lakehouse, Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint

lessons.text: A shortcut is a folder in a lakehouse (or KQL database) that points to data somewhere else. It behaves like a symbolic link. The target can be inside OneLake, such as a table in another workspace, or outside it: ADLS Gen2, Azure Blob Storage, Amazon S3 and S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage, Dataverse, OneDrive or SharePoint. Shortcuts let every Fabric engine read the data without copying it. OneLake handles the connection and credentials, so each workload does not need its own. Where you create the shortcut matters: Under Tables, point it at Delta data. The lakehouse recognises the folder as a table, and the SQL analytics endpoint and Direct Lake can use it. Under Files, it can point at data in any format. Deletes are the trap. Microsoft Learn states the rule plainly: Deleting the shortcut itself deletes only the shortcut. The target data stays. Deleting a file or folder inside the shortcut deletes it in the target, if your identity has write permission there. So a clean-up notebook that runs rm -r on Files/partner_feed/2025/ removes the partner's 2025 files from their storage account, not a local copy. Other points from Learn (checked September 2026): Moving, renaming or deleting the target breaks the shortcut. Broken shortcuts appear in the Unidentified area. For external shortcuts you can turn on caching. OneLake keeps files it has read for 1 to 28 days, which cuts cross-cloud egress costs. With Direct Lake over SQL or T-SQL in delegated identity mode, the calling user's identity is not passed through to the target. Check which identity reaches the source before relying on its permissions. A lakehouse held a shortcut Files/finance_share to a folder in the finance team's storage account. An analyst ran a notebook to free up space: it deleted every subfolder older than two years under Files/. Their identity had write access to the finance account for another project. Seven years of finance exports disappeared from the source. The storage account had no soft delete, and the files were gone. Shortcuts save copies. Treat every path under a shortcut as someone else's data.
lessons.title: OneLake shortcuts, and the delete that goes through

lessons.text: Mirroring brings an external database into Fabric as a unit. For sources that store data in their own formats, such as Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Cosmos DB, Snowflake or Google BigQuery, Fabric continuously replicates the chosen tables into OneLake as Delta tables, in near real time. You get a mirrored database item and a SQL analytics endpoint over it, read-only, like a lakehouse's. Shortcut or mirroring? Microsoft Learn's rule: Shortcut when you want specific data, already in an open format, in your OneLake view without copying it. Mirroring when you want an external database or catalog, and the data behind it, in Fabric as a unit. It replicates when the source uses a proprietary format. Cost. For database mirroring and open mirroring, the background compute that replicates data does not consume capacity. Mirrored storage is free up to 1 TB per capacity unit: an F64 includes 64 TB of mirroring storage. Queries on the mirrored data (Spark, SQL, Power BI) use capacity as usual. Limits come per source. For Azure SQL Database, checked September 2026: at most 1,000 mirrored tables per database, tables whose primary key uses datetime2(7), datetimeoffset(7) or time(7) cannot be mirrored, since April 2025 tables without a primary key can be mirrored, but existing ones are not added automatically, even with "Automatically mirror future tables" turned on. Status varies too. Most sources are generally available. Some, such as Azure Database for MySQL, Dremio and SharePoint List, were in preview in September 2026. Check the mirroring overview page before you build on a source. After you set up a mirror, compare row counts per table between source and mirror (lesson A6-L3). The limits above fail quietly: an ineligible table is simply not there. A team mirrored an Azure SQL order database and built a dashboard on it. Weeks later, finance noticed that returns were missing. The returns table's primary key included a datetime2(7) column, so it had never been mirrored. Nothing errored. A per-table row-count check between source and mirror on the first day would have listed it as absent. Mirroring replicates operational databases for free compute and generous storage, within per-source limits. Reconcile the table list after setup.
lessons.title: Mirroring operational databases into OneLake

lessons.text: Your Track A pipelines write gold tables into Unity Catalog. Mirroring Azure Databricks Unity Catalog makes them readable in Fabric without copying them. Unlike database mirroring, no data moves. Fabric mirrors only the catalog structure (catalogs, schemas, tables) and reads the underlying Delta files through shortcuts. You get a mirrored Azure Databricks item with a SQL analytics endpoint, and you can build Power BI reports on it in Direct Lake mode. By default, Automatically sync future catalog changes for the selected schema is on, so new tables appear. Propagation takes from seconds to several minutes. Three rules decide whether it works and whether it is safe (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): Some table types do not mirror: tables with row filters or column masks (RLS/CLM policies), Lakehouse federated tables, Delta Sharing tables, streaming tables, views and materialized views. The ADLS Gen2 account behind the Databricks workspace must also be reachable from Fabric. Unity Catalog permissions do not carry over. Grants on catalogs, schemas and tables in Databricks do not apply in Fabric. You rebuild access with Fabric's model: workspace roles, item permissions, SQL permissions, OneLake security. One credential reads everything. The credential used to create the connection is used for all data queries. Unity Catalog policies such as row filters, column masks or ABAC are not enforced at the storage layer, so they would not apply to direct storage access anyway. Put together: mirror tables that are safe to share at the level you grant in Fabric. For data that needs row-level rules, publish a gold table without the policy that already contains only what the audience may see, or apply the rules again in Fabric. A team mirrored their gold schema so that regional managers could build Power BI reports. In Databricks, a row filter limited each manager to their region (lesson A4-L3). The filtered table did not appear in Fabric at all, so the team created an unfiltered copy for the mirror, with a connection that could read every row. Every manager with Viewer access now saw every region. The rules had lived in Unity Catalog, and nothing had been rebuilt in Fabric. Mirroring Unity Catalog copies no data and no permissions. Decide what is shareable, scope the connection, and rebuild access rules in Fabric.
lessons.title: Mirroring Azure Databricks Unity Catalog into Fabric

lessons.text: Fabric offers several ways to move data. They overlap, and picking by habit creates pipelines nobody needs. Microsoft Learn's data movement guide (updated April 2026) gives a starting rule by layer: Curated data from an existing system, for reporting: Mirroring. If the source already does its own ETL and you need the result in Fabric, mirroring is the simplest and cheapest choice (lesson C3-L2). Raw ingestion into bronze: Copy job. It handles bulk copy, incremental copy and change data capture (CDC), with scheduling and state tracking built in, without building a pipeline. Low-latency events: Eventstream (lesson C7-L1). Then add tools only where they earn their place: Pipeline (Data Factory): orchestration. Run activities in order, branch on success or failure, loop, retry, and call notebooks, stored procedures, dataflows and Copy jobs. A pipeline with a copy activity also moves data, but you manage incremental state yourself. Dataflow Gen2: Power Query, low-code transformation for analysts, with a data destination per query. Spark notebook: code-first transformation at scale, the closest match to your Databricks work (lesson C5-L1). A simple way to decide: Does the source need to be replicated as a whole database? Mirroring. Is it a copy of tables or files into bronze? Copy job. Are there events that must arrive within seconds? Eventstream. Is there transformation? Spark for engineers, Dataflow Gen2 for low-code authors. Do several steps need ordering, branching and alerts? Wrap them in a pipeline. Two warnings. A pipeline that only copies tables re-creates what a Copy job does, with more to maintain. And Dataflow Gen2 is not a replacement for Spark on large volumes. Check your capacity usage (lesson C10-L3) before you standardise on one tool. A team built 40 pipelines, each with a copy activity, a lookup of the last loaded timestamp from a control table, and a stored procedure to update it. Two of them had an off-by-one error in the watermark and silently skipped rows every night. A Copy job per source would have tracked incremental state itself, with nothing for the team to get wrong. Mirroring for curated databases, Copy job for bronze, Eventstream for events, Spark or Dataflow Gen2 for transformation, and pipelines to orchestrate.
lessons.title: Choosing how data gets into Fabric

lessons.text: A Copy job copies data in one of two modes. Full copy moves everything on every run. Incremental copy moves everything on the first run, then only new or changed data. The job tracks the state of the last successful run itself (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026). Incremental copy works in one of two ways: Watermark. You pick an incremental column, such as a ROWVERSION, a datetime, a date or an increasing integer. Each subsequent load copies rows whose value is larger than any value copied before. CDC (preview in Copy job). If change data capture is enabled on the source database, the job reads its change stream and copies every insert, update and delete since the last run. You do not choose a column. The watermark method has two blind spots, and both follow from "larger than": It cannot see deletes. A deleted row simply stops appearing, and the destination keeps it. It misses late rows. A row committed after the run, with a watermark value at or below the one already copied, is never picked up. A modified_at set by the application clock, or several rows written in the same second, causes this. Prefer CDC when you need deletes, or a ROWVERSION column, which the database increments on every change. Microsoft also lets you reset incremental copy to a full copy, for the whole job or per table, to recover. Choose the update method for the destination on purpose. The default is Append, which keeps full history, and appends every changed row again as a new row. Merge updates existing rows by key (the primary key by default), Overwrite replaces the data, and SCD Type 2 keeps versioned history. For a silver table that must hold one row per key, choose Merge. An order table was copied incrementally on modified_at, set by the ordering app. At 23:59:59 one batch committed after the nightly run had read up to 23:59:59. Those rows carried the same timestamp as the last copied row, so they were never picked up. Finance found 212 missing orders at month end. CDC, or a ROWVERSION column, would have caught them. Watermarks copy rows above the last value seen: no deletes, no late rows. Use CDC or a ROWVERSION column, and Merge for one row per key.
lessons.title: Incremental copy with a watermark, or with CDC

lessons.text: A Data Factory pipeline runs activities: Copy job, notebook, stored procedure, Dataflow, If Condition, ForEach, Until, and more. By default a pipeline holds up to 120 activities. Three settings on each activity decide how a failure behaves (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): Timeout. How long an activity may run before it is stopped. The default is 12 hours, and the maximum is seven days, written D.HH:MM:SS. A notebook that normally takes 10 minutes and hangs will hold its slot, and its capacity, for 12 hours unless you lower this. Retry. Retries happen only if you enable them. The retry count then defaults to 1, with 30 seconds between attempts. Retry steps that fail for passing reasons, such as a busy source or a network drop. Do not retry a step that failed because its data is wrong. It will fail again, later. Dependency branches. Each activity connects to the next through a condition: Upon Success, Upon Failure, Upon Completion (either way) or Upon Skip. Put alerts and clean-up on Upon Failure. Upon Completion runs even when the step succeeded. Parameters and expressions keep one pipeline reusable across sources and environments. Expressions start with @: @pipeline().parameters.wave. Inside a string, @{...} interpolates: "landing/@{pipeline().parameters.wave}/". The result of interpolation is always a string, so "@{pipeline().parameters.max_rows}" passes text, not a number. When a setting needs a number, use the bare expression @pipeline().parameters.max_rows. Keep business logic out of the pipeline. Transformations belong in notebooks and SQL, where they can be tested (lesson A9-L1). The pipeline decides order, retries and alerts. A nightly pipeline ran a 10-minute notebook that sometimes hung on a locked source. With the default 12-hour timeout and no failure branch, each hang held its capacity until mid-morning. Downstream reports showed yesterday's data, and nobody was told. A 30-minute timeout, one retry and an Upon Failure email would have raised the alarm at 02:30 instead of 10:00. Set timeouts near the real run time, retry only transient failures, chain on Upon Success and alert on Upon Failure.
lessons.title: Pipelines that fail fast, retry sensibly and alert

lessons.text: Fabric notebooks run the same PySpark you wrote in Track A. The surroundings differ, and those differences break ported code (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026). Utilities. There is no dbutils. Fabric has NotebookUtils, formerly MSSparkUtils. The mssparkutils namespace still works but is being retired, so write notebookutils: Databricks Fabric dbutils.fs.ls(path) notebookutils.fs.ls(path) dbutils.secrets.get(scope, key) notebookutils.credentials.getSecret("https://<vault>.vault.azure.net/", "name") dbutils.notebook.run(path, timeout, args) notebookutils.notebook.run(path, timeout_seconds, arguments) dbutils.notebook.exit(value) notebookutils.notebook.exit(value) Secrets live in Azure Key Vault, not in Databricks secret scopes. You need Get permission on the vault. Output that prints a secret is redacted, but do not print secrets. Child notebooks time out at 90 seconds by default. notebookutils.notebook.run(path, timeout_seconds=90, ...). A child notebook that runs for five minutes fails unless you pass a longer timeout. For several notebooks, notebookutils.notebook.runMultiple runs a DAG of them in parallel. Default lakehouse. A notebook can attach a default lakehouse. Relative paths such as Files/landing and bare table names resolve against it. Name the lakehouse and schema in shared code (lesson C2-L1), so a changed attachment does not change what the code reads. Inline installs. %pip install affects only the current session, and inline commands are turned off by default in pipeline runs. Put libraries in an environment instead (lesson C5-L2). Runtime. Runtime 2.0 (Spark 4.1, Delta Lake 4.2, Python 3.13, Java 21) is GA and recommended for production. New workspaces still default to Runtime 1.3 (Spark 3.5), whose end of support has been announced. Set the runtime deliberately. It changes the Spark version your code meets. A team ported a Databricks orchestration notebook that called six child notebooks with mssparkutils.notebook.run(path). In development each child took under a minute. On month-end data, the largest took four minutes. Every run failed at 90 seconds with a timeout, and the error pointed at the parent notebook. Passing timeout_seconds sized to the real run time fixed it. Replace dbutils with notebookutils, secrets with Key Vault, inline installs with environments, and pass real timeouts to child notebooks.
lessons.title: From Databricks notebooks to Fabric notebooks

lessons.text: An environment is a Fabric item that fixes what a Spark session starts with: the runtime version, compute settings, libraries and small resource files. Attach it to notebooks and Spark job definitions, or make it the workspace default so every notebook set to "Workspace default" inherits it. Once an environment is the workspace default, only workspace admins can change its contents. Libraries publish in one of two modes (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): Quick mode installs libraries when each session starts. It is flexible, and it adds one to three minutes to start-up. Full mode builds a snapshot of the dependencies once. Microsoft recommends Full mode for pipelines, scheduled runs and shared workloads that need reproducible environments. It is the Fabric equivalent of the lock file in lesson B6-L3. Resource profiles set a tested group of Spark and Delta settings with one property. New workspaces default to writeHeavy, tuned for ingestion. readHeavyForSpark and readHeavyForPBI suit read-heavy work. V-Order is a Fabric write-time layout for Parquet files. It keeps files standard, open Parquet, and speeds up reads, especially for Power BI Direct Lake and the SQL engines. The cost is slower writes: Learn cites around 15% on average. Since the writeHeavy default, V-Order is off by default in new workspaces (spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default=false). Turn it on where reads dominate, at the narrowest useful level: per table: TBLPROPERTIES("delta.parquet.vorder.enabled" = "true"), the best choice for gold tables that Power BI reads, per write: the DataFrame option parquet.vorder.enabled, per session: spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default, or the readHeavyForPBI profile, which enables it. In Runtime 1.3 and later the older spark.sql.parquet.vorder.enable setting is removed. Code copied from older posts that sets it does nothing. A team moved its gold layer to a new Fabric workspace and noticed Power BI reports running noticeably slower than before. The old workspace had V-Order on for every write. The new one used the writeHeavy default, with V-Order off. Setting delta.parquet.vorder.enabled on the dozen gold tables, and optimising them once, restored read performance without slowing bronze and silver ingestion. Pin libraries in a Full mode environment, keep the writeHeavy default for ingestion, and turn V-Order on for read-heavy gold tables.
lessons.title: Environments, resource profiles and V-Order

lessons.text: Delta is an open format, so a table written by Databricks can be read by Fabric through a shortcut or Unity Catalog mirroring (lessons C3-L1 and C3-L3). Open does not mean every reader supports every table feature. A table's features decide which Fabric experiences can read it. From Microsoft Learn's Delta interoperability matrix (updated May 2026): Feature Spark Runtime 2.0 SQL analytics endpoint Direct Lake Python notebooks Deletion vectors yes yes yes no Column mapping, name mode yes yes yes no Column mapping, id mode yes no yes no TIMESTAMP_NTZ yes no no yes Liquid clustering yes yes yes no Three more limits from the same page: V2 checkpoints: only Spark notebooks and Spark jobs read and write them. The lakehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint do not list such tables correctly. Databricks-only features, such as writing identity columns and Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines tables, are not supported. Newer Delta 4.x features, such as collations and the variant type, work only in Spark notebooks and jobs, not in the SQL endpoint or Direct Lake. Fabric's own writers differ too. Runtime 2.0 writes new tables at reader version 3 and writer version 7 with deletion vectors on by default. Runtime 1.3 writes reader 1, writer 2. The practical rule: the table's writer decides which features the table has, and every reader must support all of them. For gold tables that Power BI or T-SQL users read, use timestamps with a time zone (TIMESTAMP) instead of TIMESTAMP_NTZ, avoid column mapping in id mode, and check DESCRIBE DETAIL for the protocol versions and table features before you publish. A Databricks team stored event times as TIMESTAMP_NTZ in a gold table and shared it with Fabric through a shortcut. Spark in Fabric read it fine. The SQL analytics endpoint and the Direct Lake report did not show the table's time columns, so the Power BI team built a workaround copy with converted columns. One type choice in the writer created a second dataset. Open format, but not every feature for every reader. Design shared gold tables for the weakest reader that needs them.
lessons.title: Delta tables shared between Databricks and Fabric

lessons.text: A Power BI semantic model works best on a star schema: fact tables surrounded by dimension tables. Microsoft's Power BI guidance (checked September 2026) defines the parts: Fact tables store observations or events: survey responses, orders, balances. They hold dimension key columns and numeric measure columns. The dimension keys decide the fact table's grain, for example one row per respondent per wave per brand. Dimension tables describe business entities: respondent, brand, region, date. Each has a unique key column and descriptive columns used to filter and group. A date dimension belongs in almost every model. Relationships run one-to-many from each dimension to the fact table, and filters flow from the dimension to the fact. Microsoft recommends that you minimise bi-directional relationships, which can slow queries and confuse report users with unexpected filtering. Many-to-many relationships between facts and dimensions usually mean the grain is unclear. Build the star in the gold layer, not in the model: Compute derived columns such as age bands or weighted flags in Spark or SQL, in gold tables. Direct Lake on SQL analytics endpoints does not support calculated columns, and on OneLake they are in preview with restrictions. Materialised calculated columns in Import models slow refresh. Give every fact table a clear grain in its docstring and table comment (lesson A2-L3). Use surrogate or natural keys consistently, and check they are unique in each dimension (lesson C2-L2 showed warehouse keys are not enforced). A good model is boring: one fact table per grain, conformed dimensions shared between facts, single-direction one-to-many relationships, and measures that do the arithmetic (lesson C6-L2). A brand tracker model joined a respondent table and a brand-awareness table with a bi-directional many-to-many relationship, because both held respondent_id and brand. Selecting a brand in a slicer filtered respondents, which filtered back to every brand those respondents had mentioned. Awareness for small brands showed as much higher than the survey measured. A single fact table at respondent-brand grain with one-way dimensions returned the correct figures. Facts with a stated grain, dimensions with unique keys, one-to-many single-direction relationships, and derived columns computed upstream.
lessons.title: Star schemas for semantic models
lessons.where: C6 Semantic models and Direct Lake

lessons.text: In a semantic model, arithmetic belongs in measures. A measure is evaluated at query time, in the filter context of the visual: the slicers, rows and columns that apply to that cell. A calculated column is evaluated row by row when the model refreshes and stored, which costs memory and refresh time and cannot react to slicers. Three habits make measures correct and readable (Microsoft's DAX guidance, checked September 2026): Use DIVIDE, not /. DIVIDE(numerator, denominator) returns BLANK when the denominator is zero or BLANK, instead of an error or infinity. You can pass an alternate result as a third argument. Microsoft notes it is also faster than testing for zero yourself. Use variables. VAR ... RETURN evaluates an expression once and names it. That improves performance, readability and debugging. Change filter context only with CALCULATE, and say why. CALCULATE([Weighted base], ALL(dim_brand)) removes the brand filter, which is what a share-of-total denominator needs. A weighted share, the survey version of lesson B8-L1: Weighted aware % = VAR aware_w = SUMX ( fact_awareness, fact_awareness[aware] * fact_awareness[weight] ) VAR base_w = SUM ( fact_awareness[weight] ) RETURN DIVIDE ( aware_w, base_w ) Put the unweighted base next to it as a separate measure, Base (n) = DISTINCTCOUNT(fact_awareness[respondent_key]), so report users see how many respondents stand behind each percentage. Name measures for what they return, store them in one place (a measures table or the fact table), and set their format strings. A measure that nobody can read is a measure nobody can check. A report computed awareness as SUM(aware_weight) / SUM(weight) in a measure. In a new market with no fieldwork yet, the base was zero, and the visual showed "Infinity" and "NaN" in cells that the board pack exported to PDF. DIVIDE would have returned BLANK, and the empty cells would have been left empty. Measures, not calculated columns. DIVIDE for every ratio, variables for clarity, and CALCULATE with the narrowest filter change.
lessons.title: DAX measures that state their filter context
lessons.where: C6 Semantic models and Direct Lake

lessons.text: Direct Lake lets a semantic model read Delta tables in OneLake directly, loading only the columns a query needs into memory. It combines Import-like query speed with no copy of the data. A refresh does not reload data. It performs framing: it records which Delta table versions the model uses. Framing takes seconds, and afterwards queries see the data as of that frame. Automatic updates, a schedule or an API call can trigger framing. There are two kinds (Microsoft Learn, updated September 2026): Direct Lake on OneLake reads Delta tables from one or more Fabric items. It never falls back to DirectQuery. If it cannot load data, the query fails. Direct Lake on SQL analytics endpoints reads one Fabric item through its endpoint. When it cannot load a table directly, it falls back to DirectQuery: for example when the table is a SQL view, or when the warehouse uses SQL-based granular access control. Fallback queries are slower. The model property Direct Lake behavior controls fallback for the SQL kind: Automatic (default): silently fall back to DirectQuery. Reports keep working, more slowly. DirectLakeOnly: fail with an error instead. Use it in development to find fallbacks. DirectQueryOnly: always use DirectQuery, to measure the difference. Guardrails depend on the SKU. For each table, Fabric limits Parquet files, row groups and rows. Over a guardrail, framing can fail (or, on the SQL kind, queries fall back). From Learn's table: SKU Parquet files per table Rows per table Max memory F2 to F32 1,000 300 million 3 to 10 GB F64 5,000 1.5 billion 25 GB F512 and above 10,000 12 to 24 billion 200 to 400 GB Small files hit the file guardrail first. Compact gold tables with OPTIMIZE (lesson A3-L3), and give Direct Lake tables V-Order (lesson C5-L2). A sales model on an F32 capacity was fast in testing. After six months of hourly appends, the fact table held 2,400 small Parquet files, above the F32 guardrail of 1,000. The model used Direct Lake on the SQL endpoint with the Automatic behaviour, so queries quietly fell back to DirectQuery. Reports took 40 seconds instead of two. Nobody saw an error. A nightly OPTIMIZE kept the table at a few dozen files and restored Direct Lake. Direct Lake stays fast when tables are Delta (not views), compact, within the SKU's guardrails, and fallback is made visible in development.
lessons.title: Direct Lake, framing and the fallback you did not plan
lessons.where: C6 Semantic models and Direct Lake

lessons.text: An eventstream brings real-time events into Fabric, optionally transforms them, and routes them to destinations, without code. It is Microsoft's recommended path for low-latency, event-driven ingestion (lesson C4-L1). Sources include Azure Event Hubs, IoT Hub, custom apps, and change data capture (CDC) connectors for Azure SQL Database, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server on a VM. A CDC source first captures a snapshot of the current data, then streams the changes. Transformations are no-code operators on the stream: filter, manage fields, aggregate over a time window, group by, union, join, expand. You can split one stream into derived streams for different consumers. Destinations (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): Eventhouse, for KQL analysis (lesson C7-L2). Two ingestion modes: direct ingestion, or event processing before ingestion when you apply transformations in the eventstream first. Lakehouse. Events are converted to Delta Lake format and written to lakehouse tables. Activator, to trigger actions on conditions (lesson C7-L3). A custom endpoint, to route events to your own application. Writing to an eventhouse, lakehouse or Activator destination needs Contributor or higher on the destination's workspace. Design choices that matter: Filter early. Drop events nobody needs in the eventstream, before they cost storage and query time. Keep the raw stream. Route an unfiltered copy to an eventhouse or lakehouse table as your bronze layer, and derive cleaned streams from it. You cannot replay events you dropped. Decide the event time. Events carry their own timestamp. Use it for windows and analysis, not the time of arrival, which drifts when senders buffer or reconnect. A fleet team filtered its eventstream to keep only engine-fault events and wrote those to an eventhouse. Three months later, engineers needed the normal readings before each fault to build a failure model. They had never been stored. Keeping the raw stream in a cheap table, and deriving the fault stream from it, would have preserved the history the model needed. Land the raw stream once, derive filtered streams for consumers, and route each to the destination that suits it.
lessons.title: Eventstream, events in, routed out

lessons.text: An eventhouse holds one or more KQL databases, built for high-volume, time-stamped data such as telemetry, logs and clickstreams. You query them with the Kusto Query Language (KQL): a pipeline of operators joined by , read top to bottom. telemetry_raw where event_time > ago(1h) where event_type == "reading" summarize avg_rpm = avg(rpm), n = count() by vehicle_id, bin(event_time, 5m) Put where filters first, especially on time. They cut the data every later operator touches. ago(1h) is one hour before now. bin(event_time, 5m) rounds times down to five-minute buckets. summarize ... by aggregates per group. Three KQL behaviours catch people out (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): take returns arbitrary rows. There is no guarantee which records come back, and repeated runs can differ, unless the data is sorted. For "the latest 10", use top 10 by event_time desc. summarize leaves gaps. A five-minute bin with no events produces no row, so a chart draws a straight line across an outage. make-series ... default = 0 ... step 5m fills missing bins. Empty input. summarize count() without by returns one row. With by, empty input returns no rows at all. Data policies are set per database or table. The retention policy removes old data automatically. The default is 3,650 days, the maximum 36,500, the minimum one day, and you can set it to unlimited. The caching policy decides how much recent data stays in the hot cache on local SSD: faster queries, higher cost. Set retention from the use: raw telemetry kept 90 days, daily aggregates kept for years. Turn on OneLake availability for a database or table to expose its data as Delta in OneLake, so Spark and the SQL analytics endpoint can read it without a copy. An on-call dashboard showed the "latest readings" from a KQL query ending in take 10. During an incident, the panel showed readings from two hours earlier, mixed with current ones, and the engineer concluded the sensor had recovered. It had not. take returned arbitrary rows. top 10 by event_time desc would have shown the true latest readings. Filter on time first, use top for "latest", make-series for continuous charts, and set retention and caching per table on purpose.
lessons.title: Eventhouse and KQL for time-series questions

lessons.text: Activator is Fabric's no-code event detection engine. It watches data and takes an action when a condition is met. Its sources include eventstreams, Fabric and Azure events, Power BI reports and Real-Time dashboards. Activator groups events into objects by a shared ID, such as vehicle_id. It evaluates each rule per object and keeps state for each one. "Vehicle 17 overheated" is a separate fact from "vehicle 42 overheated". Two kinds of condition behave differently (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): Change conditions fire on a transition. Increases above 100 fires when a value crosses 100 from below. Becomes true fires when a boolean changes from false to true. State conditions fire on every event that matches. Is greater than 100 fires for each reading above 100. For alerts, you want a change condition, or a state condition with an occurrence setting: "When it has been true for 10 minutes" fires only if the condition holds for the whole period. No presence of data (heartbeat) fires when no new events arrive within a set time. Use it to detect a silent sensor. Actions include an email, a Teams message, a Power Automate flow, or running a Fabric item such as a pipeline or notebook. Limits to design around: Up to 10,000 incoming events per second per rule. Above that, Activator stops the rule. Emails and Teams messages: 30 per rule per recipient per hour. Late events: by default, Activator drops events that arrive after their time window closes. The Wait time for late-arriving events setting (default two minutes) lets them in, at the cost of added latency. A plant set a rule Temperature Is greater than 80 on a stream that reports every 10 seconds. One oven ran hot for 20 minutes. The rule tried to send 120 emails to the shift lead. After 30, the rate limit throttled the rest, and the lead muted the alerts. An Increases above 80 rule, or Is greater than 80 with an occurrence of five minutes, would have sent one useful alert. Key each rule by the object it describes. Fire on change or sustained state, not on every event. Add a heartbeat for silence.
lessons.title: Activator, rules that act on events

lessons.text: Copilot in Fabric is an AI assistant built into each workload. It writes notebook code, pipelines, SQL, KQL and DAX, and summarises reports. Before you rely on it, check three things. Is it switched on for you? Copilot needs a paid Fabric capacity of F2 or higher, or Power BI Premium P1 or higher, in a supported region. Fabric administrators control it through tenant settings, scoped to security groups. If your capacity's region lacks Azure OpenAI, an admin must also allow data to be processed outside that region. Copilot stops working when a Fabric trial expires. What is its status? Release status differs by workload (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): Experience Status Copilot in notebooks (Data Engineering, Data Science) Preview Data agents GA Copilot in Data Factory (Dataflow Gen2, pipelines) GA Copilot for SQL queries in a Warehouse Preview Copilot for semantic models and reports in Power BI GA What does it cost? Copilot requests consume capacity units, metered per 1,000 tokens. About 1,000 tokens equal 750 words. Input costs 100 CU seconds per 1,000 tokens, cached input 10 and output 400. A request with 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens costs (2,000 × 100 + 500 × 400) / 1,000 = 400 CU seconds. Copilot runs as a background operation, so Fabric smooths its cost over 24 hours. On data handling, Microsoft states your data is not used to train models. It also states that Copilot output is sometimes inaccurate, and that people able to judge its accuracy should review it. Lesson C8-L3 shows you how. An analytics team put Copilot-generated SQL into a scheduled report during the Warehouse Copilot preview. Nobody recorded which features were preview. When a reviewer asked whether the process relied on anything outside GA, the team spent a week tracing it. Check status first, record it, and keep production logic reviewed and owned by a person. Confirm Copilot is enabled on a paid capacity, record the release status of each experience, and budget its CU use.
lessons.title: Copilot in Fabric, where it runs and what it costs
lessons.where: C8 Copilot and AI in Fabric

lessons.text: A Fabric data agent (GA, Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026) answers questions in plain language over your data. It picks a data source, writes a query and runs it: SQL for lakehouses and warehouses. DAX for Power BI semantic models. KQL for KQL databases in an eventhouse. One agent takes up to five data sources. Users do not write the query, but the query is still what decides the answer. Three rules keep it safe: Read-only. The agent generates only read queries. It never creates, updates or deletes data, and it does not run notebooks or other write workflows. The user's permissions. The agent runs with the credentials of the person asking, so each user only reaches data they already have access to. No unstructured files. PDFs, Word documents and text files are not supported sources. The agent is only as good as the context you give it. Microsoft's guidance: Select only the tables and columns the agent needs. Every extra table is another chance to pick the wrong one. Use clear names such as order_submission_date, not date1. Write instructions that explain business terms and which source answers which kind of question. Add example queries: question and query pairs. Each example is validated against the schema, and invalid ones are not used. Lakehouses, warehouses and KQL databases support examples. Semantic models do not. Then evaluate the agent. Build a ground-truth set of questions with known answers, run them through the agent, and measure how many it gets right. The fabric-data-agent-sdk package provides an evaluation API for this. Rerun the set after every change to instructions, examples or schema. Every query costs tokens. Instructions, example queries and conversation history all add to the input and so to CU use. A sales team published a data agent over a lakehouse with 60 tables, including three with a column called revenue: gross, net and forecast. "What was revenue last quarter?" returned the forecast. Nobody noticed for a month. Selecting only the net-revenue table, plus an instruction defining revenue as net of returns, fixed it. A 20-question ground-truth test would have caught it on day one. Narrow the schema, define your terms, add validated examples, and measure accuracy against known answers.
lessons.title: Data agents, questions in plain language
lessons.where: C8 Copilot and AI in Fabric

lessons.text: Microsoft's own guidance for Copilot in notebooks (preview, Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026) says: always review AI-generated code before you apply it. Output might be inaccurate, incomplete, or based on outdated library syntax. The chat pane shows changes as an approval diff. Approving the diff is your review, so make it a real one. Code that runs without error proves only that the names exist and the syntax parses. Use four checks, in this order. Read every line. Check each table, column and function against the schema and the docs. Check the grain: one row per what? Check joins: inner joins drop unmatched rows. Run it on known data. Build five to ten rows where you have worked out the answer by hand. Include the awkward cases: a null, a zero denominator, a duplicate key, an empty group. Compare with a second method. Compute the same number another way: a plain count() against the generated aggregate, SQL against PySpark, the new query against last month's report. Keep the checks. Turn steps 2 and 3 into tests that run with the pipeline, so the next edit, by you or by Copilot, is checked too. Errors to look for first, because they run cleanly and give plausible numbers: Average of averages. AVG(avg_basket) over stores weights a small store the same as a large one. Divide total sales by total baskets instead. Wrong join type. An inner join to a dimension drops facts with no match. COUNT(*) for distinct things. Customers with two orders count twice. Unguarded division. A zero denominator fails in some engines and returns null or infinity in others. Invented names. A column or function that does not exist. This one fails loudly. An analyst asked Copilot for average basket value by region. The query ran and the numbers looked sensible. It averaged each store's average, so a pop-up store with four baskets counted as much as a flagship with 40,000. The regional figure was 11% too high. A five-row test with two stores of different sizes shows the difference at once. Read it, run it on data with a hand-worked answer, compare it with a second method, and keep those checks as tests.
lessons.title: Verify what Copilot writes
lessons.where: C8 Copilot and AI in Fabric

lessons.text: A tenant with 400 workspaces needs two things before anyone trusts its data: a way to find data by business area, and a way to tell the authoritative copy from the rest. Fabric gives you domains and endorsement. Microsoft Learn shows neither with a preview label (checked September 2026). Domains group workspaces by business area, such as Finance or Marketing. You can split a domain into subdomains. You associate workspaces with a domain. Every item in the workspace inherits the domain. Users filter the OneLake catalog by domain to find relevant data. Some tenant settings can be delegated to domain level, so each area sets its own rules. Domain assignment does not grant or restrict access. Workspace roles and item permissions decide who sees what. Three roles manage domains. Fabric admins create domains and name domain admins. Domain admins, ideally the business owners, edit their domain and associate workspaces. Domain contributors are workspace admins allowed to assign their own workspaces to the domain. Endorsement labels an item with one of three badges: Badge Meaning Who applies it Promoted The creators think it is ready to share Anyone with write access to the item Certified An authorised reviewer confirms it meets the organisation's standards Only users a Fabric admin names Master data The authoritative source for core data such as customer lists Only users a Fabric admin names Any item except a Power BI dashboard can be promoted or certified. Master data applies only to items that hold data, such as lakehouses and semantic models. Certification and master data work only after a Fabric admin enables them. Endorsed items get a badge and appear first in some lists. That helps people pick the right copy. It does not stop anyone using an uncertified one. A company had five semantic models called "Sales" across four workspaces. Two finance directors presented different quarterly revenue to the board. Both had used a model called "Sales". Certifying one model, retiring the others, and filing the finance workspaces under a Finance domain made the right model the first result anyone found. Domains help people find data. Endorsement tells them which copy to trust. Neither controls access.
lessons.title: Domains and endorsement, finding the right data

lessons.text: OneLake security controls who reads which data in OneLake: tables, folders, schemas, rows and columns. Every supported engine enforces it (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026). Roles. Each role has a permission (Read or ReadWrite), the data it covers, and its members: Entra users or groups. The model is deny by default and supports only grant roles. There are no deny roles. A lakehouse starts with a DefaultReader role that gives users with the ReadAll permission access to its data. Remove or narrow it before your own roles mean anything. Who it restricts. OneLake security governs Viewers and users with Read permission on the item. Workspace Admins, Members and Contributors already have data access through their workspace role. Make analysts Viewers. Row and column security. A role can filter rows (RLS) and hide columns (CLS) on a table. Within one role, access is the intersection of its table, row and column rules. Across roles, access is the union: row filters combine with OR, so a user in roles for city = 'Leeds' and city = 'York' sees both cities. Two exceptions: In the SQL analytics endpoint, CLS uses deny semantics: if any of the user's roles hides a column, the endpoint blocks it. SELECT * on a table with hidden columns returns the allowed columns in Spark, but fails in the SQL analytics endpoint. Keep row and column rules that belong together in the same role. OneLake rejects a combination where two roles allow different columns of a table and either role also filters its rows. Roles with ReadWrite cannot carry RLS or CLS. Engines. RLS and CLS are GA in Spark notebooks, lakehouses, Direct Lake on OneLake semantic models, and the SQL analytics endpoint in user's identity access mode. Eventhouse supports RLS only, in preview. A team added a OneLake security role limiting analysts to UK rows of fact_sales, then found the analysts still saw every country. Two causes. The analysts were Contributors on the workspace, so roles did not restrict them. And the DefaultReader role was still in place, granting full reads to every Viewer with ReadAll. Making analysts Viewers and removing DefaultReader fixed both. Readers are Viewers, defaults are removed, related row and column rules share a role, and every engine runs in a mode that enforces them.
lessons.title: OneLake security, roles down to rows and columns

lessons.text: Access control decides who opens an item. Sensitivity labels say how sensitive its content is, and travel with it. Fabric uses labels from Microsoft Purview Information Protection. You need a Purview licence, and labelling Power BI items also needs a Pro or Premium Per User licence (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026). How labels spread: Downstream inheritance. A label on a semantic model flows to the reports and dashboards built on it. It never overwrites a label someone applied manually, and never replaces a label with a less restrictive one. Default and mandatory labelling. Admins can apply a default label to new items, or require users to pick one before they save. Export. Labels, and the protection a Purview policy attaches, stay with data exported to Excel, PDF and PowerPoint. Protection policies link a label to access. When an item carries the label, users and groups named in the policy keep the permissions they already have. Everyone else is blocked. The user who last applied the label is not blocked. Purview also gives you: Unified Catalog: metadata about Fabric items, visible in Purview. Data loss prevention (DLP): detects sensitive data uploaded to OneLake and raises policy tips and alerts. It also restricts access to sensitive assets in KQL databases, SQL databases and warehouses. Audit: compliance admins track label activity. Lineage shows how items connect. Every workspace has a lineage view that any user with a workspace role can open. It covers all items in the workspace, plus external sources one step upstream. Impact analysis starts from one item and lists the downstream items and workspaces a change might affect, and lets you notify their contacts. Run impact analysis before a schema change. A label names the risk. A protection policy acts on it. An engineer renamed a column in a lakehouse table on a Friday. Monday morning, 14 reports in three other workspaces showed errors, and a finance close was delayed. Impact analysis on the table would have listed all 14 reports and their workspaces, and notified their owners before the change. Run impact analysis before changes. Label sensitive items, attach protection policies, and let inheritance carry the label downstream.
lessons.title: Sensitivity labels, Purview and lineage

lessons.text: Git integration connects a Fabric workspace to a branch and folder in a Git repository. Supported providers are Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitHub Enterprise, all cloud-based only. Some item types are still in preview, so check the supported-items list for each one you use (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026). What Git holds. Item definitions, not data. Each item gets its own folder of definition files. For a lakehouse, Git tracks metadata only: its name, shortcuts and OneLake security roles. Tables and files are not tracked, and Git operations never overwrite them. Rebuilding a workspace from Git gives you empty lakehouses. Your pipelines must reload the data. Two directions: Commit exports workspace changes to the branch. Update imports branch changes into the workspace and overwrites the workspace version. The source control panel shows each item's state. If an item changed in both places, you have a conflict to resolve before you continue. Who does what. Only a workspace Admin connects or disconnects the workspace. Members and Contributors commit and update, limited by their permissions in the Git repository. Viewers see no Git information. One workspace, one branch. A workspace is a shared runtime. Anything one person changes there affects everyone using it. Microsoft's recommended pattern is a separate workspace per developer, each connected to its own feature branch. You develop in your workspace, commit to your branch, and open a pull request into the main branch. The shared workspace connected to main then updates from Git. Alternatively, develop in client tools such as VS Code for notebooks or Power BI Desktop for reports, and push to your branch. Keep notebooks small and parameterised, and keep configuration in files your pipeline reads. Reviewers read diffs. A 900-line notebook with hard-coded paths produces diffs nobody can review. Three engineers shared one development workspace connected to main. One of them updated from Git while another had an hour of uncommitted notebook edits. The update overwrote the workspace version, and the edits were lost. With a workspace and branch per developer, each person's work stays isolated until it merges. One workspace per developer on its own branch, pull requests into main, and a data reload plan, because Git holds definitions, not data.
lessons.title: Git integration for Fabric workspaces

lessons.text: Git integration (lesson C10-L1) versions your items. Deployment pipelines move them between environments. A pipeline has 2 to 10 stages, with Development, Test and Production as the default three. Each stage is a workspace (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026). What a deployment copies. When you deploy from one stage to the next, Fabric copies item content and metadata to the target stage. It does not copy data. After deploying a semantic model, you refresh it in the target stage. After deploying a lakehouse, you load its tables there. Overwrite, not replace. If the item already exists in the target stage, Fabric overwrites its content. The item's ID, URL and permissions stay the same, so reports and links in production keep working. Deployment rules give each stage its own settings: Data source rules: point a semantic model at the production database, not the test one. Parameter rules: set a parameter's value per stage. Default lakehouse rules: attach a notebook to the stage's own lakehouse. You define a rule in the target stage, on the item. It applies from the next deployment into that stage. Autobinding. If a deployed item depends on another item, such as a report on a semantic model, and the linked item exists in the target stage, Fabric binds to the target copy automatically. Compare shows which items differ between two stages before you deploy. Use it every time. The deployment pipelines REST APIs automate the same steps from a build system. Many teams combine the tools. Developers work in Git-connected workspaces and merge through pull requests. The merged branch updates the Development stage, and deployment pipelines promote tested content to Test and Production. Microsoft's CI/CD guidance also describes Git-only release options, so pick one and document it. A team deployed a notebook from Test to Production. It still pointed at the test lakehouse, so for a week the production job wrote its gold tables into Test. The dashboard in Production read stale tables and nobody noticed. A default lakehouse rule on the notebook in the Production stage would have attached it to the production lakehouse on every deployment. Stage-specific settings belong in deployment rules. Compare before you deploy. Reload data after, because deployments copy items, not data.
lessons.title: Deployment pipelines, dev to test to production

lessons.text: Every Fabric operation draws capacity units (CUs) from its workspace's capacity (lesson C1-L1). Fabric lets operations burst above the capacity's size, then smooths the cost over future time (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026). Smoothing. Fabric measures usage in 30-second timepoints, 2,880 per day. Interactive operations, such as report queries, are smoothed over at least 5 minutes and up to 64 minutes. Background operations, such as scheduled Spark jobs, pipeline runs and model refreshes, are smoothed over 24 hours. Example: an F2 has 2 CUs, or 48 CU hours per day. A background job that uses 1 CU hour adds 1 / 48, about 2.1%, to every timepoint for the next 24 hours. Throttling starts when smoothed usage borrows too much future capacity: Future capacity already used What happens Up to 10 minutes Overage protection: no throttling Over 10, up to 60 minutes Interactive jobs are delayed by 20 seconds Over 60 minutes, up to 24 hours Interactive jobs are rejected Over 24 hours All requests are rejected, background too Background jobs keep running well after users feel the delay. A capacity deep in debt takes hours to recover, because only idle capacity pays it back. Surge protection lets capacity admins reject background jobs earlier, before the capacity reaches deep throttling. At workspace level, it caps a workspace's share of CU use over a rolling 24 hours, unless you tag the workspace Mission Critical. The Capacity Metrics app shows what happened. A capacity admin installs it and shares it. The Health page flags throttling and rejections across your capacities. The Compute page gives 14 days of utilisation by item and operation. Practical rules: schedule heavy background jobs away from business hours, keep production on its own capacity, and check the Compute page before you buy a larger SKU. A team scheduled a full rebuild of 40 gold tables at 08:00 on an F16. By 09:30 the capacity had borrowed more than an hour of future use, and Power BI reports started failing for every user. The rebuild itself kept running. Moving it to 02:00, and making it incremental, kept the morning reports responsive without a larger SKU. Know which of your jobs are background, run them off-peak, protect production with surge protection, and read the Metrics app before you resize.
lessons.title: Capacity, smoothing and throttling

lessons.text: This track is about finding what is wrong in code, quickly and for certain. Start with three kinds of problem, from cheapest to most expensive. A syntax error stops Python before anything runs. It points at the line. An exception stops the program while it runs, with a traceback that names the error type and the line, such as KeyError: 'R2'. A wrong result raises nothing. The code finishes and reports the wrong number. These silent bugs cost most, because nobody knows to look. Use precise words. A defect (bug) is the mistake in the code. A failure is what someone sees: a crash, or a total that is 3% too high. The symptom is where it shows. The root cause is the first place it went wrong, often far from the symptom. Work through every bug with the same method: Reproduce it, then shrink the input to the smallest one that still fails. Three rows beat three million. Read the evidence: the last line of the traceback, or the first value that differs from what you expected. Form one hypothesis that would explain everything you see. Test it with one small check: an assert, a print of a single value, or the debugger (lesson D2-L1). Write a test that fails because of the bug, so it cannot return unnoticed. Fix the root cause, not the symptom, and watch the test pass. Look for the same mistake elsewhere. Copied code copies bugs. Two habits undo the method. Changing several things at once means you never learn which change mattered. Catching every exception and returning a default, such as except Exception: return 0.0, turns a loud failure into a silent one. A weight loader caught every exception and returned 0.0 so that "the pipeline never breaks". When a supplier changed its file encoding, every read failed, every weight became 0.0, and the gold tables showed zero respondents for three regions. The pipeline reported success for a week. Without the catch-all, the first run would have stopped with a clear UnicodeDecodeError naming the file. Reproduce small, read the evidence, test one hypothesis at a time, pin the bug with a failing test, fix the cause, and never silence an error with a default.
lessons.title: Bugs, errors and failures, the words and the method
lessons.where: D0 Start here: foundations for finding errors

lessons.text: Most code you debug was written by someone else: a colleague, your past self or an AI assistant. Read it in a fixed order, so you understand it before you trust it or change it. The contract. Read the name, the signature and the docstring. What does it promise to take and return? get_unprocessed_waves(...) -> list[str] promises a list and no side effects. Inputs and outputs. Which values come in, and what leaves: the return value, a written table, a printed line? Side effects. Look for anything that changes the world: writing files or tables, network calls, print, and changes to arguments, such as list.remove or df[col] = ... on a frame passed in. A function named get_ or check_ should have none. Trace by hand. Pick a tiny input, three values, and follow the code line by line. Write each variable's value in a small table after every step. It is slow for one minute and saves an hour. Edges. Ask what happens with an empty input, a zero, a None, a duplicate key and one row. Most bugs live there. Assumptions. Note what the code takes for granted: sorted input, unique IDs, a column that is never missing. Each one is a question for its author, or a check to add. Only then run it, on a small input whose right answer you worked out by hand. While you read, watch for code that changes a list while looping over it. for w in weights: weights.remove(w) skips the element after each removal, so some values survive. If the code is hard to read, restate it: rename variables, add type hints, and split it into small functions. Rewriting it clearly, with the same behaviour, is often how you find the bug. A helper called clean_weights was reused in four notebooks. It also sorted the caller's list in place, which nobody noticed from its name. One notebook relied on the original order to pair weights with respondent IDs, and every respondent after the first got someone else's weight. Reading the helper for side effects, step 3 above, finds the sort() in seconds. Read the contract, the inputs and outputs and the side effects first, trace a tiny input by hand, then probe the edges and list the assumptions.
lessons.title: Read code you did not write
lessons.where: D0 Start here: foundations for finding errors

lessons.text: A traceback lists the calls that led to an error, oldest first. The line that matters most is at the bottom. Read it in this order: The last line names the exception type and message: NameError: name 'uuid' is not defined. That is what went wrong. The frame just above it shows where: file, line number, function, and the source line. Python 3.11 and later add ^ or ~ marks under the exact expression. Walk up until you reach the first frame in your own code. Frames inside site-packages or the standard library are rarely the cause. The call from your code that fed them bad input usually is. Here is your reference log_pipeline_run, cut down, on Python 3.13: Traceback (most recent call last): File "observability.py", line 7, in <module> main() ~~~~^^ File "observability.py", line 5, in main log_run() ~~~~~~~^^ File "observability.py", line 2, in log_run return str(uuid.uuid4()) ^^^^ NameError: name 'uuid' is not defined. Did you forget to import 'uuid'? Python 3.12 added the "Did you forget to import" hint. Python 3.11 prints the same error without it. Chained exceptions print two tracebacks. The joining sentence tells you how they relate: "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" means someone wrote raise NewError(...) from err. The first traceback is the root cause. "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred" means a second error happened inside an except block. Your error handler has its own bug. Fix both. When you catch an exception to add context, use raise ... from err. The original traceback stays attached, so the next person sees both. Never read only the first line of a traceback, and never read only the message. KeyError: 'row_count_max' names the missing key. The frame tells you which dictionary, and so which config file, lacks it. A contract validator failed with a 60-line traceback. The on-call engineer read the top frames, which pointed at the job scheduler, and restarted the job three times. The last line said KeyError: 'row_count_max', and the frame above it named _check_row_count. The new tracker's contract file lacked one key. Reading from the bottom would have found it in a minute. Read the last line, then the frame above it, then walk up to your own code. When you re-raise, add context and chain with from err.
lessons.title: Read a Python traceback from the bottom up
lessons.where: D1 Reading tracebacks and stack traces

lessons.text: A Spark error message is long, but it has a fixed shape. In PySpark 4.0 (Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS) most errors start with an error condition in square brackets and end with a SQLSTATE: [UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column, variable, or function parameter with name final_wieght cannot be resolved. Did you mean one of the following? [final_weight, age, wave_id, respondent_id]. SQLSTATE: 42703 Read three things: The condition names the problem. Search for it in the Databricks error conditions reference. The SQLSTATE class, its first two characters. Class 42 is a syntax error or access rule violation: your code names something that does not exist. Class 22 is a data exception: the code is valid but a value is not. The origin line. Runtime errors show == DataFrame == and "cast" was called from ... with your file and line. When the error appears. Transformations are lazy, so a data error appears at the action (collect, count, write), not at the line that caused it. The origin line points you back. In classic Spark, a missing column fails at once, when you call select. Python UDF errors arrive as PythonException wrapping a normal Python traceback. Read that inner traceback bottom up (lesson D1-L1). Shadowed built-ins give a misleading message. Your data_contracts.py imports sum from pyspark.sql.functions. Then sum(1 for c in checks) raises [NOT_COLUMN_OR_STR] Argument col should be a Column or str, got generator. The code never meant to call Spark. Import functions as F. ANSI mode is on by default in Spark 4.0 and Databricks Runtime 17.0 and above. A cast of 'abc' to INT now raises [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] instead of returning null. Use try_cast where bad values are expected, and count the nulls it produces. In code, catch pyspark.errors.AnalysisException and read err.getCondition() and err.getSqlState(), not the message text. After a runtime upgrade to Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS, a silver job that had run for two years failed with [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value 'n/a' ... cannot be cast to "INT". The engineer's first thought was a Spark bug. The SQLSTATE started with 22, a data exception: the data had always held 'n/a', and the old runtime had turned it into null without a word. The new error exposed a data quality problem that was two years old. Read the condition, the SQLSTATE class and the origin line. Class 42 means fix the code. Class 22 means look at the data.
lessons.title: Spark errors, the condition and the real cause
lessons.where: D1 Reading tracebacks and stack traces

lessons.text: PySpark talks to the Spark engine in one of two ways, and each shapes the errors you see. Facts below were checked on PySpark 4.0.4 and the Databricks docs in September 2026. Spark Classic runs your Python next to a JVM driver through Py4J. PySpark converts most engine errors into Python classes such as AnalysisException. Some still arrive raw, as py4j.protocol.Py4JJavaError: Py4JJavaError: An error occurred while calling z:org.apache.spark.api.python.PythonRDD.collectAndServe. : org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure ... Caused by: org.apache.spark.api.python.PythonException: Traceback ... File "/repo/job.py", line 5, in <lambda> ZeroDivisionError: division by zero Skip the Java frames. Search for the last Caused by: line and the Python traceback inside it. That is your bug. Spark Connect sends a query plan to a remote server over gRPC. Databricks serverless compute uses Spark Connect, and supports only Spark Connect APIs. Three differences matter when you debug: Analysis is deferred. Classic Spark rejects a misspelt column when you call select. Spark Connect accepts the select and raises AnalysisException at the action, or when you read df.columns or df.schema. A try around the select catches nothing. Error classes live in pyspark.errors.exceptions.connect. They subclass SparkConnectGrpcException and the familiar base classes, so except pyspark.errors.AnalysisException still works. The message ends with a JVM stacktrace: section from the server. JVM-only attributes fail. spark.sparkContext raises [JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED]. RDD code, such as sc.parallelize, does not run on serverless. Two habits follow. Catch pyspark.errors classes, never Py4JJavaError, so the same code works on both. And place error handling around the action, where both modes raise, not around the transformation. A notebook wrapped df.select(col(name)) in try/except AnalysisException to skip columns missing from older waves. It worked on a classic cluster. After the team moved the job to serverless, the except never fired: the select succeeded, and the write failed with the same AnalysisException two cells later. Checking name in df.columns before the select works in both modes. Find the last "Caused by" in a Py4J error. Under Spark Connect, expect errors at the action, and catch pyspark.errors classes.
lessons.title: Py4J and Spark Connect errors
lessons.where: D1 Reading tracebacks and stack traces

lessons.text: A traceback shows where code failed. A debugger shows the values at that moment. Python ships one: pdb. Stop at a line. Put breakpoint() in your code. When Python reaches it, pdb opens a prompt, (Pdb), with every local variable in scope. Setting the environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 turns every breakpoint() call into a no-op, so a forgotten one cannot hang a scheduled job. Remove them before you commit anyway. Stop where it crashed. Run a script under pdb with post-mortem on: python -m pdb -c continue run_qa.py ... ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero Uncaught exception. Entering post mortem debugging /repo/run_qa.py(2)weighted_pct() -> ratio = reach / base (Pdb) p reach, base (5.0, 0.0) You land in the frame that raised, with its variables intact. Checked on Python 3.13. The commands you use most: Command Does p expr, pp expr Print, or pretty-print, a value w Show the stack, newest frame last u, d Move up to the caller, or down again n Run the next line, stepping over calls s Step into a call c Continue to the next breakpoint l List source around the current line q Quit A useful pattern: after a crash, p the inputs of the failing frame. If they look wrong, u to the caller and p what it passed. Repeat until you find the first frame where a value went bad. That is the frame to fix. In Databricks notebooks, the built-in interactive debugger gives breakpoints, stepping and a variable view for Python cells. It runs on serverless and on recent runtimes, after you turn it on in your editor settings. In Spark code a debugger stops only the driver. Code inside a UDF runs on executors, where your breakpoint never fires. Test UDF logic as a plain Python function first. A weighted-reach function returned 0.0 for one subgroup. An analyst added eleven print statements over two hours and still missed it. A post-mortem pdb session on a forced failure showed in one command that base was the unweighted count, passed in by a caller that swapped two arguments. u, then p, found the caller. Let the crash open the debugger, print the failing frame's inputs, then walk up until the values go wrong.
lessons.title: breakpoint() and pdb, stop and look

lessons.text: A job that failed overnight leaves you its logs and nothing else. Good logs answer three questions fast: what ran, with what inputs, and where it stopped. Python's logging module does this better than print. One logger per module: import logging logger = logging.getLogger(name) Levels, lowest to highest, with their numbers: Level Number Use it for DEBUG 10 Detail you need only while investigating INFO 20 Normal progress: step started, rows written WARNING 30 Unexpected but handled: a WARN check ERROR 40 A step failed CRITICAL 50 The pipeline cannot continue A logger passes on records at or above its effective level. The root logger's default is WARNING, so logger.info(...) prints nothing until you configure logging. Checked on Python 3.13: logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) configures the root logger once. A second call does nothing, unless you pass force=True. logger.exception("...") inside an except block logs at ERROR and appends the traceback. Pass values as arguments: logger.info("wrote %d rows to %s", n, table). The string is built only if the record is emitted. ruff rule G004 flags f-strings in logging calls. Logging is not control flow. logger.critical(...) records a message. It does not stop anything. Your standard says a CRITICAL check raises. Log, then raise. Logging is not your run log. Text logs are for people debugging. The Delta run log table, with one structured row per run, is for queries and dashboards. Write both. Every log line in a pipeline should carry the identifiers that let you find the data: tracker, wave, table, run id. A silver job logged "Processing..." and "Done" at INFO for every wave, and nothing else. When wave W14 produced 30% fewer rows, the logs could not say which step dropped them.
