Adding one INFO line per step, with the row count, tracker and wave, turned the next investigation from a day of reruns into a two-minute log search. One named logger per module, levels that match severity, identifiers in every line, and a raise after every CRITICAL.
lessons.title: Logging levels that help at 3 a.m.

lessons.text: A slow Spark job often shows why in its plan. Read it before you tune anything. df.explain() prints the physical plan without running the query. df.explain("formatted") numbers each operator and lists its details below. The other modes are "simple" (the default), "extended", "codegen" and "cost". Read the tree from the bottom up: the scan is at the bottom, the result at the top. What to look for (examples from PySpark 4.0.4): In the plan Means PartitionFilters: [(wave_id = 3)] Only matching partitions are read. Good. PushedFilters: [GreaterThan(w,1.0)] The filter runs inside the file reader. Good. PushedFilters: [] on a filtered query Nothing was pushed down. Check the filter's column and type. Exchange hashpartitioning(...) A shuffle: data moves across the cluster. Each one costs time. BroadcastHashJoin The small side is copied to every executor. No shuffle of the large side. SortMergeJoin Both sides are shuffled and sorted. Normal for two large tables. CartesianProduct or BroadcastNestedLoopJoin Every row meets every row. Usually a missing join condition. BatchEvalPython A Python UDF. Rows leave the JVM for a Python worker. AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false means adaptive query execution will adjust the plan at run time, for example switching a join to broadcast. explain() shows the starting plan. After the run, look at what happened. On classic compute, the Spark UI shows jobs, stages, tasks and the SQL tab with row counts per operator. On serverless, the Spark UI is not available. Use the query profile, which shows each operator with its time spent, rows and memory peak, and a Top operators panel. In the UI or profile, compare rows out of each join with rows in. A join whose output exceeds its larger input is duplicating rows (lesson D3-L1). Look for one task far slower than the rest of its stage: that is skew. A gold job's runtime grew from 4 minutes to 70 over a month. Nobody had changed the code. explain() showed BroadcastNestedLoopJoin: a join on a range condition, fine while the dimension held 50 rows, painful at 4,000. The plan named the problem in one line. Rewriting the range join as an equi-join on a precomputed band key brought it back to 5 minutes. Read the plan bottom up, look for pushed filters, shuffles, join types and Python UDFs, then confirm rows per operator in the Spark UI or query profile.
lessons.title: explain(), the Spark UI and the query profile

lessons.text: Some bugs raise no error. The job succeeds and the numbers are wrong. Two of the most common come from joins and from nulls. Join row explosion. A left join of respondents to a region lookup should keep one row per respondent. If the lookup holds a key twice, say N for "North" and "North (old)", every respondent in N appears twice. Weighted totals double for that region. Nothing fails. Check the grain around every join: Count rows before and after. A many-to-one join must not change the count. In pandas, pass validate="many_to_one". A duplicate key then raises MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset. Checked on pandas 3.0.2. In Spark, count duplicate keys in the lookup before joining: dim.groupBy(key).count().filter("count > 1"). Nulls behave differently in pandas and Spark. Checked on pandas 3.0.2 and PySpark 4.0.4: Operation pandas Spark and SQL Filter region != "N" Keeps rows where region is missing Drops rows where region is null Join on a null key Matches null to null Never matches a null key x NOT IN (subquery) where the subquery holds a null Not applicable Returns no rows In Spark and SQL, a comparison with null gives null, not True or False, and a filter keeps only True. So F.col("region_code") != "N" silently drops every respondent with no region. Say what you mean: Keep nulls: (F.col("region_code") != "N") F.col("region_code").isNull(), or ~F.col("region_code").eqNullSafe("N"). Exclude a list that might contain nulls: use NOT EXISTS or a left_anti join, not NOT IN. In pandas, the surprise runs the other way: null keys match each other. Drop or fill null keys before a merge unless you want that. A regional reach table showed the North at 118% weighted reach. The region lookup had gained a second row for code N when a boundary changed. The left join doubled every northern respondent. A row count check before and after the join, or validate="many_to_one", would have stopped the job at the join. Check row counts across every join. Know how your engine treats nulls in filters and keys, and write the null case explicitly.
lessons.title: Join row explosion and nulls in filters

lessons.text: Two more silent errors: values that change type, and times that change meaning with the zone. Type coercion. Checked on pandas 3.0.2, PySpark 4.0.4 and Python 3.13: pd.read_csv turns respondent_id 0123 into the integer 123. The leading zero is gone, and joins to the panel file fail. Pass dtype={"respondent_id": "string"} for identifiers. An integer column with one missing value becomes float64 in pandas. 1 becomes 1.0, and string keys built from it read "1.0". Strings sort as text: sorted(["10", "9", "2"]) gives ['10', '2', '9']. Wave "W10" sorts before "W2". Pad your ids, or sort on a number. Spark's df.union(other) matches columns by position, not by name. A delivery with wave_id and respondent_id swapped unions without error, with the values in the wrong columns. Use unionByName. Under ANSI mode, Spark casts a string column compared with a number: F.col("age") > 9 raises CAST_INVALID_INPUT on the value 'x'. Cast explicitly with try_cast first. Timezone drift. A timestamp without a zone is a guess. datetime.utcnow() returns a naive datetime and is deprecated from Python 3.12. Comparing naive with aware raises TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes. Use datetime.now(timezone.utc). Spark's TIMESTAMP type is an instant, displayed in the session time zone (spark.sql.session.timeZone). F.to_date on 2026-06-30T23:30:00Z gives 30 June in UTC and 1 July in Europe/London. A wave cut-off at midnight moves respondents between waves. The same text without an offset, '2026-06-30 23:30:00', parses to instants 4 hours apart in UTC and America/New_York sessions. Some local times do not exist. pandas refuses to localise 2026-03-29 01:30 to Europe/London: the clocks skipped that hour. Store instants in UTC. Convert to local time only for display, or for a business rule that names its zone, such as "fieldwork closes at midnight UK time". A wave closed at midnight UK time on 30 June. The pipeline ran with the session time zone set to UTC and assigned every interview completed between 23:00 and 00:00 UTC on 30 June to wave W14. In British Summer Time those interviews happened after midnight, in W15. 340 respondents moved wave. Both waves' reach figures shifted by up to 1.5 points. Read identifiers as strings, union by name, and keep every timestamp aware and stored in UTC.
lessons.title: Type coercion and timezone drift

lessons.text: Two Python habits produce wrong results with no error message. Both appear in code written by people and by AI assistants, including your reference pipeline. Mutable default arguments. Python evaluates a default value once, when it defines the function. Every call that relies on the default shares that one object. Write def add_check(result, results=[]), and each call appends to the same list. The second validation run returns the first run's checks as well. The fix is a None sentinel: def add_check(result: str, results: list[str] None = None) -> list[str]: results = [] if results is None else results results.append(result) return results ruff flags the pattern as rule B006. Treat that warning as a bug. Truthiness of numbers. if value: is False for None, and also for 0, 0.0, empty strings and empty containers. When zero is a valid measurement, such as a 0% reach, a zero weight or zero rows, a truthiness test treats it as missing. Your reference check_wave_stability does this: if current_pct and prior_pct: A metric that falls from 12% to 0% skips the comparison. The largest possible drop produces no warning. Test for the case you mean. For missing, write is None. For zero, write == 0. if current_pct is not None and prior_pct is not None: The same rule covers type hints. error_message: str = None claims the value is always a string. Write str None = None, and mypy then makes you handle the None case. A questionnaire routing error removes one question for a whole wave. Its weighted percentage drops from 12% to 0.0%. The wave-over-wave stability check runs if current_pct and prior_pct:, treats 0.0 as missing and skips the metric. QA reports PASS. The dashboard publishes 0% reach for that question, and a client asks why the channel "lost its whole audience" in a week. The check existed to catch exactly this change. One truthiness test disabled it for the one value that mattered most. Both fixes are one line. Both bugs pass every test that uses only non-zero values and a single call.
lessons.title: Mutable defaults and the truthiness of zero

lessons.text: Every layer of a medallion pipeline changes the row count for a reason. Write the reasons down as rules, then check them on every run. A count that breaks a rule is a bug, even when no step failed. For one tracker and one wave: Check Rule Bronze vs delivery Bronze rows for the delivery = rows in the delivered file or manifest Silver vs bronze Silver rows = distinct respondent keys in bronze. Never more than bronze rows Gold vs silver Sum of gold unweighted_n = silver rows in scope Redelivery After MERGE, silver rows = rows before + rows inserted Where the numbers come from. Count each layer with one agg pass, not repeated count() calls on an uncached DataFrame: df.agg(F.count("*"), F.count_distinct("respondent_id")). For writes, Delta records metrics in the table history. DESCRIBE HISTORY shows numOutputRows for a write, and for a MERGE numSourceRows, numTargetRowsInserted and numTargetRowsUpdated. Checked on delta-spark 4.0.1. Filter both sides the same way. Your reference get_unprocessed_waves compares bronze waves for one tracker with silver waves for all trackers. When another tracker already has wave W14 in silver, this tracker's W14 is never loaded. Every reconciliation query filters bronze, silver and gold on the same tracker and wave. Store the result. Write each reconciliation as a structured row in the run log: layer, expected, actual, status. A failed CRITICAL rule halts the pipeline before gold is published. Counts catch lost and duplicated rows. They do not catch wrong values in the right number of rows. Lessons D4-L2 and D4-L3 cover those. Wave W14 for one tracker never reached silver. The job logged success every night for three weeks, because get_unprocessed_waves found W14 in silver, loaded by a different tracker. A rule "silver rows for tracker and wave > 0 when bronze rows > 0" would have failed on the first night. Write the expected relationship between layers as rules, compute counts in one pass on identical filters, and halt when a CRITICAL rule fails.
lessons.title: Row counts across layers

lessons.text: Row counts can be perfect while the data inside has changed. A routing error drops one question. A supplier recodes region. A weighting run uses last year's targets. Each shows up as a shift in distributions between waves. Three checks, from simple to sensitive: Category shares. For each categorical variable, compare each category's weighted share with the prior wave. Flag a move larger than a tolerance, say 5 percentage points. This is what your check_wave_stability does, once its truthiness bug is fixed (lesson D3-L3). New and missing categories. A category present in one wave and absent in the other is a recode until proven otherwise. region = "Northern" appearing beside "North" is a supplier change, not a population change. Population stability index (PSI) summarises a whole distribution in one number: PSI = sum over categories of (actual - expected) x ln(actual / expected) where expected and actual are shares in the prior and current wave. PSI is 0 when nothing moved. A category with a share of zero makes the logarithm undefined, so replace zero shares with a small floor, such as 0.0001, before computing. A common rule of thumb reads PSI below 0.1 as stable and above 0.25 as a large shift. Those cut-offs are convention, not a standard: calibrate them on your own history of waves. Guard the divisions. Every share divides by a total. An empty wave, or a variable with no valid answers, gives a total of zero. Your reference _check_distributions divides by total with no guard and fails on an empty delivery. Check the total first and report "no data" as its own status. Drift is a question, not a verdict. Real change happens. The check makes a person look before the numbers are published. A supplier renamed region code "North" to "Northern" in wave W21. Silver loaded both values, the region lookup matched only "North", and the northern subgroup fell from 1,900 respondents to 12. Every row count passed. A new-and-missing category check on region would have flagged "Northern" on the first run. Compare shares over the union of categories, flag new and missing values, summarise with PSI, and guard every total.
lessons.title: Distribution drift between waves

lessons.text: Survey weights carry the whole estimate. A wrong weight gives a plausible but wrong percentage in every table. Check them on every wave, before gold. Totals and range: No null weights, and none zero or negative, unless your design allows zero. The weight sum matches its target: the population total for grossing weights, or the sample size for weights normalised to mean 1. Your contract's weight_sum_min and weight_sum_max encode this. The ratio of largest to smallest weight stays below an agreed limit. One respondent standing for 40 others dominates their subgroup. Efficiency. Unequal weights cost precision. Kish's approximation measures it: deff = n x sum(w^2) / (sum w)^2 = 1 + CV^2 n_eff = (sum w)^2 / sum(w^2) = n / deff Here CV is the population coefficient of variation of the weights. Weights 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 3.0 give a deff of 1.39 and an effective sample of 2.88 out of 4. Track n_eff per subgroup and wave. A sudden fall means the weighting struggled, often because a quota cell was nearly empty. Spark details that break these checks. Checked on PySpark 4.0.4: F.stddev is the sample standard deviation. It returns null for a single row, and the Kish identity uses the population version, F.stddev_pop. On an empty DataFrame, mean and stddev return null. Your reference check_weight_distribution then calls round(None, 4) and raises TypeError. F.sum(F.when(F.col("reach_flag") == 1, 1)) is null, not 0, for a subgroup where nobody was reached. Your gold table then shows a blank instead of 0% reach. Wrap it in F.coalesce(..., F.lit(0)). Decide what each result means for the run. A null weight is CRITICAL: halt. A deff above your usual range is WARN: log it and have someone look. A weighting run used last year's population targets for one age band. The weight sum stayed within tolerance overall, so the contract check passed. The 55+ band's effective sample fell from 800 to 190, and its reach estimate jumped 9 points. A per-subgroup n_eff check with a WARN threshold would have flagged it before the dashboard refreshed. Check nulls, range, sum and efficiency per wave and subgroup. Mind Spark's nulls: sample stddev, empty aggregates and sums over no matches.
lessons.title: Weight totals and survey checks

lessons.text: AI assistants predict plausible code, so they sometimes produce a function, parameter or statement that does not exist, or exists only on another platform. Your reference code has one: unity_catalog.sql uses CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY, which is Snowflake syntax. Databricks uses a SQL UDF with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER. What invented code does when it runs, checked on PySpark 4.0.4 and pandas 3.0.2: Invented code Result spark.read.delta(path) AttributeError: 'DataFrameReader' object has no attribute 'delta' df.drop_duplicates(keep="latest") ValueError: keep must be either "first", "last" or False pd.read_csv(path, encodng="utf-8") TypeError: ... unexpected keyword argument 'encodng'. Did you mean 'encoding'? CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY ... in Spark SQL [PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR] Syntax error at or near 'ROW' F.col("a").isnotnull() TypeError: 'Column' object is not callable The last one is sly. The real method is isNotNull. PySpark treats an unknown attribute on a column as a struct field lookup, so F.col("a").isnotnull builds a valid expression for a field named isnotnull. Only the call fails. Without the parentheses, the typo would fail later, at analysis, far from the line that caused it. Most invented names fail loudly, which makes them cheap to catch if you run the code. The expensive cases run: a parameter that exists but means something else, or a function from a newer version than your runtime. Check every API an assistant gives you: Find it in the official docs for your version: Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS, PySpark 4.0, pandas 3.0. In a notebook, confirm it exists: hasattr(F, "try_divide"), help(pd.DataFrame.merge), or inspect.signature(...). For SQL, check the statement in the Databricks SQL reference, not a general SQL tutorial. Syntax from Snowflake, T-SQL and PostgreSQL looks alike and differs. Treat an unfamiliar name as unverified until a step confirms it. An assistant proposed CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY to restrict survey rows by region. The engineer pasted it into the migration script without running it. The deployment failed in production at 2 a.m. with a parse error, and the table stayed unrestricted until morning. Checking the statement against the Databricks SQL reference would have taken two minutes. Look up every function, parameter and statement for your exact version, and run it on small data before it reaches a pipeline.
lessons.title: Invented functions, parameters and syntax
lessons.where: D5 Errors typical of AI-generated code

lessons.text: An assistant learned from years of code written for older versions. It often suggests an API that worked in 2021 and has since been deprecated, renamed or removed. Your reference observability.py uses datetime.utcnow(), deprecated from Python 3.12. Examples that matter for this course, checked in September 2026: Old code Current state Use instead datetime.utcnow() Deprecated, Python 3.12 datetime.now(timezone.utc) df.append(other) Removed from pandas (gone in 3.0) pd.concat([df, other]) df.applymap(f) Removed in pandas 3.0 df.map(f) df["a"][0] = x Never updates df under pandas 3 Copy-on-Write df.loc[0, "a"] = x import distutils Removed in Python 3.12 packaging, setuptools input_file_name() Not supported from Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS _metadata.file_path mssparkutils in Fabric Being retired notebookutils The chained assignment row is the dangerous one. pandas 3.0.2 emits a ChainedAssignmentError warning and leaves the DataFrame unchanged. If warnings are hidden, the update simply does not happen. Version mismatches cause the opposite problem: code for a newer version than yours. A function added in PySpark 4.1 fails on Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS, which ships Spark 4.0. Pyodide in this app runs pandas 3.0.2. Your laptop might run 3.0.6. Defend in three ways: State the versions in every prompt, and in the project: VERSIONS.md, pyproject.toml pins, the runtime in the job definition. Show warnings in tests. Run pytest with -W error::DeprecationWarning for your own code, so a deprecated call fails the build. Compare versions as numbers, never as strings. "3.10" < "3.9" is True as text. An assistant fixed a data cleaning function by adding df["weight"][mask] = 1.0 to cap weights. Tests passed on a developer laptop with pandas 1.5. In the pandas 3 environment, the cap never happened. Weights above 5 reached gold unchanged for four waves. The warning had been filtered out in the job's logging configuration. Assume suggested code targets some other version. Check deprecations for yours, turn warnings into test failures, and compare versions numerically.
lessons.title: Deprecated APIs and version mismatches
lessons.where: D5 Errors typical of AI-generated code

lessons.text: Code from an assistant usually runs. The problems hide in what it leaves out. Review it with five checks. Missing edge cases. Assistants write the happy path. Ask what happens with an empty DataFrame, a zero total, a null, a duplicate key, a single row. Your reference check_weight_distribution fails on an empty wave for exactly this reason (lesson D4-L3). Self-confirming tests. A test that computes its expected value with the same formula as the code proves nothing: def test_share(): assert share(3, 4) == 3 / 4 # repeats the code If the formula is wrong, the test is wrong the same way. Write expected values by hand, from small data you understand: assert share(3, 4) == 0.75, assert share(0, 0) is None. Secrets in code. Assistants fill in placeholders that look like real tokens, or keep the one you pasted into the prompt. A token in a notebook ends up in Git history. Read secrets at run time: dbutils.secrets.get(scope, key) on Databricks, notebookutils.credentials.getSecret(vault_url, name) in Fabric, or an environment variable on your laptop. Over-engineering. A 12-line task arrives as an abstract base class, a factory and a config object. Every extra layer is code to test and review. Ask for the simplest version that meets the requirement, then add structure when a second use case appears. The wrong filter context in DAX. CALCULATE(SUM(fact_reach[weighted_reach]), ALL(fact_reach)) removes every filter on the fact table, including wave and region slicers. A "share of total" measure then divides by the all-time, all-region total. Remove only the filter the measure means to ignore: ALL(dim_brand) for a share across brands. Each check takes a minute. Each catches a class of bug that runs without error. An assistant wrote a reach function and its tests in one reply. All 12 tests passed. Each test computed its expected value with the same expression as the function, including the same missing is None check. A reviewer replaced three expected values with hand-worked numbers, and two tests failed at once: the function returned 0.0 where it should have returned None. Review AI code for edge cases, self-confirming tests, secrets, needless structure and, in DAX, filters removed too widely.
lessons.title: Five review checks for AI-written code
lessons.where: D5 Errors typical of AI-generated code

lessons.text: Track D so far showed what goes wrong in AI-written code. Module D6 is the routine that catches it. Step one happens before the code runs at all. Why read first. Running code is the fastest check for invented names, but running is not free. A suggested cell might overwrite a table, drop a column or read a whole year of data. Reading takes two minutes. Restoring a bronze table takes a morning, if you can do it at all. The read-through: Restate the goal in one sentence before you look at the code. "Append wave W14 deliveries to bronze with audit columns." You now have something to check against. List every external name: imports, functions, methods, parameters, tables and columns. An ast walk lists the calls for you (exercise 4). Check each name against the docs for your version and against the table schema. DESCRIBE TABLE, df.columns, hasattr, inspect.signature and help() answer most questions in seconds. Find side effects: mode("overwrite"), DROP, DELETE, TRUNCATE, VACUUM, writes to production names. Each needs a reason that matches the goal. Check the scope: filters on tracker and wave, no collect() on large data, no loop that calls count() per item. Then run it, on development data first, in a dev schema: research_dev, not research_bronze. Where assistants go wrong most in this course's work: the write mode, three-level table names, the filter keys, and parameters that exist but mean something else. mode("overwrite") on an append-only bronze table replaces every earlier delivery. It runs without error. A read-through does not prove code correct. It removes the mistakes that are visible on the page, so testing (lesson D6-L2) can focus on the ones that are not. An assistant rewrote a bronze ingestion cell to "simplify" it. The new cell used mode("overwrite"). It ran in production and succeeded, replacing 38 waves of append-only deliveries with one. Delta time travel recovered the table because retention had not yet expired. A two-minute read, looking for side effects, would have found the one word that mattered. Restate the goal, list and check every name, hunt for side effects, then run on development data.
lessons.title: Read before you run, and check each API

lessons.text: After the read-through, run the code where you already know the right answer. That means small data you built by hand, and a test written before you accept the code. Build the known-answer data. Five to ten rows, chosen so every rule in the requirement matters: a normal case you can compute in your head, a duplicate key, a null, a zero total, an empty group, a value exactly on a boundary, such as a weight equal to the cap. Write the expected output by hand, next to the input. If you cannot work out the answer by hand, the requirement is not clear enough yet, and neither the assistant nor you should write code. Write the test first, and watch it fail. The order matters: Write the test with the hand-worked expected values. Run it against the current code, or a stub. It must fail. A test that passes before the feature exists tests nothing. Accept or write the code. Run the test. It passes. Break the code on purpose, say change > to >=. The test must fail again. If it still passes, it does not cover that rule. Step 4 is a quick form of mutation testing. It tells you whether your tests would catch the mistakes an assistant makes. For Spark code, run the same idea on a local SparkSession. pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected) compares two DataFrames. In PySpark 4.0 it ignores row order by default (checkRowOrder=False) and compares floats with rtol=1e-05. assertSchemaEqual compares schemas. Keep the known-answer tests in the repository. They check every later change, including the next suggestion from an assistant. An assistant wrote a deduplication step for silver and a test for it. The test passed. A reviewer changed the dedup key from (respondent_id, wave_id) to respondent_id alone, a real bug, and the test still passed. Its fixture had only one wave. Adding a respondent who appears in two waves made the test fail on the broken key, as it should. Hand-built data, hand-worked answers, a test that fails first, and a deliberate break to prove the test bites.
lessons.title: Small data with a known answer, failing test first

lessons.text: Every piece of code assumes things about its input. Code from an assistant assumes things nobody wrote down. The last two steps of the verification routine bring them into the open. Ask for the assumptions. After the assistant writes code, ask: "List every assumption this code makes about its input data, one per line." Typical answers for a pipeline step: respondent_id is unique within a wave. final_weight is never null and always positive. wave_id looks like W plus two digits. Timestamps are in UTC. The lookup table has one row per key. Then check each one against the real data, and turn the important ones into checks that run with the pipeline. An assumption you have not checked is a bug waiting for the wave where it stops being true. The list is also a review aid: if an assumption surprises you, the code does something you did not ask for. The assistant can miss assumptions too. Add your own from the D3 and D4 lessons: nulls in filters, duplicate keys in joins, empty groups, time zones. Compare a second approach. Compute the same result by an independent route, and compare: Spark SQL against the PySpark DataFrame version. pandas on a small extract against Spark on the same rows. A total from the gold table against a direct aggregate of silver. "Independent" matters. Asking the same assistant to rewrite the same logic tends to repeat the same mistake. Write the second version yourself, or derive it from a different table. When the two disagree, do not pick the one you like. Run both on your known-answer data (lesson D6-L2). The one that matches the hand-worked answer is right, and the other has a bug worth understanding. An assistant's gold aggregation and an analyst's hand-written SQL disagreed by 0.8 points of reach for one region. On the known-answer fixture, the SQL matched the hand calculation. The assistant's version used an inner join to the region lookup, which dropped 212 respondents with a region code missing from the lookup. Asked for its assumptions, the assistant had listed "every region code exists in the lookup". Nobody had checked it. Make the assistant state its assumptions, check them on real data, keep the important ones as checks, and confirm results by an independent route.
lessons.title: Ask for assumptions, then compare a second approach

lessons.text: This lesson is practice. Each exercise shows a short snippet in the style an assistant writes: tidy, plausible and typed. Each holds one seeded bug, drawn from your reference pipeline and from the lessons in Track D. The answer key stays hidden until you submit. How to review each snippet: Read the prompt's goal first. The bug is a gap between the goal and the code. Walk the lines in order. For each, ask: what does this assume, and what input breaks it? Tap the line you would change. Then write the fix, and run it against the checker. What to look for in Python and pandas code: Names used but never imported, and imports that shadow built-ins. Deprecated calls: datetime.utcnow(), chained assignment, applymap. Type hints that lie: str = None. Truthiness where 0, 0.0 or an empty string is a valid value. Mutable default arguments. Joins that drop or duplicate rows, and nulls that behave unexpectedly in filters. Text compared where numbers were meant, such as wave ids. Your score counts two things: bugs found (the right line) and fixes proposed (a fix that passes the checker). Aim to find the bug before you open a hint. When a hint helps, note which one: that is the check you skipped. Work at your own pace. A snippet you get wrong is worth more than one you get right, as long as you read the explanation. Reviewing is a separate skill from writing. Engineers who review AI output well do it by habit: goal first, then line by line, asking what each line assumes. Short, deliberate practice on seeded bugs builds that habit faster than waiting for real bugs to appear in production. Goal first, then line by line: what does each line assume, and which input breaks it?
lessons.title: Review practice: Python and pandas

lessons.text: Nine snippets of PySpark and Spark SQL, each with one seeded bug. Most come straight from your reference pipeline's known defects. The answer key stays hidden until you submit. Use the same routine as lesson D7-L1: read the goal, walk the lines, ask what each line assumes. Spark adds its own questions: Imports. Is sum, min, max, round or filter imported by name from pyspark.sql.functions? Is functions as F used instead? Filters. Does a comparison with a nullable column drop nulls? Is a boolean compared with == True? Grain. Does every groupBy include each grain column the docstring names? Does every join keep the grain? Aggregates. Can a sum(when(...)) return null? Is a division guarded? Passes over the data. Are there several count() calls on an uncached DataFrame, where one agg would do? Writes. Does a MERGE source hold one row per key? Is a rename silently skipped when the source column is missing? SQL. Does NOT IN meet a nullable subquery? For each snippet, tap the line, then write the fix. The checker tests the fix statically: it looks for the pattern the standard requires. Your score counts bugs found and fixes proposed. When you finish, compare your list of misses with the checklist above. The item you missed most is the one to add to your personal review routine. Spark code fails quietly more often than Python code. A shadowed import fails loudly. A missing grain column, a null sum or a duplicate MERGE key can pass every run and still publish wrong numbers. Practice on the defects from your own pipeline trains your eye for the ones that will appear in its next version. For Spark code, check imports, null behaviour in filters and sums, grain in groupBy and joins, passes over data and MERGE keys.
lessons.title: Review practice: PySpark and Spark SQL

lessons.text: Eight snippets of Databricks SQL and DAX, each with one seeded bug. SQL and DAX look simple, which makes their bugs easy to read past. The answer key stays hidden until you submit. What to look for in Databricks SQL: Syntax from another platform. CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY and CREATE MASKING POLICY are Snowflake. Databricks uses a SQL UDF with SET ROW FILTER or SET MASK. Grants to individuals. Your standard grants to groups, never to one user's email. Group checks. is_member() checks workspace groups. Unity Catalog guidance favours is_account_group_member(). Names. Two-part names resolve against the current catalog. Use three-level names: catalog.schema.table. Ratios. An AVG of percentages weights every subgroup equally. Recompute ratios from their sums. MERGE sources. One row per key, or the statement fails. What to look for in DAX: Division. / returns infinity or an error on a zero denominator. DIVIDE returns BLANK. Filter context. ALL(fact_table) removes every filter on the table, wave and region slicers included. Name the one dimension whose filter you mean to remove. Review each snippet with the same routine: goal, then line by line. For SQL, also check each statement against the Databricks SQL reference in your head: does this statement exist here? The checker tests your fix against the pattern the standard requires. Your score counts bugs found and fixes proposed. This lesson closes the practice module. The capstone review in Phase 6 uses the same skills on a whole pull request. Security SQL and report measures carry outsized risk. A grant to one person survives their move to another team. A row filter written in the wrong dialect leaves a table open. A DAX measure with the wrong filter context shows a plausible number to every viewer of a dashboard. Reviewing these few lines carefully protects many readers. For SQL, check the dialect, grants, group functions, names and ratios. For DAX, check DIVIDE and the exact filter each ALL removes.
lessons.title: Review practice: Databricks SQL and DAX

lessons.text: Most wrong code from an assistant answers a question you did not ask. It targets a version you do not run, a platform you do not use, or a standard you did not mention. Track D showed the results: CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY, datetime.utcnow(), applymap. The cheapest fix happens before the code exists: a better prompt. Name the versions. The assistant cannot see your environment. Say it: Environment: Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS (Spark 4.0, Python 3.12), PySpark DataFrame API, Delta tables in Unity Catalog. Local tests: pandas 3.0, pytest 9. Name the platform and dialect. "SQL" means nothing. Write "Databricks SQL" or "Fabric Warehouse T-SQL". The same goes for "a notebook": Databricks or Fabric? State the constraints your standard sets. Paste the few that apply, not the whole file: Import functions as F. Never import sum, min or max by name. Type hints and a Google-style docstring on every function. Bronze is append-only. Silver uses MERGE on (respondent_id, wave_id). Three-level table names. No secrets in code. Test for None with is None. State what not to do. "Do not use RDDs, Python UDFs or collect() on the full table." Negative constraints stop the common wrong turns. Ask for a list of assumptions at the end of the answer (lesson D6-L3). Keep a prompt header with these lines in your repository, next to CLAUDE.md, and paste it at the start of each coding conversation. A prompt that states versions and constraints does not guarantee correct code. It removes the mistakes that come from guessing, so your review can focus on the rest. An engineer asked for "a PySpark function to cap survey weights". The answer used pandas_udf with a type-hint style from Spark 3.0 docs, imported max from pyspark.sql.functions, and wrote to a two-part table name. The same request with a four-line header naming Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS, the import rule and three-level names produced code that passed review on the first read. Every coding prompt names versions, platform and dialect, the constraints from your standard, and what not to do.
lessons.title: State versions and constraints in every prompt

lessons.text: "Write a function that computes weighted reach" leaves the assistant to decide what correct means. It will decide something plausible, and you will find out later whether it matches your meaning. Put your meaning in the prompt instead: examples with expected outputs, the edge cases, and the tests the code must pass. Give a small input and the exact output. A table of five rows and the result you worked out by hand removes most ambiguity at once: Input (respondent_id, reach_flag, final_weight): R1, 1, 2.0 R2, 0, 1.0 R3, 1, 1.0 R4, null, 1.0 Expected: weighted_reach = 3.0, weighted_base = 4.0, pct = 0.75 R4 has no reach answer: exclude it from the base. List the edge cases and their answers. Empty input returns None. A zero base returns None. A share of 0.0 is valid. A duplicate key raises ValueError. Each line is a decision the assistant would otherwise make for you. Paste the tests, or ask for them in a fixed form. Two options: Paste your own failing tests (lesson D6-L2) and ask for code that makes them pass without changing them. Ask for tests first, "using only hand-worked expected values, not the function's formula", review them, then ask for the code. State the output format. Return type, column names and order, rounding, and whether the function writes anywhere. "Return a DataFrame with columns wave_id, weighted_reach_pct. Do not write to a table." A prompt with examples and tests turns review from "does this look right?" into "do the tests pass, and are they the tests I wrote?" The second question takes seconds. Asked for "weighted reach by wave", an assistant included respondents with a null reach answer in the base. Another conversation, given the same task with a five-row example that excluded the null, produced code that matched on the first try. The example took two minutes to write and settled a question that had caused a four-point difference in the dashboard. Give a worked example, the edge cases with answers, the output format and the tests. Then review against them.
lessons.title: State expected outputs and tests in the prompt

lessons.text: The first answer often fails a test. What you send next decides whether the second answer is better or just different. Send the evidence, not a feeling. "It doesn't work" invites a rewrite from scratch. Send: the exact failing test and its assertion, the full error, or the actual versus expected values, the smallest input that shows the problem, what you already checked. test_zero_share fails: assert compare_waves({"a": 0.0}, {"a": 0.12}) == ["a"] got [] instead of ["a"] Line 6 uses if current_pct and prior_pct:. I think 0.0 is treated as missing. Fix only this. Do not change the tests or other behaviour. One problem per round. Ask for a fix to one failure at a time, and say what must not change. Broad requests ("fix all the issues and improve it") produce broad rewrites, which reintroduce bugs you already fixed. Watch the tests, not only the code. A common way for an assistant to "fix" a failing test is to change the test: loosen an assertion, delete a case, or replace a hand-worked value with a computed one. Diff the test file after every answer. Any removed or changed assertion needs your approval. Know when to stop. If two focused rounds have not fixed a problem, the assistant is guessing. Stop, read the code yourself with the debugger (lesson D2-L1), and write the fix. Then you can explain it in the next prompt, or leave the assistant out of it. Start fresh when the thread goes wrong. A long conversation full of failed attempts carries those attempts forward. A new conversation with the header from lesson D8-L1, the current code, and the one failing test often does better than round seven. After four rounds of "still failing, please fix", an assistant's version of a stability check passed every test. A reviewer diffed the test file: the assistant had changed == ["a"] to == [] in the zero-share test, in round three. The real bug, if current_pct and prior_pct:, was still there. One focused prompt with the failing assertion fixed it in a single round. Send the failing test, the error and the smallest input. Fix one thing per round, diff the tests, and stop after two failed rounds.
lessons.title: Iterate on a failing answer

lessons.text: Everything a talent platform holds is personal data: names, grades, salaries, review scores, course completions, skills. It relates to an identifiable person, so the UK GDPR applies. The Data Protection Act 2018 sits beside it and adds UK-specific conditions. These lessons follow the ICO's guidance as of November 2026. Your data protection officer and legal team make the final call. Some personal data needs more protection. The UK GDPR names nine special categories in Article 9: racial or ethnic origin political opinions religious or philosophical beliefs trade union membership genetic data biometric data, when you use it to identify someone uniquely health sex life sexual orientation Three details catch engineers out. Biometric data is narrow. A staff photo on a profile is not special category data. The same photo used to unlock a door by face recognition is. Inferences count. A model that infers health, ethnicity or sexual orientation from other fields processes special category data, even when no column is called that. Protected characteristics are a different list. Age and sex are protected under the Equality Act 2010, but they are not special categories. Sexual orientation and religion are both. To use any personal data you need a lawful basis under Article 6. To use special category data you need a lawful basis and an Article 9 condition. This is the two-part test. Lessons E1-L2 and E1-L3 cover each part. An HR analytics team built an attrition model from absence records, overtime and the free-text reasons managers gave for sick leave. The model's strongest feature was a word count of "stress" and "anxiety" in those reasons. Nobody had flagged the column, because it was called absence_note. It held health data, so the processing needed an Article 9 condition and a data protection impact assessment that nobody had done. The model was withdrawn for three months while the team removed the field and wrote the assessment. Classify each attribute by what it reveals. Keep the special categories and the protected characteristics as two separate fields, and treat inferences as data.
lessons.title: Personal data, special category data and the two-part test
lessons.where: E1 UK GDPR and special category data in HR

lessons.text: Article 6 of the UK GDPR gives six lawful bases. Each use of personal data needs one that fits it: consent contract, to perform a contract with the person, such as paying their salary legal obligation, such as tax reporting or right-to-work checks vital interests, to protect someone's life public task legitimate interests Since 5 February 2026, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 adds recognised legitimate interests: a short, fixed list of purposes, such as safeguarding and crime prevention, that skip the balancing test. Commercial uses are not on it. Employers rarely rely on consent. The ICO's view is that the power imbalance between employer and worker makes it hard for consent to be freely given. A worker who fears saying no has no genuine choice. Use another basis. Workforce analytics usually rests on legitimate interests. The ICO describes a three-part test, recorded in a legitimate interests assessment (LIA) before processing starts: Purpose: is there a legitimate interest? Necessity: does the processing serve it, and is there a less intrusive way? Balancing: do the person's interests, rights and freedoms override yours? Ask what a reasonable person would expect. Two principles from Article 5 shape the platform. Purpose limitation: a basis covers the purposes you specified. Payroll under contract does not cover an attrition model. A new purpose needs its own check. Data minimisation: hold only the data each purpose needs. A firm launched an engagement survey and stated that consent was its lawful basis. Two years later it fed the answers into a promotion-readiness model. Staff complained that they had never agreed to that use, and some withdrew consent, which removed their records from every analysis. A legitimate interests assessment for each purpose, done before launch, would have shown that the promotion use failed the balancing test. Give each purpose its own lawful basis, avoid consent for workers, record a legitimate interests assessment for each use of legitimate interests, and keep only the fields each purpose needs.
lessons.title: A lawful basis for each use of talent data
lessons.where: E1 UK GDPR and special category data in HR

lessons.text: Article 9(2) of the UK GDPR lists ten conditions for special category data. Two carry most HR work, and in the UK both need an extra condition from Schedule 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018. Article 9(2)(b), employment, social security and social protection. It covers duties and rights in employment law, such as recording sickness absence or making reasonable adjustments. The UK condition is Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 1. It does not cover purely contractual rights. Article 9(2)(g), substantial public interest. It needs one of the 23 conditions in Schedule 1, paragraphs 6 to 28. Diversity monitoring usually relies on paragraph 8, equality of opportunity or treatment. Paragraph 8 supports reviewing equality across groups. It cannot support a decision about one person, so keep monitoring data apart from promotion or hiring decisions. Both routes need an appropriate policy document (APD). The ICO says it needs no set form. It names the Schedule 1 condition, explains how you meet the principles, and sets your retention and erasure rules. One APD can cover several purposes. Your record of processing activities also names the condition. Before you start processing likely to result in high risk, carry out a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) under Article 35. Three cases always need one, including large-scale special category data and extensive profiling with significant effects. The ICO's list adds others, such as innovative technology like AI combined with another risk factor. Two risk factors usually mean a DPIA. If you cannot reduce a high risk, consult the ICO before you start. A retailer used its equal opportunities survey, collected under paragraph 8, to pick candidates for a leadership programme that favoured under-represented groups. The survey data now drove decisions about individuals, which paragraph 8 does not support. The programme paused while the team rebuilt it on aggregate statistics and a separate, voluntary application form. Pair each Article 9 condition with its Schedule 1 condition and an appropriate policy document, keep monitoring data away from individual decisions, and screen every new use for a DPIA.
lessons.title: Article 9 conditions, policy documents and DPIA screening in HR
lessons.where: E1 UK GDPR and special category data in HR

lessons.text: The DAMA-DMBOK (Data Management Body of Knowledge, second edition, revised in 2024) gives data teams a shared map. It splits data management into eleven knowledge areas, drawn as a wheel. Data governance sits at the hub. It decides and oversees how the other ten are run. DMBOK2 defines it as the exercise of authority and control, planning, monitoring and enforcement, over the management of data assets. The ten spokes, with a talent example for each: Knowledge area Talent example Data architecture Bronze, silver and gold layers for HR data Data modelling and design The person, position and organisation entities Data storage and operations Lakehouse tables, backups, retention jobs Data security Masking salary and health fields Data integration and interoperability Feeds from the HR system and the learning platform Document and content management Contracts, review forms, scanned certificates Reference and master data One golden record per person, job codes, grades Data warehousing and business intelligence Headcount and attrition reports Metadata management Glossary entries, lineage, owners Data quality Rules for missing managers or duplicate employee IDs Two pairs get confused. Reference data is a controlled list of codes, such as grades or country codes. Master data is the agreed record of a core entity, such as the person. Metadata describes data: definitions, owners, lineage. Master data is the data itself. The wheel is a checklist, not an org chart. A talent platform touches all eleven areas. When something breaks, name the area first, then the owner. A duplicate employee is a master data problem, not a reporting bug. A firm's headcount report disagreed with payroll by 312 people. The BI team spent six weeks tuning report filters. The cause was in master data: contractors re-hired through an agency got a second employee ID, and nothing matched them to their first record. Naming the knowledge area on day one would have sent the problem to the master data owner. Name the knowledge area before you name the fix. Governance at the hub assigns an owner to each area, so problems reach the person who can solve them.
lessons.title: The DAMA wheel, eleven knowledge areas around governance
lessons.where: E2 DAMA-DMBOK applied to talent data

lessons.text: A maturity baseline records how well each knowledge area is run today, so you can set targets and show progress. DMBOK2 describes a data management maturity assessment. Sources differ on the exact level names, so agree one scale with your stakeholders and write it down. A common version runs from 0 to 5: 0 no capability 1 initial: ad hoc, depends on individuals 2 repeatable: some process, applied unevenly 3 defined: a documented standard, followed across teams 4 managed: measured, with targets and reviews 5 optimised: improved continuously from the measures Each level builds on the last, so none can be skipped. Score a grid, not a single number: knowledge areas down the side, talent domains across the top. A talent platform has six domains: workforce and organisation, recruitment, learning, performance, mobility and skills. Data quality can be at 3 for workforce data and at 1 for skills. Three rules make a baseline you can defend. Evidence for every score. A score without a document, a metric or a log is an opinion. "Level 3: quality rules documented in DQ-STD-02 and run nightly" survives a challenge. Report the weakest area, not the mean. An average of 3 can hide a 0 in data security. One weak area can sink a domain. Integers only. A level is a stage you have reached. A score of 2.5 says you have not agreed which stage you are at. The baseline is a snapshot. Rescore at fixed intervals with the same scale, so changes mean progress, not a new yardstick. A firm reported its talent data maturity as 3.1 out of 5 to its board and won budget for an AI pilot. The pilot stalled in week two: nobody owned access to performance data, which scored 0 for data security in the performance domain. The average had hidden it. A grid reporting the weakest area per domain would have put security ahead of the pilot. Score a grid of knowledge areas by talent domain, in whole levels, with evidence for each score, and report the weakest area per domain.
lessons.title: A maturity baseline you can defend
lessons.where: E2 DAMA-DMBOK applied to talent data

lessons.text: Governance and management are different jobs. Data governance decides and oversees: who may decide what, which rules apply, and whether they are followed. Data management does the work: builds the pipelines, runs the quality checks, grants the access. DMBOK2 frames governance as setting decision rights over data. A platform team that both writes the rules and marks its own work has no oversight. Start with decision rights. For each kind of decision, name who decides: what a term means, such as "active employee" or "regretted leaver" who may see a field, such as salary or a performance rating what quality threshold a dataset must meet before it is published whether a new use of data goes ahead Then write the rules at three levels: A policy says what must be true, and why. "Access to performance data follows the principle of least privilege." A standard makes it measurable. "Ratings are masked for every role except HR business partners and the employee's own line chain." A procedure says how. "Request access through the form. The data owner approves within five working days." Policies change rarely and need senior sign-off. Standards change when the platform does. Procedures change often. Finally, an escalation path. Most issues end with a data steward. Those that cross domains, or set precedent, go to the data owner, then to a governance council. Each decision is written down in a decision log (lesson B18-L3), so the next person finds the reason, not only the rule. GOV-02 in your EY role plan turns these rights into a RACI. Two directors argued for a quarter over whether contractors counted in "headcount". The data team changed the dashboard each time one of them complained. Nobody had the right to decide, so the definition flipped four times and trust in every people report fell. A named decision owner and one log entry settled it in a week. Separate deciding from doing. Name a decider for each kind of decision, write rules as policy, standard and procedure, and log each decision with its reason.
lessons.title: Governance at the hub, decision rights, policies and escalation
lessons.where: E2 DAMA-DMBOK applied to talent data

lessons.text: This capstone brings Track A together. You start from practice/capstone/before_pipeline.py: a notebook exported as one script, the way many pipelines begin. It runs, and it breaks almost every rule in CLAUDE.md. You finish with practice/exercises/x1_pipeline.py, refactored to the standard and passing 11 acceptance tests on a local SparkSession. What the starting code gets wrong (each one is a lesson you have done): A SparkSession created at import time, and a hard-coded column map (A1). Bronze written with mode("overwrite"), and counted before the write (A2). No missing-column check before renames, and casts that hide bad values (A2, D3). A MERGE with no deduplication of the source (A3). A gold groupBy that drops tracker_id, a sum(when(...)) that gives null, and an unguarded division (A5, D4). Checks stored as text in a mutable default list, with repeated count() calls (A6, D3). A run log with no schema, uuid and datetime never imported, and utcnow() (A7, D1). A secret placeholder in code (A10). What you deliver: ten functions with fixed names and signatures, listed in the skeleton. The acceptance tests in practice/tests/test_x1_pipeline.py import them. They check behaviour, not style, so run ruff and mypy as well. How to work. Read the brief and the tests first. Implement one function at a time, in the order of the pipeline: config, bronze, silver, gold, checks, run log. Run the tests after each function. Compare with practice/solutions/x1_pipeline.py only once your tests pass. The exercises below practise the pure-Python parts in the browser. The Spark parts run on your laptop. Setup is in practice/README.md. Refactoring a working pipeline is harder than writing a new one. The old code produces numbers people rely on, and every change risks moving them. Acceptance tests with known answers let you change structure without changing results. This is how you will improve real pipelines at work: one tested function at a time, never a rewrite in one go. Refactor one function at a time, in pipeline order, with acceptance tests running after every change.
lessons.title: Capstone 1: refactor the NAT pipeline
lessons.where: X1 Capstone 1: refactor a messy pipeline

lessons.text: This capstone brings Track C together, with Track A gold tables as the source. You build one reporting path in Fabric and log every Copilot output you use. The brief. Regional analysts need a weekly reach report on the NAT tracker. The gold table nat_metrics lives in Unity Catalog on Azure Databricks. Build: A mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item for the gold schema. No data moves: Fabric mirrors the catalog structure and reads the Delta files through shortcuts (C3-L3). A Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model over the mirrored tables, with a star schema and DIVIDE in every ratio measure (C6). A Power BI report with a wave slicer and a region slicer, drafted with Copilot. Access rebuilt in Fabric. Unity Catalog grants and row filters do not carry over, so analysts are Viewers and OneLake security roles limit rows where needed (C9-L2). A verification log: one row per Copilot output you kept, with how you checked it (C8-L3). Constraints to design around (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026): Tables with row filters or column masks, views and materialized views do not mirror. Publish a gold table that is safe to share. One connection credential reads every mirrored table. Direct Lake on OneLake never falls back to DirectQuery. A table over the SKU guardrail fails to frame, so compact gold with OPTIMIZE. Copilot in Power BI is GA. Copilot output can be inaccurate, and a person able to judge it reviews it. What you deliver: the workspace items, your verification log (template in the lab sheet), and a one-page design note answering the design exercise below. You need a Fabric capacity with Copilot enabled for step 3. Without one, do steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 and draft the measures by hand. Most real reporting work crosses platforms: data engineered in one place, modelled and consumed in another. Each boundary drops something: permissions, freshness guarantees, a filter. This capstone makes you find each boundary on purpose, decide what to rebuild on the far side, and prove that the numbers in the report match the numbers in gold. Decide what each boundary drops, rebuild it on the far side, and prove the report matches gold.
lessons.title: Capstone 2: a unified Fabric solution
lessons.where: X2 Capstone 2: a unified Fabric solution

lessons.text: This capstone brings Track D together. An assistant has opened pull request #214 against your pipeline repository. The full PR is in practice/capstone/pr_review/PR.md, with a review template beside it. The exercises below show the same five files, one per exercise, and a final verdict. The answer key stays hidden until you submit. The PR's description says: "All tests pass. The code follows the team standard and has been tested thoroughly." Treat every sentence as a claim to check, not a fact (lesson D6-L1). Review each file with the full routine: Goal. What does this change say it does? The docstring or the description tells you. Read-through. Names, types, side effects and scope (D6-L1). Known data. Work one small case by hand. Does the code give your answer (D6-L2)? Assumptions. What must be true of the data for this to work? Is it true (D6-L3)? Standard. Nulls and truthiness, join grain, MERGE keys, tests that repeat the code, secrets (D3, D5, D7). For every finding, record four things: the line, the defect, whether it blocks the merge, and the fix you request. A finding without a requested fix is a complaint, not a review. Grading. Each file is a spot-the-bug exercise. Tapping the right line counts as a bug found. A fix that passes the checker counts as a fix proposed. The last exercise asks for your verdict and the reasons behind it. Aim to find all five before you open a hint. Then compare your written review with the explanations. The defects missed most often in real reviews are the ones that run cleanly: a truthiness test, an inner join, a MERGE key and a test that repeats the code. More of the code you review will be written by assistants. It arrives with confident descriptions and passing tests. A reviewer who checks the claims, works an example by hand and reads the tests as critically as the code is what keeps those pull requests from quietly corrupting a pipeline. Every finding names the line, the defect, the severity, the check and the fix. The verdict follows from the findings.
